lead: The Church opens the civil year with a name. On the eighth day after his birth the Child is circumcised and named, and today’s readings ask what a name means before God. In Genesis, God gives Abram a new name and a sign in the flesh. In Isaiah, he tells a people in exile that he has called them by name. In Philippians, the one who emptied himself receives “the name that is above every name”. In Matthew and Luke, the angel’s word to Joseph and the rite of the eighth day come together: he is called Jesus, because he saves.
The line runs from a name given to one man to a name before which every knee bends. The key words are covenant, called by name, emptied and Jesus.

r.h: A new name and a sign in the flesh
set: Abram has already heard God’s promises (Genesis 12; 15), and he has already tried to secure them his own way through Hagar (Genesis 16). Now he is ninety-nine and still has no son by Sarai. Into that dead end God speaks again. Many scholars think this chapter received its final form in priestly circles around the time of the exile, when a people without land or Temple held on to circumcision and the sabbath as signs of who they were.
str: vv. 1–2: God appears and calls Abram to walk before him.
vv. 3–8: God’s side of the covenant: many nations, a new name, kings, the land, and “I will be their God”.
vv. 9–14: Abraham’s side of the covenant: the sign of circumcision on the eighth day, for every male of the household.
¶ The word “covenant” comes ten times in these fourteen verses. It is the thread of the whole passage.
kw: A solemn bond with promises and duties. Here God is the one who sets it up: “I will establish my covenant”. Israel does not earn it; Israel keeps it.
An ancient name of God. The exact meaning of šadday is uncertain. “Almighty” is the traditional rendering, and it suits the moment: God promises what an old man and an old woman cannot bring about.

Abram can be understood as “exalted father”. The new name is explained by its sound, ’ab hămôn, “father of a multitude”. This is a play on sound rather than a strict derivation. Abraham carries his mission in his name before he has the child who will begin it.
The same word is used for the rainbow (Genesis 9:13) and the sabbath (Exodus 31:13). A sign is a visible thing that points to a bond with God.
vv: I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless.
The word for “blameless”, tāmîm, means whole, undivided. God does not ask Abraham for a spotless record but for a whole heart.
No longer shall your name be Abram, but your name shall be Abraham; for I have made you the ancestor of a multitude of nations.
God speaks in the past tense, “I have made you”, of something that has not yet happened. His promise is as good as done.
to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
This is the centre of the covenant. Land and descendants are gifts, but the greatest gift is God himself.
You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.
The sign reaches into the household: the child eight days old, who can decide nothing, and the slave bought from a foreigner (17:12). Belonging begins with God’s gift, and it is wider than blood.
ch: The Catechism sees in the call of Abraham God’s plan to gather scattered humanity (CCC 59). St Paul says that Abraham “received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11). When the Son of God is circumcised, “the sign of his incorporation into Abraham’s descendants”, says the Catechism, he enters the people of the covenant and submits to the Law; and the same sign prefigures Baptism, “the circumcision of Christ” (CCC 527; Colossians 2:11–12). The Church honours the Jewish people, for whom this sign remains holy to this day, because “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).

r.h: I have called you by name, you are mine
set: Isaiah 40–55 speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon. They have lost land, king and Temple, and they think that God has finished with them. The chapter just before ends with Israel’s blindness and the fire of punishment (42:24–25). Then comes “But now”. The words that follow are among the tenderest in the Old Testament.
str: v. 1: God who created and formed Israel says “Do not fear”.
vv. 2–3a: through waters and fire, “I will be with you”.
vv. 3b–4: how precious Israel is to him.
vv. 5–7: a second “Do not fear”: the scattered children are gathered from every direction.
kw: The gō’ēl was the near relative who bought back a family member sold into slavery, or family land that had been lost (Leviticus 25). God speaks as Israel’s next of kin.
I have called you by name
To name someone is to know and claim that person. Similar words are spoken to Cyrus in 45:3–4, and of the stars in 40:26. God knows what he has made, one by one.
The word is used of costly things. “You are precious in my sight” is the reason given for everything God does. It is not a reward for faithfulness, since Israel has just been called blind.
vv: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.
The last three words are the heart of the passage. The exile has not cancelled them.
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you
Waters recall the sea of the Exodus and the Jordan. God does not promise that there will be no waters and no fire. He promises to be there.
everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory
The promise ends with a people who carry God’s name. Today’s feast shows how far that will go: the Name will be carried in human flesh.
ch: The Catechism applies these words to each believer: “God calls each one by name” (CCC 2158). Everyone’s name is sacred, and in Baptism the Christian receives a name in the Church (CCC 2156, 2158). The passage through water and fire is easily heard by Christians as a word about Baptism and about trial, where the Lord does not spare us the river but goes through it with us.

r.h: The name that is above every name
set: Paul writes from prison (1:13) to the Christians of Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia (Acts 16:12), a community he loves. They have disputes and rivalries (2:3; 4:2). To heal them he does not give a rule but points to Christ. Many scholars think that vv. 6–11 are an early Christian hymn which Paul quotes; others think he wrote them himself. Either way, this is among the oldest statements we have of faith in Christ’s divinity.
str: v. 5: the call: have this same mind.
vv. 6–8: the way down: form of God, emptying, form of a slave, human likeness, obedience, death, the cross.
vv. 9–11: the way up: God exalts him and gives him the Name, and all creation confesses him.
¶ In the first half Christ is the one who acts. In the second half God the Father acts. The turning point is the word “Therefore”.
kw: Not an outward appearance only. “Form” here points to what he truly is. The same word stands in the contrast “form of a slave”, which is what he truly became.

A rare word, found only here in the New Testament, and its exact sense is debated. It points to something to be seized or held on to for one’s own advantage. The Son did not use his equality with God for himself.
From this verb comes the word kenosis. He did not stop being God. He “emptied” himself by taking on what he was not: our nature, in its lowly condition.
The word by which the Greek Old Testament regularly renders the divine name. To say “Jesus Christ is Lord” in this setting is to give him the name of God.
vv: who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness.
In the Roman world a slave had no rights over his own life. Roman emperors accepted divine honours; this one, who was truly equal with God, goes the other way.
he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death
The verse goes on to add “even death on a cross”. In Philippi, a Roman colony, everyone knew that this was the death for slaves and rebels. It is the lowest point of the descent.
so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth,

These words echo Isaiah 45:23, “To me every knee shall bow”, spoken there by the Lord God himself. Paul applies them to Jesus. What was said of God alone is now said of the crucified one, “to the glory of God the Father” (2:11).
ch: The Catechism quotes this hymn as the Church’s song of the Incarnation (CCC 461), and teaches that the Son became truly man without ceasing to be truly God (CCC 464, 469). It reads the Name as revealed in the Resurrection (CCC 434), and it says that the name of Jesus is at the heart of Christian prayer (CCC 435). St Leo the Great, in his letter to Flavian, says that this emptying was a bending down in compassion, not a failure of power (in substance). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Philippians, argues that the Son could lay aside his glory because it was his by nature and not something seized (in substance).

r.h: He named him Jesus
set: Matthew has just given the genealogy, which ends with “Joseph the husband of Mary” (1:16). The problem is plain: the line runs through Joseph, and yet the child is not Joseph’s. Vv. 18–25 explain how Jesus is both conceived by the Holy Spirit as Son of God and son of David through Joseph, who names him and so receives him as his own.

Betrothal in that world was a binding bond, commonly lasting some months before the couple lived together. A betrothed man was already called husband, and the bond could be ended only by divorce. That is why Joseph plans to “dismiss her quietly”.

Luke’s single verse (2:21) adds the rite. As with John the Baptist (Luke 1:59), the child is circumcised and named on the eighth day, as the Law says (Leviticus 12:3). Matthew tells of the naming and Luke tells of the day; the feast joins them.
str: vv. 18–19: Mary is found with child; Joseph, a righteous man, decides.
vv. 20–21: the angel in the dream: take her, and give the name.
vv. 22–23: the prophet’s word (Isaiah 7:14).
vv. 24–25: Joseph obeys, without saying a word.
Luke 2:21: the eighth day.
kw: Yeshua is a short form of Yehoshua, “the Lord saves”. It was a common name. Only in this child does it become exactly true: “God saves” in person (CCC 430, 432).
Faithful to God’s Law, and here also merciful. Joseph’s righteousness will not expose Mary to public disgrace.
The Gospel of Matthew opens with this name and closes with the promise, “I am with you always” (28:20). The whole Gospel stands between the two.
vv: She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.

The angel gives Joseph a father’s task, since a father gave the name. By naming the child, Joseph places him in the line of David (CCC 437). The saving announced here is salvation from sins, not first from Rome.
Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son

The Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 has ‘almâ, a young woman; the Greek translation which Matthew quotes has parthenos, a virgin. The Church reads Matthew’s words as he meant them: the Child is conceived by the Holy Spirit, without a human father (CCC 496–497).
When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him
Matthew records no word from Joseph. His answer is his obedience.
and he named him Jesus.
and he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
Luke 2:21
The name came from God before the child came to his mother. It is a gift and a mission from the beginning.
ch: St Bernard of Clairvaux, preaching on the Song of Songs, calls the name of Jesus honey in the mouth, music in the ear, and joy in the heart (in substance). The Catechism says that this one name contains everything, and it speaks of the prayer of the Name handed on in Sinai, Syria and Mount Athos: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners” (CCC 2666–2668). On Mary’s virginity the Church teaches that it was real and perpetual (CCC 499–501).

qa: Why was the Son of God circumcised?

Not because he needed purifying. By this rite he entered his people, Israel, and placed himself under the Law, “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). It is a first sign of his obedience, and it prefigures Baptism (CCC 527).
Why do Christians not circumcise, if Genesis calls it an everlasting covenant?

The first Christians faced this question directly, and the apostles decided in Jerusalem that Gentile believers were not to be bound by it (Acts 15). In Christ the sign of entry is Baptism (Colossians 2:11–12). This is no contempt for the Jewish people’s fidelity: God’s covenant with them has not been revoked (CCC 121, 839).
Does “until she had borne a son” (Matthew 1:25) mean that Mary and Joseph later lived as husband and wife?

No. The Greek “until” says what happened up to a point and says nothing of what came after. Matthew’s concern here is that the child was not Joseph’s. Compare 28:20, “to the end of the age”, which does not mean that the Lord will then leave us. St Jerome argued this against Helvidius, and the Church teaches Mary’s perpetual virginity (CCC 499–501).
rite: The Malayalam ഈശോ comes through the Syriac form of the name, Isho‘. Syriac is a dialect of Aramaic, the family of languages our Lord himself spoke, so a Syro-Malabar Christian who says ഈശോ stands close to the sound his Mother used. In the Holy Qurbana the Lakhumara hymn addresses him by that name: Lord of all, we praise you; Jesus Christ, we glorify you. Today, at the start of a new year, the whole of what we hope for can be gathered in this one Name.
study: God gave Abraham his mission in his name. What did my baptismal name mean to those who gave it, and what could it mean now?
Isaiah 43 promises God’s presence in water and fire, not an escape from them. Where do I need to hear “I will be with you” this year?
Philippians 2 was written to heal quarrels. In which relationship is Christ’s way of not holding on to my own rights asked of me?
How might the Name be said more often in my family this year, in the day’s work and at the end of the day?

lead: Paul says that the things of God can be known only through God’s own Spirit; Jesus tells his disciples to stay awake for a master who will surprise them. Both readings are about being able to recognise the Lord. The Child of Bethlehem was seen by many and recognised by few, and the same is true when he comes again.

r.h: The Spirit that is from God
set: Paul founded the church in Corinth (Acts 18) and writes to it, probably from Ephesus (16:8), about its divisions. Some of the Corinthians prized eloquence and “wisdom”. Paul has answered with the cross. Now he explains how anyone can grasp a wisdom like that: only by the Spirit.
str: v. 11: only a person’s spirit knows that person; only God’s Spirit knows God.
vv. 12–13: we have received that Spirit, and we speak in words he teaches.
vv. 14–15: the unspiritual person and the spiritual person.
kw: Literally “of the soul”: a person living by natural powers alone. It is not a word for a bad person but for someone who has not yet received the Spirit’s light.
A person led by the Holy Spirit. It does not name a special class. Paul soon tells the Corinthians that they are behaving as infants in Christ (3:1).
To sift and judge. It is the key verb of vv. 14–15. Faith has its own way of seeing.
vv: So also no one comprehends what is truly God’s except the Spirit of God.
The comparison runs from the human to the divine: no one can see into my heart from outside. Still less can anyone see into God from outside, unless God gives his own Spirit.
Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may understand the gifts bestowed on us by God.
The Spirit is given so that we may recognise what we have already been given.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 11 in teaching that only the Spirit knows the things of God (CCC 687), and it says that no one can confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Spirit (CCC 683). This gift belongs to all the faithful, who have received the Spirit’s anointing (CCC 91). So v. 15 does not put an individual above the Church’s teaching: Paul writes these words while correcting the very people who thought themselves spiritual.

r.h: Have your lamps lit
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem (9:51). He has just told the disciples not to worry about possessions (12:22–34). He now turns to how they must live while they wait for him.
str: vv. 35–36: dressed and with lamps, like servants waiting for their master.
vv. 37–38: the surprise: the master serves the servants.
vv. 39–40: the thief, and the unexpected hour.
kw: Literally “loins girded”: the long robe tucked into the belt for work or travel. Israel ate the Passover this way, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11).
The same word as in the Beatitudes (6:20–22). The watching slave is a happy person, not an anxious one.
vv: Be dressed for action and have your lamps lit;
Blessed are those slaves whom the master finds alert when he comes; truly I tell you, he will fasten his belt and have them sit down to eat, and he will come and serve them.
No master in that world did this. The roles are reversed, and we see it happen at the Supper: “I am among you as one who serves” (22:27). The one we wait for comes to wait on us.
You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an unexpected hour.
The early Church often used the image of the thief (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 3:3). It is about the timing and nothing else: he comes as a surprise. It says nothing about his character.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, reads the girded loins as self-control and the burning lamps as good works that give light to others (in substance). The Catechism connects watchfulness with prayer: the disciple keeps watch, remembering the first coming in lowliness and hoping for the second in glory (CCC 2612). At this time of the year the Church holds both comings together.

study: Where have I recognised God’s gift only long afterwards? What helped me to see it?
If the Lord comes to serve those who wait for him, how does that change the way I think of waiting?

lead: Three days before Denha the readings already look to the Jordan. Each of them is about one whom God calls and sends. Moses, an exile keeping sheep, is sent to Pharaoh with the promise “I will be with you”. Cyrus, a foreign king, is called God’s anointed without knowing it. Timothy is told to hold on to the Scriptures he learned as a child. Then in Nazareth, Jesus reads from Isaiah in the synagogue of his boyhood and says that the anointed one is here, “today”.
So the Sunday moves from anointed figures who point forward to the Anointed himself. The key words are I have come down, anointed, continue and today.

r.h: I have come down to deliver them
set: Moses has fled from Egypt to Midian (2:15), married there, and is keeping another man’s sheep. Meanwhile the Israelites cry out in slavery, and God hears them and remembers his covenant (2:23–25). The reader knows this; Moses does not. He is on an ordinary working day when the mountain of God comes into his life. Horeb is the name which some parts of the Old Testament use for Sinai.
str: vv. 1–3: the shepherd and the bush that is not consumed.
vv. 4–6: the call by name, the holy ground, the God of the fathers.
vv. 7–10: what God has seen and what he will do: “I have come down”, and then “I will send you”.
vv. 11–12: Moses’ objection and God’s answer.
¶ God’s revelation of his name (3:13–15) comes right after this reading.
kw: A word found only here and in Deuteronomy 33:16, probably a thorn bush. God does not appear in a cedar. A Jewish midrash says that God chose a lowly thorn bush to show that he shares his people’s pain (in substance).
The Bible’s word for God’s entering into human need (compare Genesis 11:5). Christians hear in it the mystery the Church has just celebrated at Christmas: the Son who “came down from heaven”.
“I know their sufferings” does not mean only having information. In Hebrew this verb includes experience and care.
’Ehyeh, “I will be”, is the very word God uses two verses later when he reveals his name (3:14). Moses asks who he is, and God answers by saying who is with him.
vv: he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.
Fire that does not destroy what it fills: this is the first thing Moses learns about the holy God.
Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.

The Catechism says that before God’s presence man discovers his own littleness; Moses takes off his sandals and veils his face (CCC 208). God draws him close and keeps him at a distance at the same time.
I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry on account of their taskmasters. Indeed, I know their sufferings,

Four verbs in vv. 7–8 are the creed of Exodus: observed, heard, know, come down. God does not stand far from slaves. Then comes a surprise: “So come, I will send you” (3:10). God’s coming down takes the form of a man’s going.
Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?
It is an honest question. God does not reply by praising Moses.
I will be with you; and this shall be the sign for you that it is I who sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall worship God on this mountain.
This is a strange kind of sign: it can be seen only after obedience. The goal of the deliverance is worship, and that is fulfilled at Sinai (Exodus 19).
ch: The Catechism treats this scene as one of the primordial images of prayer: God calls first, and his call waits for an answer (CCC 2575), and it hears in it the God who reveals himself and is near (CCC 204–208). St Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, sees the bush as a figure of the Virgin: the divine light shone from her without destroying her virginity (in substance).

r.h: Cyrus, the Lord’s anointed
set: These verses speak to the Jewish exiles in Babylon, at the time when Cyrus II of Persia was rising to power. He took Babylon in 539 BC and let the deported peoples go home; the exiles were allowed to return and to rebuild the Temple (Ezra 1:1–4).

Cyrus’s own clay cylinder, found at Babylon in the nineteenth century and now in the British Museum, gives Marduk, the god of Babylon, the credit: Marduk took him by the hand and called his name. Isaiah uses the same kind of language for the opposite claim. It was the Lord, whom Cyrus did not know, who did this.
str: 44:28: Cyrus is my shepherd; Jerusalem will be rebuilt.
45:1: he is called anointed; God holds his right hand.
45:2–3: God goes before him: mountains, gates, hidden treasure.
45:3b–4: the purpose: “so that you may know”, and “for the sake of my servant Jacob”.
kw: The word that gives us “Messiah”. It was used of kings and priests of Israel. Cyrus is the only non-Israelite in the Old Testament to receive this title. The Greek Old Testament here has christos. He is not the Messiah in the later sense; he is someone God has set apart for a task.
A royal title in the ancient Near East, and a title Israel gave to its God (Psalm 23). The pagan king is made to serve as a shepherd for the Lord’s flock.
To give a title of honour. God gives the honour; Cyrus has done nothing to merit it.
vv: Thus says the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped
This must have shocked the exiles. Many commentators think that the next verses (45:9–13), about the clay that questions the potter, answer those who objected to it.
so that you may know that it is I, the Lord, the God of Israel, who call you by your name.
For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I surname you, though you do not know me.
Twice now God says “I call you by your name”. God’s plan does not depend on whether the instrument understands it. Cyrus’s success is not the point. The small, defeated people is.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God guides history with care and carries out his plan by making use of his creatures, who do not always know it (CCC 303–308). The Church also recognises that God is at work beyond her visible limits, and that those who do not yet know him are not outside his care (Lumen Gentium 16). In this reading the title “anointed” is given only for a time and for a task. It prepares us to hear what Jesus claims for himself at Nazareth.

r.h: Continue in what you have learned
set: This letter reads as the last testament of Paul, a prisoner who expects death (4:6–8), writing to his younger co-worker. The Church has received it among Paul’s letters. Many scholars today think that the Pastoral Letters come from a disciple writing in Paul’s name; others defend Paul’s own authorship. The teaching stands as inspired Scripture either way.

The list of places is not accidental. Antioch, Iconium and Lystra are the towns of Paul’s sufferings in Acts 13–14, and Lystra is where Acts first meets Timothy (Acts 16:1), so he may well have known those events at first hand.
str: vv. 10–11: what Timothy has seen in Paul: teaching, life, sufferings, and the Lord’s rescue.
vv. 12–13: this is the normal lot of believers; there are also deceivers.
vv. 14–15: “But as for you”: stay with what you learned and with the Scriptures.
kw: A disciple’s word: to walk beside someone and take in his way of life. Christian teaching is passed on from life to life, not only as ideas.
The same verb that John uses for abiding in Christ (John 15). In a time of trouble the task is to stay.
Here this means the Jewish Scriptures, our Old Testament, which Timothy learned as a child from his mother and grandmother (1:5).
vv: Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them.
Yet Paul is writing in chains. Rescue does not mean that suffering never comes, but that the Lord does not abandon his servant (compare 4:17–18).
Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.
This was true for Paul, and it remains true for those who suffer for their faith in many lands today. We pray for them, and for those who wrong them.
But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it,
Faith is received from people whom we can trust. Paul has in mind himself, and also a mother and a grandmother.
how from childhood you have known the sacred writings that are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
The Scriptures lead to salvation when they are read in faith in Christ. Note how today’s Gospel shows the same thing: a boy brought up in a village synagogue reads the same Scriptures.
ch: The Second Vatican Council urges all the faithful to read Scripture often, and it quotes St Jerome: “Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ” (Dei Verbum 25; CCC 133). The Church holds the Old Testament as an indispensable part of Scripture, whose inspired books remain permanently valid (CCC 121). The Catechism also reminds us that all must be ready to confess Christ before others, and to follow him on the way of the cross amid the persecutions the Church always meets (CCC 1816).

r.h: Today this scripture has been fulfilled
set: In Luke, Jesus has just been baptized, and the Spirit has come down on him (3:21–22). He is “full of the Holy Spirit” in the desert (4:1), and he returns “filled with the power of the Spirit” (4:14). This scene at Nazareth is Luke’s opening picture of the whole mission, placed at the head of the public ministry. That is why the Church reads it as she approaches Denha.

A synagogue service of the time included the reading of the Law and the Prophets, followed by a word of exhortation (compare Acts 13:15). We do not know for certain how fixed the readings were at this date, and Luke’s wording, “found the place”, may suggest that Jesus chose it. The reading stops at v. 22a, at the moment of wonder, before the question and the anger that follow.
str: vv. 16–17: Jesus in his own town, “as was his custom”. He stands and receives the scroll.
vv. 18–19: Isaiah’s words.
v. 20: scroll closed, Jesus seated, all eyes on him.
v. 21: “Today”.
v. 22a: their wonder.
kw: From the same root as christos. The anointing is the Spirit himself, given at the Jordan (Acts 10:38).
Used twice in v. 18 in the Greek, for captives and for the oppressed. It is also the word for the forgiveness of sins (24:47). This is the release of the whole person.
the year of the Lord’s favor
This recalls the jubilee year of Leviticus 25, when debts were cancelled and land returned.
A word Luke loves: “to you is born this day” (2:11), “Today salvation has come” (19:9), “today you will be with me” (23:43). The promise is not only for later.
vv: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.

The quotation is from Isaiah 61:1–2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next line, “the day of vengeance of our God”. Many commentators remark on this ending: the emphasis of this hour is mercy.
The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him.
Luke slows down and builds the silence. The reader is drawn into the room.
Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.
This is his entire sermon as Luke gives it. The scroll is about a person, and the person is standing in front of them.
All spoke well of him and were amazed at the gracious words that came from his mouth.
“Gracious words” in Greek are literally “words of grace”. The Word made flesh speaks grace.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ begins the proclamation of the Good News by making this passage of Isaiah his own (CCC 714), and that “the kingdom belongs to the poor and lowly” (CCC 544). Christ means the Anointed (CCC 436), and the Spirit’s anointing reveals his mission (CCC 438). Origen, in his homilies on Luke, says that the synagogue where all eyes were fixed on Jesus was blessed, and he asks that our assemblies also have the eyes of the heart fixed on him (in substance).

qa: Why is this Sunday called a Sunday of Denha when Denha comes three days later?

The calendar this year counts the Sunday falling before 6 January as the first of Denha. Its readings prepare for the feast by speaking of the one God anoints and sends. Please check your local parish calendar, since arrangements can differ.
Was Cyrus a believer?

The text says twice that he did not know God (45:4–5). His own inscription credits Marduk. Scripture does not make him a convert; it says that God used him. God’s plan is larger than any ruler’s understanding of it.
Why did the people turn on Jesus at Nazareth?

The reading stops before that, at v. 22a. The verses that follow tell of the question “Is not this Joseph’s son?” and of a sharp conflict with his own townspeople. This is a matter of one town’s reaction in one hour, and Luke tells it as a warning to every hearer, including us, not as a judgment on a people.
rite: The East Syriac year has moved from the Annunciation and the Nativity toward Denha, the rising of the light at the Jordan. Syro-Malabar Christians call our Lord Mishiha, the Anointed, in nearly every prayer. This Sunday shows what the word means. Moses is sent, Cyrus is used, and Timothy holds on to what he learned, but only one person can read Isaiah 61 and say “today”. When the Gospel is proclaimed in the Holy Qurbana, it is this same “today”: he is present, and his word is being fulfilled in our hearing.
study: Moses was called in the middle of an ordinary working day. Where might God be speaking to me in my usual work?
“Who am I?” God answers, “I will be with you”. What am I refusing because I am looking at myself and not at that promise?
Who taught me the faith? Have I thanked God for them, and who is learning it from me?
If the “today” of Luke 4:21 were true of my parish, who are the poor, the captive and the oppressed who should be hearing good news from us?

lead: Two days before Denha, both readings speak of a Father and a Son. John’s letter says that to believe in Jesus is to be born of God, and that this faith conquers the world. In the Gospel, Jesus says that he does what he sees the Father doing. The feast will show the Son in the water and the Father’s voice from above; these readings prepare us to hear what that means.

r.h: The victory that conquers the world
set: The First Letter of John addresses a community that has been through a painful split (2:19), over what it means to confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. Against those who left, the writer offers plain tests of true faith: right belief, love of the brethren and obedience. In these verses, the three are woven together.
str: v. 1: believing in Jesus is the mark of being born of God; such a person loves God’s other children.
vv. 2–3: love of God and keeping his commandments belong together.
vv. 4–5: faith is the victory.
kw: God’s act comes first. Believing is the sign that a new birth has taken place (compare John 3:5).
This noun occurs only here in the New Testament, though the verb “conquer” is common in John (John 16:33). It was the word for a victory in war or in the games.
Literally “heavy”. Compare Matthew 11:30: “my burden is light”.
vv: And his commandments are not burdensome,
He does not say that they are easy. A command is heavy until one loves the one who gives it, and grace gives the strength.
And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.
“The world” in this letter means human life organised apart from God (2:15–17), not creation itself. The victory is already won in Christ, and the believer shares it.
Who is it that conquers the world but the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
The reading ends on the title which the voice from heaven will give to Jesus at the Jordan.
ch: The Catechism says that to become children of God we must be “born from above” or “born of God” (CCC 526). St Augustine, in his sermons on this letter, returns again and again to the point that faith and charity cannot be separated (in substance). For the Church, this new birth happens in Baptism, the sacrament that Denha brings to mind.

r.h: The Son does what he sees the Father doing
set: Jesus has healed a sick man at the pool on a sabbath (5:1–18). When challenged, he says, “My Father is still working, and I also am working” (5:17). Jewish thinkers of the time, such as Philo, also said that God does not stop working on the sabbath. The conflict comes from Jesus’ claim to share that work. When John says “the Jews” in this chapter, he means the religious authorities who opposed him, not the Jewish people as a whole (CCC 597–598). Vv. 19–23 are Jesus’ answer.
str: vv. 19–20: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, in love.
v. 21: the Son gives life, as the Father does.
vv. 22–23: judgment is given to the Son, so that all may honour him.
kw: A double “amen” at the start of a saying, found only in John’s Gospel. It marks words of special weight.
Both a judge’s verdict and the moment of decision. In John, a person’s response to Jesus is already part of it (3:18–19).
The word used of honouring parents and God. This is the honour due to God alone, and it is claimed for the Son in v. 23.
vv: the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.

Many commentators hear a picture from daily life, of a son learning his father’s trade at his side. It does not make the Son lesser: “whatever the Father does” is everything. He and the Father work as one.
just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.
Only God gives life to the dead. In the verses that follow, Jesus gives life by his word.
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
This is a very high claim. To honour the Father one must honour the Son.
ch: The Church teaches that the works of the Trinity are one: the Three Persons are as inseparable in what they do as in what they are (CCC 258). The Catechism says that full right to judge belongs to Christ as redeemer of the world, and it cites this passage (CCC 679). St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, explains that the Son’s “seeing” is not a pupil’s learning; he has from the Father all that he is (in substance).

qa: If “the Son can do nothing on his own”, is he less than the Father?

No. These words speak of perfect unity, not of weakness. The Son has everything from the Father, and he does everything with the Father. The same passage demands equal honour for both (5:23). The Church confesses him as “one in being with the Father” (CCC 242, 262).
study: John says that the commandments are not heavy. Which command feels heavy to me, and what would it mean to carry it in love?
Jesus does what he sees the Father doing. Where do I need to stop and look first, before I act?

lead: On the eve of Denha the readings are sober. The letter to Titus insists that those who believe must devote themselves to good works, and warns against quarrels. In the Gospel, Jesus replies to a curious question about numbers by telling the questioner to strive for the narrow door. Before the feast of Baptism, both readings ask how seriously we take the life we entered through that door.

r.h: Devote yourselves to good works
set: Titus is presented as Paul’s co-worker, left on Crete to organise the churches (1:5). This is one of the Pastoral Letters, which the Church receives among Paul’s letters; many scholars think that they come from a disciple writing in his name, while others defend Paul’s own authorship. V. 8 comes straight after one of the letter’s great statements about the grace of Baptism (3:4–7).
str: v. 8: the saying is sure; believers must do good works.
v. 9: stay away from useless disputes.
vv. 10–11: how to deal with one who divides the community.
kw: A formula found only in the Pastoral Letters (for example 1 Timothy 1:15), pointing to a teaching held firmly by the Church.
Literally “beautiful” or “excellent” works. Salvation is not by works (3:5), yet the saved are to devote themselves to them. Grace bears fruit.
The word that later gave us “heretic”. Here it has its earlier sense: a person who makes factions. The later technical meaning should not be read back into it.
vv: I desire that you insist on these things, so that those who have come to believe in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works
The word for “devote” suggests taking the lead in something. Good works are not a side matter.
But avoid stupid controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless.
We do not know exactly what these disputes on Crete were. The test Titus is given is a practical one: does this argument build anyone up?
ch: The Catechism recalls that “faith apart from works is dead” (CCC 1815). It defines heresy as the obstinate denial of a truth of faith after Baptism (CCC 2089), and it says that those born today into communities separated from the Catholic Church cannot be charged with the sin of separation; the Church accepts them with respect and affection as brothers and sisters (CCC 818). The letter’s severity is about protecting the community’s unity, not about hating a person.

r.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
set: Jesus is making his way to Jerusalem (13:22). Someone asks him about numbers. Jesus does not give a figure; he turns a question about others into a warning for the questioner. Matthew has a similar saying about the narrow gate (Matthew 7:13–14) and the people from east and west (8:11–12); Luke puts them together here as a picture of a house whose owner shuts the door.
str: v. 23: “will only a few be saved?”
v. 24: the narrow door.
vv. 25–27: the shut door: “We ate and drank with you”; “I do not know where you come from”.
vv. 28–29: those shut out and the banquet with people from everywhere.
v. 30: the last and the first.
kw: From agōn, the contest or struggle of an athlete. The verb is in the present tense: keep striving. The word points to effort, not to anxiety.
A door one must enter deliberately, not a wide road one drifts along. In John, Jesus calls himself the gate, the same Greek word thyra (John 10:9).
vv: Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.
The failure lies in coming too late or wanting to come without change.
We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.
Being near Jesus is not the same as following him. This warning reaches every believer, and it reaches us who eat at his table in the Holy Qurbana.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.

Isaiah promised such a feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6). Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets are already at the table (13:28). The warning is not about any one nation; it is for all who assume that their place is safe.
ch: The Catechism quotes the saying about the narrow gate as a call to take responsibility for our eternal destiny (CCC 1036). It also says that the Church prays that no one should be lost (CCC 1058), and it teaches that those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel, yet seek God sincerely, can attain salvation (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). Everyone is called to enter the Kingdom (CCC 543). So the Church holds both things: God’s wide mercy and each person’s real responsibility.

qa: Does this Gospel say that only a few will be saved?

Jesus refuses to give a number. What he does say is that entering takes effort, that it cannot be assumed, and that people will come from all directions. The Church does not say how many are saved, and she prays for all (CCC 1058).
rite: The eve of Denha had its own custom among Kerala’s Christians: rakkuli, the bath at night in river or pond, recalling the Jordan. Whether or not a family keeps this today, the eve is a good time to remember one’s own Baptism, the door through which each of us has already been brought.
study: Am I more interested in how others will fare with God than in my own response to him?
“We ate and drank with you”. How can I keep my reception of the Holy Qurbana from becoming a mere habit?

lead: Denha is the Syriac word for a rising or a dawning. The East Syriac tradition celebrates on this day the Baptism of the Lord, because at the Jordan the mystery of God shines out: the Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down, and the Father’s voice is heard.

The readings show the dawn from far off to close at hand. A seer from outside Israel sees a star rising from Jacob, “but not now”. Isaiah sees a shoot from a cut-down stump, with the Spirit resting on him. In Matthew that person stands in the Jordan, and the Spirit rests on him as the Father speaks. And Titus tells us where we come into it: “the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit”. The key words are star, Spirit, righteousness and appeared.

r.h: A star shall come out of Jacob
set: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab at the end of the desert journey. Balak, the king of Moab, hires Balaam son of Beor, a famous seer from the Euphrates region (22:5), to curse them. Three times Balaam opens his mouth and blesses them instead. Now, unasked, he speaks a fourth oracle about the future.
A plaster inscription found at Deir ‘Alla in Jordan in 1967, from about the eighth century BC, speaks of a seer called Balaam son of Beor. So he was remembered outside the Bible as well.
str: vv. 15–16: Balaam introduces himself as one who sees.
v. 17: the star and the scepter.
vv. 18–19: Edom and Seir.
vv. 20–24: brief oracles on Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur and the ships from Kittim. The Hebrew is obscure in places, especially in the last verses.
v. 25: Balaam goes home.
kw: In the ancient Near East a star was often an image for a king, and “scepter” in the parallel line confirms this. Compare “the bright morning star” in Revelation 22:16.
The staff of a ruler (compare Genesis 49:10). Many scholars think that the oracle first had David in view, who subdued Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 13–14). Later readers looked beyond him.
The Hebrew word in v. 15 is rare and its meaning uncertain. It could mean “opened” or “closed”. The NRSV reads “clear”.
vv: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near
The seer knows that what he sees is far off. Those who come to the Jordan and see Jesus are living in the “now” that he could not reach.
a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel;

The Greek Old Testament says that a star “shall rise”, and this is the language of dawn. Matthew’s Magi say, “we observed his star at its rising” (Matthew 2:2). Zechariah speaks of “the dawn from on high” (Luke 1:78). Jewish readers around the time of Jesus also read this verse of a coming leader, as the Dead Sea Scrolls show.
Then Balaam got up and went back to his place
He goes home. The seer who saw so far does not walk in that light; later Scripture remembers him unfavourably (Numbers 31:16; 2 Peter 2:15). Seeing truly is one thing, and following is another.
ch: St Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 106) and Origen (Against Celsus 1) link this oracle with the star of the Magi (in substance). The Catechism says that Epiphany celebrates the manifestation of Jesus as Messiah of Israel, Son of God and Saviour of the world, and that the Magi represent the nations who come to him (CCC 528). The East Syriac feast of Denha centres on the Jordan, but the theme is the same: the light that had been promised is seen.

r.h: The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him
set: Isaiah preaches in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, in the shadow of Assyria. Just before this reading (10:33–34) the Lord cuts down a great forest, a picture of proud powers brought low. The royal house of David itself will look like a stump. But from that stump something grows.
str: v. 1: the shoot from Jesse’s stump.
v. 2: the Spirit and his gifts.
vv. 3–4: how this king judges: not by appearance, but with justice for the poor.
v. 5: righteousness and faithfulness are his clothing.
kw: The prophet says Jesse, not David. He goes back behind the royal glory to the shepherd’s father in Bethlehem. God starts again from the beginning.
Some scholars think that this word lies behind Matthew’s saying that Jesus would be called a Nazorean (Matthew 2:23), though this cannot be proved.
In Israel’s history the Spirit came on judges and kings for a moment. Here he “shall rest” on this one, and remain.
vv: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots.
New life comes from what looks dead. This is the way God works in Scripture, and the feast of Denha rests upon it.
The spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord.

The Hebrew has six gifts in three pairs. The Greek and Latin versions render “fear of the Lord” in two ways, adding “piety”, and so the Church’s list of seven gifts of the Holy Spirit took shape (CCC 1831).
He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide by what his ears hear;
Compare “the Lord looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). A king who judges by appearances will favour the rich and the well-connected.
but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth;
The test of the Spirit’s presence in a ruler is what happens to the poor.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the prophets announced that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the hoped-for Messiah, and that the descent of the Spirit on Jesus at his baptism was the sign that he was the one to come (CCC 1286; see also CCC 712). The gifts “belong in their fullness to Christ, Son of David” (CCC 1831), and they are given to us who are joined to him.

r.h: The water of rebirth
set: The letter instructs Titus on how the Christians of Crete are to live among their neighbours. The Church has received it among Paul’s letters, while many scholars think that a disciple wrote the Pastoral Letters in his name and others defend Paul’s own authorship. In the middle of practical advice comes one of the most compact summaries of salvation in the New Testament (3:4–7). The verses that follow it were read on the eve of this feast (3:8–11).
str: vv. 1–2: how to behave in society: respect, gentleness, courtesy to all.
v. 3: what we once were.
vv. 4–7: what God has done: he appeared, he saved, he poured out the Spirit, and we have become heirs.
¶ The structure is a “before” and an “after”. The hinge is the word “But” in v. 4.
kw: From the same root as epiphaneia, “manifestation”, which gives this feast its Greek name. For Titus the manifestation is of God’s kindness itself.
Literally “love of human beings”. The Greeks praised it in kings. Titus says that it has appeared in God our Saviour.
Loutron means a washing or bath. Palingenesia, new birth, is used in the New Testament only here and in Matthew 19:28. This is Baptism.
vv: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared,
he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
Grace comes first, and it comes through a real sacramental act. Water is not a mere symbol here; God saves through it.
This Spirit he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
Notice the three: God our Saviour, the Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ. The Jordan’s revelation of the Trinity becomes the believer’s own experience.
so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
What the Father says of the Son at the Jordan now reaches us: those who are baptized into him are heirs with him (Romans 8:17).
ch: The Catechism names Baptism with these very words, “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1215). Through it the baptized become a new creature and an adopted child of God (CCC 1265). Paul’s teaching on justification (Romans 3:24) is echoed here: it comes from God’s grace and mercy (CCC 1987, 1996).

r.h: This is my Son, the Beloved
set: John the Baptist has been preaching repentance at the Jordan and has announced one more powerful who will baptize “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (3:11). Now, as a grown man, Jesus appears in Matthew’s Gospel for the first time since his childhood. John’s baptism was a sign of repentance. This raises a question which only Matthew records, and John himself asks it.
str: v. 13: Jesus comes to John from Galilee.
v. 14: John tries to prevent him.
v. 15: Jesus’ first words in Matthew’s Gospel.
vv. 16–17: the heavens opened, the Spirit, the voice.
kw: A key word in Matthew (5:6; 6:33): doing God’s saving will. “All righteousness” means all that the Father’s plan asks.

Luke says “in bodily form” (3:22). The dove may recall the Spirit over the waters of creation (Genesis 1:2) or the dove after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12). The Catechism sees here a prelude of the new creation (CCC 1224).
The voice combines Psalm 2:7, of the royal son, and Isaiah 42:1, of the servant in whom God delights. Many also hear Genesis 22:2, the beloved son of Abraham. King and Servant meet in one person.
vv: I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?
John sees that the order seems to be wrong.
Let it be so now; for it is proper for us in this way to fulfill all righteousness.
Jesus has no sin to confess. He comes to stand where sinners stand, in solidarity with them. The word “us” includes John: each has a part in the Father’s plan.
suddenly the heavens were opened to him and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting on him.
Isaiah had cried, “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). What Isaiah 11 promised is happening: the Spirit rests on him.
This is my Son, the Beloved, with whom I am well pleased.
In Mark and Luke the voice says “You are”. In Matthew it says “This is”, as an announcement to all. This is the manifestation that gives Denha its name.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus’ baptism is his acceptance and inauguration of his mission as God’s suffering Servant, that he lets himself be numbered among sinners, and that the Spirit comes to remain on him (CCC 536). It sees here the manifestation of his self-emptying, and a prelude of the new creation (CCC 1224). St Ignatius of Antioch says that he was baptized so that by his passion he might purify the water (To the Ephesians 18, in substance). St Gregory Nazianzen says in his Epiphany sermons: Christ is baptized; let us go down with him so as to rise with him (in substance). Mar Ephrem sings in a hymn of faith of fire and Spirit in the womb that bore him and in the river where he was baptized (in substance). In Baptism, the Christian is sacramentally joined to Jesus (CCC 537).

qa: Why was the sinless Jesus baptized?

Not for his own sins. He took his place among sinners, began his mission as the Servant, and by entering the water made it holy for us (CCC 536, 1224). The Catechism sees this as a first form of the self-giving that will be fulfilled on the cross.
Is Denha the same feast as the Latin Epiphany of the Magi?

It falls on the same date and comes from the same ancient feast of God’s manifestation. The Catechism says that Epiphany celebrates the Magi, the Baptism and the wedding at Cana together (CCC 528). The Latin tradition places the Magi first, and the Syriac and other Eastern traditions place the Baptism first. These are two windows on one light.
Why would God speak through a seer like Balaam?

Because God is not limited by who is speaking. Balaam was hired to curse, and he was made to bless. Scripture does not hide his later failure. God’s word can be true on the lips of one who does not live by it, and this is a warning to all who speak in God’s name.
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church keeps Denha as one of her great feasts, and its season runs on from here, showing week by week who Jesus is. In Kerala the feast was kept with lights and water. In pindikuthi, lamps were set on a plantain stem and the family gathered around them, confessing Christ as the light. In rakkuli, families bathed by night in river or pond to recall the Jordan. Both customs teach the same thing as the readings: the Light has risen, and we belong to him through water. At the Holy Qurbana today, we who were baptized into the Son hear the Father’s word again, and we may hear it as said over us too.
study: Balaam saw truly but went home unchanged. Where have I seen something true about God without letting it move me?
Isaiah says that the king judges for the poor. If the same Spirit was given to me in Baptism and Chrismation, what does that ask of me this week?
Do I know the date of my own Baptism? How could my family remember it each year?
Jesus stood among sinners in the river. Whom do I keep my distance from, where he would stand close?

lead: The day after Denha, the manifestation continues. Paul speaks of a wisdom hidden from the rulers of the age and revealed by the Spirit. Luke shows Jesus stopping a funeral at Nain and giving a dead son back to his mother. What God had hidden now shows itself as compassion.

r.h: God’s wisdom, secret and hidden
set: Paul has told the Corinthians that he came preaching only “Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (2:2). Yet he insists that this is real wisdom. It is not the kind that the world’s powerful people recognise, for it is the wisdom of the cross, planned by God before the ages.
str: v. 6: a wisdom for the mature, not of this age.
v. 7: God’s hidden wisdom, decreed before the ages.
v. 8: the rulers did not understand.
vv. 9–10: what no eye has seen is revealed through the Spirit.
kw: In Corinth a word of high prestige. Paul keeps the word and changes its content: the wisdom of God is the crucified Christ (1:24).
Translated here as “secret”. It does not mean a puzzle, but God’s plan, once hidden and now revealed.
The human rulers responsible for the crucifixion, and perhaps, as some think, the unseen powers behind them. Paul’s stress is on their failure to understand.
vv: None of the rulers of this age understood this; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

“Lord of glory”, the highest title, is joined to the most shameful death. The Catechism uses this verse to teach that we must not place the blame for the Cross on the Jewish people; all sinners were its authors (CCC 597–598).
What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived, what God has prepared for those who love him

Paul’s source is uncertain. The words seem to echo Isaiah 64:4 and 65:17. They are often used about heaven, as the Catechism uses them (CCC 1027), but Paul applies them first to what the Spirit is revealing now.
these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
The Spirit who came down at the Jordan is the one who opens this to us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that sinners were the authors of Christ’s Passion, and it quotes the Roman Catechism on those who keep crucifying the Lord by their sins (CCC 598). It describes the blessedness of heaven with the words of v. 9 (CCC 1027). So what the rulers could not see is offered to all “who love him”.

r.h: Young man, I say to you, rise
set: This story is found only in Luke. Nain is a village in Galilee, on the slope of the hill of Moreh, not far from Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37). Luke has just told of the centurion’s servant (7:1–10), and next come John’s disciples asking, “Are you the one who is to come?” Jesus answers, “the dead are raised” (7:20–22).
A widow who lost her only son lost her protection and her livelihood as well as her child. The crowd of mourners and the crowd of disciples meet at the town gate.
str: vv. 11–12: two crowds meet at the gate.
v. 13: he sees her, has compassion, and speaks.
vv. 14–15: he touches the bier, gives the command, and returns the son.
vv. 16–17: fear, praise, and the report that spreads.
kw: Here Luke, as narrator, first calls Jesus “the Lord”. He uses the title at the very moment of compassion.
A verb from the word for the inward parts: to be moved in one’s depths. Luke also uses it for the good Samaritan and for the father of the prodigal son (10:33; 15:20).
Literally “visited”, as God visits to save. Zechariah sang the same word (1:68). The Malayalam POC keeps the sense of visiting.
vv: When the Lord saw her, he had compassion for her and said to her, “Do not weep.”
No one asks him to act. She does not ask, and there is no statement of faith. The whole initiative is his.
Then he came forward and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still.
The Law treated contact with the dead as a cause of ritual impurity (Numbers 19:11–16). Jesus does not hesitate, and his touch carries life.
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
These are almost the same words as in the Greek of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah gives a widow’s son back to her. So the crowd says “A great prophet”, and the reader knows that he is more than that.
ch: The Catechism lists the son of the widow of Nain among those raised before Easter, and it makes a distinction: they returned to ordinary life and would die again, whereas Christ’s Resurrection is of another order (CCC 646). St Augustine, in a sermon, sees three kinds of sinners in the three dead whom Jesus raised: the girl in the house, the young man carried out through the gate, and Lazarus in the tomb (in substance). St Ambrose sees in the weeping widow an image of the Church, a mother who prays for her children (in substance).

study: Where has the wisdom of the cross turned my ideas about success upside down?
Jesus saw the widow before she said anything. Who around me is grieving without asking for anything? What would it mean to stop for them?

lead: On the Fridays of Denha the Church honours the great witnesses who made Christ known, and the first of them is John the Baptist. Each reading gives one side of his witness. Isaiah supplies the voice in the wilderness that the Gospels hear in John. Paul, preaching in a synagogue, places John at the turning point of Israel's story. Ephesians, in Paul's voice from prison, shows what such witness builds: a household resting on apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone. Mark tells the price: a prison, a banquet, a sword and a tomb. The line runs from a voice, to a story, to a house, to a martyr, and its key words are word, witness and foundation.

r.h: A voice in the wilderness
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah, often called the Book of Consolation, speak to the people exiled in Babylon, in the years before Cyrus allowed them to return (539 BC). Many scholars think that a prophet of the exile, in the school of Isaiah, gave these oracles; the Church receives them as one book of Scripture. The great empire looks permanent and the promise looks dead. These eight verses are the opening of a new message: the sentence is served, and God is coming home with his people.
str: vv. 1–2: comfort: Jerusalem's term of suffering is over.
vv. 3–5: a road through the desert, and the glory of the Lord seen by all.
vv. 6–8: human strength withers; the word of God stands.
¶ The whole passage is made of voices. No speaker is named. The attention falls on what is said, a point the Baptist himself will make when he calls himself only a voice (John 1:23).
kw: The Hebrew is doubled for force, and the command is plural: God tells a group of messengers to go and comfort. Many scholars picture God addressing his heavenly court.
Literally “speak to the heart”. It is the language of a lover winning back a beloved; compare Hosea 2:14, “speak tenderly to her”.

Usually God's steadfast love. In v. 6 the word is used of human beings: their faithfulness does not last. The Greek Old Testament has “glory” here, which 1 Peter 1:24 follows, and the Malayalam POC's “beauty” stands close to that line.
vv: Comfort, O comfort my people, says your God.
“My people” and “your God” are the words of the covenant. The exile has not cancelled them.
A voice cries out: “In the wilderness prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

A note on the text. In the Hebrew, as the NRSV sets it out, the road is prepared in the wilderness. The Greek Old Testament can be read so that the voice itself is in the wilderness, and that is the form the Gospels quote (Mark 1:3; John 1:23). John, preaching in the desert, fits it perfectly. The picture is of the great processional roads of Babylon, but this road is for the God of a defeated people.
All people are grass, their constancy is like the flower of the field.
The prophet's first response is discouragement: what is there to say about creatures who fade? The answer takes in the mighty as well. Herod, in today's Gospel, is grass too.
The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God will stand forever.
This is the centre of the reading. 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes it and adds that this word is the good news preached to us. John dies, and Herod's rule ends; the word John served remains.
ch: All four Gospels apply this passage to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4–6; John 1:23). The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner, the last of the prophets, who bears witness to Christ by his preaching, by his baptism of conversion and finally by his martyrdom (CCC 523; see also 719). St Augustine liked to draw the contrast: John is the voice, which passes, and Christ is the Word, who remains (in substance). Every preacher and catechist stands in that place: a voice that serves a Word greater than itself.

r.h: Paul tells the story and names the forerunner
set: On their first missionary journey Paul and Barnabas reach Antioch in Pisidia, in the south of Asia Minor. It is not the great Antioch in Syria. On the sabbath they go to the synagogue, and after the reading of the law and the prophets the officials invite them to give “any word of exhortation” (13:15). This is the first long sermon of Paul that Acts reports. He speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews and to devout Gentiles, and he calls them “brothers”. The promise is “our” story.
str: v. 16: the address: Israelites and God-fearers.
vv. 17–19: Egypt, the wilderness, the land.
vv. 20–22: judges, Samuel, Saul and David.
v. 23: from David's line, Jesus the Savior.
vv. 24–25: John prepares his coming and points away from himself.
v. 26: this message is for you who are listening.
kw: Many scholars take this as a term for Gentiles who were drawn to Israel's faith and worship in the synagogue without becoming full converts. Such people were often the first to welcome the gospel in Acts (compare Cornelius, 10:2).
God himself is Savior in the Old Testament. Paul uses the title of the descendant of David (v. 23).
Metanoia is a turning of mind and life. John's rite prepared people; it pointed beyond itself to the one who was coming.
vv: For about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.

A note on the text. Greek manuscripts differ here by one letter. One reading says God “put up with” them, which the NRSV and the POC follow. The other says he “cared for” them, as a nurse carries a child (compare Deuteronomy 1:31). Both are true of God in the desert.
Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised;
All the earlier history leads here. God's fidelity to his promise is the thread of Paul's sermon; David is named so that the promise to David can be recalled.
before his coming John had already proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
Far from Galilee, years after his death, John is already part of the Christian message. The Church's preaching of Jesus begins from John's baptism (Acts 1:22; 10:37).
What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but one is coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.
Untying sandals was a slave's task. John's whole greatness lies in knowing who he is not (compare John 1:20).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the coming of God's Son was prepared over many centuries, and that John, the last of those who prepared the way, sums up that long preparation (CCC 522–523). Paul's sermon is a model for the Church's teaching: it does not begin with an idea but with a history, in which God has kept faith with a people. The Church honours that people still, for from them comes the Christ according to the flesh (Romans 9:4–5; CCC 839).

r.h: A household built on a foundation
set: The letter comes in Paul's name, from prison (3:1). Many scholars think a close disciple wrote it in his name after his death; others hold that Paul himself wrote it. Either way the Church receives it as the inspired word of God. Its great theme is the unity in Christ of Jews and Gentiles. The reading joins the end of chapter 2 to the beginning of chapter 3: first the house, then the prisoner who serves it.
str: 2:19: no more strangers, but citizens and members of the household.
2:20–22: the building: foundation, cornerstone, temple, dwelling place.
3:1: “I Paul”, a prisoner for the Gentiles. The sentence breaks off and resumes only at 3:14.
3:2–5: a mystery revealed, hidden from earlier generations.
3:6: its content: Gentiles are fellow heirs.
3:7: Paul is its servant, by grace.
kw: The stone that sets the line of the whole building. The word comes from the Greek of Isaiah 28:16, and 1 Peter 2:6 quotes it of Christ.
Not a riddle, but God's plan, once hidden and now made known (3:3–5).
In 3:6 three Greek words in a row begin with “with”: fellow heirs, members of the same body, sharers. The grammar itself pulls people together.
vv: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The move is from a legal status to a family. A stranger may be tolerated, but a member of the household has a place at the table.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.

The prophets are probably those of the early Church, since 3:5 names them with the apostles as receiving the revelation now. Yet John, the last of the old prophets, prepared the ground on which this foundation was laid.
This is the reason that I Paul am a prisoner for Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles
Today the letter's prisoner stands beside the prisoner in the Gospel. A jail does not stop the building; it often serves it.
that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
The Gentiles join a promise already given. They do not replace those who received it first.
ch: The Catechism gathers the images of this passage: the Church is God's building, resting on the apostles, with Christ as its stone (CCC 756), and she remains built on the foundation of the apostles (CCC 857). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is one people drawn from Jews and Gentiles, called together in Christ (Lumen Gentium 9). To call the Church apostolic means that our faith does not float; it stands on witnesses who gave their lives.

r.h: The price of telling the truth
set: Mark places this story between the sending out of the Twelve (6:7–13) and their return (6:30). While the disciples go out to preach, we are told what can happen to a preacher. It is the only story in Mark that is not directly about Jesus, and it is told as a flashback, when Herod hears of Jesus and fears that John has come back.

The “King Herod” here is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great. Rome gave him only the title of tetrarch of Galilee and Perea (compare Matthew 14:1). Josephus, the Jewish historian, also reports John's death: he says that Herod feared John's influence over the people and had him killed at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea (Antiquities 18). The two accounts give different sides of the event and do not need to exclude each other.
str: vv. 14–16: who is Jesus? John, Elijah, a prophet? Herod's guilty fear.
vv. 17–20: why John was in prison.
vv. 21–25: the banquet, the dance and the request.
vv. 26–28: the king's grief and the order.
v. 29: John's disciples bury him.
kw: Herod himself gives this description (v. 20). He knows who John is, and that makes his act worse.
A note on the text. Many manuscripts read instead “he did many things” after hearing John. The older witnesses support “perplexed”, which the NRSV follows and with which the POC agrees in sense.
A blunt word. Mark uses it again of the body of Jesus (15:45). John's end foreshadows the Lord's: a ruler who knows better, an order given to save face, and a burial in a tomb.
vv: For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
The verb suggests he said it repeatedly. The Law forbade this marriage (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John did not soften God's word for a ruler.
for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he protected him. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed; and yet he liked to listen to him.
A striking picture of a divided heart: someone can enjoy a good preacher for years and never change.
And he solemnly swore to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, even half of my kingdom.”
The words echo Esther 5:3. There is irony here: Herod has no kingdom of his own to give. Josephus reports that he was later banished by Rome after seeking the title of king.
The king was deeply grieved; yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests, he did not want to refuse her.
He fears losing face more than he fears doing evil. A man with soldiers is ruled by what his dinner guests will think.
When his disciples heard about it, they came and took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
The story ends without a miracle. Nothing suggests that God has failed; the reader knows what is coming for Jesus, and what comes after his tomb.
ch: St John Paul II names John among those who refused to compromise with evil and gave their lives in witness to truth and justice, and says that he so became the forerunner of the Messiah in the way he died (Veritatis Splendor 91). The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). St Bede observes that John was not asked to deny Christ, but he died for justice and truth, and Christ is the truth; so he died for Christ (in substance).

qa: Why does Mark call Herodias's first husband Philip, when Josephus calls him Herod?

It is a real difficulty. Josephus names her first husband as a Herod, and speaks of a Philip as the husband of Salome, her daughter. Some suggest that the man bore both names; others that Mark's tradition confused members of a family in which names were often repeated. The point of the story, John's witness to God's law, is not affected.
Why did Herod feel bound by his oath?
Mark presents this as weakness, not as piety. An oath does not make a grave wrong right. Herod's real motive is shown in the words “for the guests”.
Who was the girl who danced?

The NRSV follows manuscripts that say “his daughter Herodias”; other manuscripts say the daughter of Herodias herself, as the POC's “her daughter” does. Josephus names Herodias's daughter as Salome, and tradition has taken that name from him, though Mark does not give it.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar calendar the Fridays of Denha are given to the witnesses of the Lord, and John rightly comes first: at the Jordan, which the Church has just celebrated, he saw the Spirit come down on the Lord (John 1:32). For our Church, built on the witness of the apostle Thomas, the reading from Ephesians speaks directly: we are members of the household because someone came and told the truth at a cost. The Holy Qurbana we offer today joins John's witness to the one sacrifice he foretold.
study: Isaiah sets the fading of “all people” against the word that stands. What do I treat as permanent that is really grass?
John says, “I am not he.” Where am I tempted to take the place that belongs to Christ?
Herod liked to listen to John and did not change. How do I respond to a word that troubles me?
Who has been part of the foundation of my own faith, and at what cost to them?

lead: Both readings are about people who stumble at what God has done. Paul grieves that many of his own people have not received Christ, and he speaks of a stone laid by God himself. In John, Jesus is in the Temple and is accused of blasphemy for calling himself God's Son. In this season of Denha, the manifestation of the Lord, we hear that manifestation is not the same as acceptance: the light shines, and each person must still respond.

r.h: The stone laid in Zion
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long wrestling with one question: why have so many of Israel, to whom the promises belong, not come to believe in the Messiah? He begins with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his own people (9:2) and ends with the mercy of God for all (11:32). This short reading must be heard inside that whole movement. It is not the last word on Israel. Paul himself says that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).
str: v. 30: Gentiles who were not seeking have found righteousness through faith.
vv. 31–32a: Israel, striving, did not reach the goal of the law.
vv. 32b–33: the reason is given with a quotation about a stone.
kw: In Paul, being set right with God, God's own saving gift. It is not first of all a human achievement.
a rock that makes them fall
The word skandalon gives us “scandal”. Paul joins two passages of Isaiah (28:16 and 8:14). The stone is laid by God: what trips us is his own gift.
vv: Gentiles, who did not strive for righteousness, have attained it, that is, righteousness through faith;
A surprise for anyone who thinks in terms of merit: the outsiders receive what they did not chase. Grace is not a wage.
Because they did not strive for it on the basis of faith, but as if it were based on works.
Paul is not attacking the Law, which he calls holy (7:12). He warns against treating a relationship with God as something we earn. Christians too can fall into this.
and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.
The same stone that trips one person holds up another. The verse ends with a promise.
ch: The Church teaches that “our justification comes from the grace of God” (CCC 1996), and that faith and the works of love belong together, as gift and response. On Israel she follows Paul's own conclusion: God does not take back his gifts, and the Jewish people may not be spoken of as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). This passage gives no room for Christian pride; a few chapters later Paul warns the Gentile believers, “do not become proud, but stand in awe” (11:20).

r.h: The one whom the Father sanctified
set: It is winter, at the feast of the Dedication, the feast that recalls the rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 4:36–59), and Jesus is walking in the Temple, in the portico of Solomon (10:22–23). He has just said, “The Father and I are one” (10:30).

When John writes “the Jews” here, he means those authorities and opponents who confronted Jesus in the Temple on this occasion, not a whole people. Jesus and his disciples were themselves Jews. The Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people as such for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
str: vv. 31–33: stones in their hands, and the charge of blasphemy.
vv. 34–36: Jesus answers from Scripture.
vv. 37–38: believe the works.
v. 39: he escapes from their hands.
kw: Insulting God's honour. From the point of view of those who do not believe, the charge follows logically: a man makes himself God. The Gospel's point is that they have the matter backwards.
To set apart for God. At the feast of the Temple's consecration, Jesus says that he himself is the one the Father has consecrated. The true Temple is standing in front of them (compare 2:21).
vv: It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you, but for blasphemy, because you, though only a human being, are making yourself God.
Without intending it, they state the mystery the Gospel will overturn. He is not a man making himself God; he is the Word, who is God, made man (1:1, 14).
Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?

The quotation is from Psalm 82:6. “Law” here means Scripture as a whole. The argument moves from the lesser to the greater: if those who received God's word could be called “gods”, how much more the one whom the Father sent. Scholars discuss who the “gods” of the psalm were; the argument does not depend on settling that.
can you say that the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world is blaspheming because I said, ‘I am God’s Son’?
Two verbs carry the weight: sanctified and sent. His mission comes from before his appearing in the world.
so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.
The works are signs. They lead beyond themselves to the deepest truth: the communion of the Father and the Son.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus asked the religious authorities to believe in him because of the works of the Father he accomplished (CCC 591), and it recalls that this faith was a hard step: the authorities could not make it without a kind of death to what they had known. Verse 38 is at the root of the Church's language about the Trinity: because of their unity, the Father is wholly in the Son and the Son wholly in the Father (CCC 255).

qa: By quoting “you are gods”, did Jesus deny that he is God in a unique way?
