No. He does not say that he is a god in the same sense as those in the psalm. He argues from the lesser to the greater, and he goes on at once to say that the Father is in him and he in the Father. His opponents understood him: “they tried to arrest him again”.
study: Paul says some people stumble over God's gift because they want to earn it. In what ways do I try to deserve what God wants to give?
Jesus says, “believe the works”. What works of God in my life or in the Church lead me to believe?

lead: The name Denha means dawning: the Lord shows himself. Today's four readings ask how God can be with us and still be God. In Numbers the ark goes ahead of a people on the road, under the cloud. In Isaiah the Creator who stretched out the heavens is confessed as “a God who hides himself”. Hebrews sets Moses the faithful servant beside Jesus the Son. And John gathers all these threads in one sentence: the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. The hidden God travels with us, and at last he has a face. The key words are tent, house and glory.

r.h: The ark goes before them
set: Israel has been at Sinai since Exodus 19. At Numbers 10:11, in the second year after leaving Egypt, the cloud lifts and the people set out at last. This reading is the moment of departure: the book's turn from receiving God's law at the mountain to following him through the desert. The rest of Numbers tells how hard that road will be.
str: vv. 29–32: Moses asks Hobab to come with them as a guide.
vv. 33–34: three days' march, with the ark going before and the cloud above.
vv. 35–36: the two short prayers of Moses, as the ark sets out and as it rests.
¶ In the Hebrew manuscripts vv. 35–36 are marked off by special signs (inverted letters), and an old rabbinic tradition treats them almost as a book of their own.
kw: ark of the covenant of the Lord
The chest holding the tablets of the covenant (Deuteronomy 10:1–5), the sign of God's presence with his people. In Numbers it travels; God is not fixed to one mountain.
The goal of the journey (v. 33). The ark itself looks for rest for the people. Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3–4 will take up this word: the promised rest is more than a piece of land.
A battle cry that became a prayer. It returns in Psalm 68:1 and Psalm 132:8.
vv: Do not leave us, for you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as eyes for us.

There is a lovely tension here. The ark goes ahead and the cloud gives direction, and yet Moses asks an experienced desert man for help. God's guidance does not make human skill and friendship unnecessary. Hobab is a Midianite; the people of God, from the beginning, travel with outsiders' help. Judges 1:16 suggests that his descendants did come.
So they set out from the mount of the Lord three days’ journey with the ark of the covenant of the Lord going before them three days’ journey, to seek out a resting place for them,
God scouts the way for his people. The picture is of a God who goes ahead, not one who waits at the end.
Arise, O Lord, let your enemies be scattered, and your foes flee before you.
Moses prays this each time the ark sets out. It is not a prayer of confidence in Israel's strength; the march depends on God going first.
Return, O Lord of the ten thousand thousands of Israel.
And this each time it rests. The people's day begins and ends with a prayer about God's presence.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Israel on its way through the desert was already called the Church of God, and that the Church too is a people on pilgrimage (Lumen Gentium 9). The Catechism sees the cloud of the Old Testament as a sign of the Spirit, who both reveals and hides God (CCC 697). Christian tradition also sees in Mary a new ark of the covenant, “the place where the glory of the Lord dwells” (CCC 2676), for in her the Word took flesh.

r.h: A God who hides himself
set: We are again in the Book of Consolation, among the exiles of Babylon. This chapter opens with a startling claim: the Persian king Cyrus, a foreigner who does not know the Lord, is called God's “anointed” (45:1). It seems some of the exiles objected, for vv. 9–10 scold anyone who questions the potter. Our reading answers them: the Creator has the right to use whom he chooses.
str: v. 11: will you question me about my children?
vv. 12–13: I made the earth, and I have raised up this man to let the exiles go.
v. 14: the nations will come and confess that God is with Zion.
v. 15: the confession: you are a God who hides himself.
vv. 16–17: idol makers are shamed; Israel is saved for ever.
kw: The verb used in the Old Testament only with God as subject (Genesis 1:1). In v. 12 he himself says it: “created humankind”.
The verb form suggests a God who actively keeps himself hidden. He is not absent; his ways cannot be read off from the surface of events. Who would have looked for salvation in a Persian conqueror?
Literally “salvation of ages”. The name Yeshua, Jesus, comes from the same root.
vv: I have aroused Cyrus in righteousness, and I will make all his paths straight; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward, says the Lord of hosts.

The Hebrew says only “him”; the NRSV supplies the name Cyrus from the context, whereas the POC says “one”. Cyrus's decree allowed the exiles to return (Ezra 1:1–4). God can use even those who do not know him.
God is with you alone, and there is no other; there is no god besides him.

The nations, once captors, confess it. The picture of chains is the poetry of its time, and the point is the confession. St Paul echoes these words when he says that an outsider will cry, “God is really among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25).
Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior.
The verse joins two words we would keep apart: hidden and Savior. God saves in ways we fail to recognise at first.
But Israel is saved by the Lord with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity.
The promise stands. The Church hears in it God's lasting fidelity to Israel, and the hope of all the nations.
ch: “Even when he reveals himself, God remains a mystery beyond words”, says the Catechism, and it quotes St Augustine: if you understood him, it would not be God (CCC 230). Blaise Pascal returned to this verse: he saw that God hides himself as well as shows himself, and thought any teaching that does not say so is untrue. Denha does not remove the mystery. Even in Jesus God is seen by faith, in a child, a man in the waters of the Jordan, the Holy Qurbana under the form of bread.

r.h: Servant in the house, Son over the house
set: Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It is a sermon to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were growing tired; the author is not named. Having shown the Son above the angels and our brother in suffering (chapters 1–2), the preacher now turns to Moses, the greatest figure of Israel. He uses Numbers 12:7, where God himself praises Moses as the one entrusted with all his house. This is not a put-down of Moses. Moses is the standard, the highest comparison there is.
str: v. 1: consider Jesus.
v. 2: both he and Moses were faithful.
vv. 3–4: the builder has more honour than the house, and God is the builder of all.
vv. 5–6a: Moses as a servant in the house, Christ as a son over it.
v. 6b: we are that house, if we hold firm.
kw: The only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called “apostle”, the one sent. Sent from God to us, as high priest he goes from us to God.
The word returns again and again in these verses. It means both a building and a household. The people themselves are God's home.
Not the common word for a slave, but an honoured attendant, the word used of Moses in the Greek of Numbers 12:7.
vv: Therefore, brothers and sisters, holy partners in a heavenly calling, consider that Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
“Consider” is the whole aim of the sermon. Tired Christians are told to look hard and long at Jesus.
Yet Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.
Moses belongs to the house; Christ belongs to its builder's side. The next verse says plainly that the builder of all things is God.
Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that would be spoken later.
Moses points forward. His whole service is a witness to what God would say at last in his Son (compare 1:1–2).
Christ, however, was faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.

A note on the text. Some ancient manuscripts add “to the end”, and the POC has these words; the NRSV follows the older witnesses that lack them. In either form the warning is the same. “Confidence” translates parrēsia, the boldness of those who have nothing to hide.
ch: The Catechism calls Jesus the Father's Emissary, the one on whose mission all the Church's mission depends (CCC 858). It also lists “the house of God in which his family dwells” among the images of the Church (CCC 756). Hebrews gives this image a condition: we are that house “if we hold firm”. Faith is a long fidelity, like that of Moses on the road.

r.h: The Word pitched his tent among us
set: These verses are the climax of John's Prologue (1:1–18), the opening of the Gospel, written as a kind of hymn. Until now the Word has been spoken of as being with God, as the maker of all things and as the light. At v. 14 comes the sentence for which the Prologue was written. The Word's coming among us is the true manifestation that Denha celebrates. The Old Testament background is the Exodus: tent, glory, Moses, law, and God's refusal to let Moses see his face (Exodus 33:18–23; 34:6).
str: v. 14: the Word became flesh, and we have seen his glory.
v. 15: John's witness.
v. 16: from his fullness, grace upon grace.
v. 17: Moses and Jesus Christ.
v. 18: no one has seen God; the Son has made him known.
kw: Not a pious word for “a person”, but the human condition in its weakness and mortality. John chooses the strongest word.
From skēnē, tent, the word for the tent of meeting in the Greek Old Testament. The sound also recalls the Hebrew for dwelling. What the ark and the tent stood for, the flesh of Jesus now is.
Many scholars hear in this the Hebrew ḥesed we’emet, “steadfast love and faithfulness”, by which God describes himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6.
Literally “he led out, he explained”. Our word “exegesis” comes from this verb. Jesus himself is the Father's exegesis.
vv: And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father’s only son, full of grace and truth.

“We” is the voice of those who saw: the community of witnesses. The verb “became” is strong, yet the Word does not cease to be God. The glory Moses asked to see is now seen, above all in the Cross (compare 12:23–24).
From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.
Literally “grace in place of grace”. Scholars debate the sense: an unending supply of grace, or the grace of Christ following the grace of the Law. Both agree on abundance.
The law indeed was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
The Greek has no “but”. The Law is God's gift; in Christ the gift reaches its fullness. This is the first time the Gospel uses the name Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known.

A note on the text. The oldest Greek manuscripts have “only-begotten God”, which the NRSV and the POC follow in their own ways. Many others read “only-begotten Son”. Both are firmly Catholic faith. The literal image is of the Son “in the Father's bosom”, the place of closest love, the place the Beloved Disciple has at the Supper (13:23).
ch: The Catechism says that the Church calls the Son's assuming a human nature the Incarnation, and it quotes this verse (CCC 461); Jesus is true God and true man, not part God and part man (CCC 464). It calls the Son the Father's “one, perfect and unsurpassable Word” (CCC 65), and repeats that only he has seen the Father and made him known (CCC 151). St Athanasius says that the Son of God became man so that we might become God (quoted in CCC 460). St John Chrysostom notes that the word “lived among us” guards the mystery: the Word did not change into something else, but truly dwelt in our flesh (in substance).

qa: If “no one has ever seen God”, what of Moses and Isaiah?

They experienced God through signs: the cloud, the fire, the vision. Exodus 33:11 speaks of friendship, and 33:20 denies that Moses saw God's face. John says that all this looked toward Jesus: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9).
Did the Word turn into a human being and stop being God?
No. The Word remained what he was and took up what he was not. The Church confesses one person in two natures, truly divine and truly human (CCC 464–469).
Is Isaiah's “hidden God” the same as a God who does not care?
No. The verse says hidden and Savior in one breath. The Psalms and the prophets, and the Cross itself, teach that God is at work even when we do not see him.
rite: At Denha the Syro-Malabar Church celebrates the baptism of the Lord and his manifestation as the Son. In many Kerala parishes the feast is kept with lights, in the custom of Pindikuthi, a reminder that the Light has come into our dark. Today's Gospel gives the reason. On this Sunday, as we stand before the altar in the Holy Qurbana, we receive the same flesh of which John says, “we have seen his glory”. The hidden God still comes under signs, and those who receive him are his house.
study: Moses asked Hobab, “you will serve as eyes for us”. Who has God sent to be eyes for me on my road? For whom can I be eyes?
Isaiah calls God hidden and Savior at once. When has God been at work in my life in a way I recognised only later?
Hebrews tells tired Christians to “consider” Jesus. How could I give more time to looking at him?
John says Jesus is the one who has explained God. What in the Gospel has changed my picture of who God is?

lead: Today's readings set a broken table beside a prayer for unity. In Corinth, Christians who gather for the Lord's Supper shame the poor among them. In John, on the night before he dies, Jesus prays for all who will ever believe, “that they may all be one”. Division among Christians is not a small matter of manners. It hides from the world the God whom Denha makes known.

r.h: When you come together
set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8), probably in the mid-50s, to a young and divided community in a busy Roman port. Christians then met in private houses for a shared meal, with the Eucharist as part of the gathering. Many scholars think that the better-off arrived early and ate and drank in plenty, while poorer members and slaves, who had to work, came late to find little left. Immediately after this reading Paul gives the oldest written account of the Lord's Supper (11:23–26).
str: v. 17: “I do not commend you.”
vv. 18–19: divisions when you gather.
vv. 20–21: what you are eating is not the Lord's Supper.
v. 22: you show contempt for the church of God.
kw: Literally tears, as in cloth. These are not yet separate churches, but rifts within one assembly, here along lines of wealth and class.
The only place in the New Testament where this name is used. The meal belongs to the Lord, and it cannot be treated as “your own supper” (v. 21).
vv: For, to begin with, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you;
“Church” here is the people assembled. For Paul the church takes visible shape when they gather.
When you come together, it is not really to eat the Lord’s supper.
This is a shocking sentence. The rite may go on, and it is still contradicted by the way the poor are treated.
Or do you show contempt for the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?
To shame a poor brother or sister is to despise God's Church. For Paul the two offences are one.
ch: The Catechism teaches that “the Eucharist commits us to the poor”, and it quotes St John Chrysostom: you have tasted the Blood of the Lord, yet you do not recognise your brother (CCC 1397). The Eucharist makes the Church (CCC 1396), so that what is done to the unity of the people touches what is done at the altar.

r.h: That they may all be one
set: John 17 is the long prayer that closes Jesus' words at the Last Supper. He has prayed for himself and for his disciples; at v. 20 the prayer widens to those not yet born. The Church's tradition has often called this the priestly prayer of Jesus. The reader of every age is meant to hear his own name in it.
str: vv. 20–21: for all who will believe: that they may be one, so that the world may believe.
vv. 22–23: the glory given, so that they may be completely one.
v. 24: that they may be with him and see his glory.
vv. 25–26: the world does not know you; I have made your name known.
kw: The Greek is neuter: not one person, but one reality, the same word as in “The Father and I are one” (10:30). The unity of the Church has its source in the unity of God.
The revealing brightness of God. In John it is seen above all on the Cross. Jesus gives us a share in it.
Jesus says he has made God's name known and will do so (v. 26). Past and future join in the same work; through the Spirit the Church goes on growing in the knowledge of him.
vv: I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word,
Faith comes through the word of witnesses. Each of us is in this verse.
As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
The measure is impossibly high: the Father and the Son. And unity has a purpose outside itself. Division among Christians makes the gospel hard to believe.
Father, I desire that those also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory,
He ends by asking for what every love asks: to be together. Heaven is described simply as being with him.
so that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.
These are the last words of the prayer: the Father's love for the Son is to live in us. Then Jesus goes out to the garden (18:1).
ch: The Catechism calls this “the prayer of the Hour of Jesus”, the priestly prayer (CCC 2746–2751), and says that the desire to recover the unity of all Christians is Christ's gift and a call of the Spirit (CCC 820). The Second Vatican Council teaches that division among Christians contradicts Christ's will and is a scandal to the world (Unitatis Redintegratio 1). St John Paul II took his encyclical's title from this verse (Ut Unum Sint, 1995). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this chapter, sees our unity as a work of the Spirit and of the Lord's own body received in the Eucharist (in substance).

qa: Does Paul say that “there have to be factions”? Does God want division?

No. The tone of v. 19 is sharp, close to irony, or else it reflects the view that the last days bring testing: such strains show who is genuine. Paul has just told them he does not commend them. Elsewhere he begs them to have no divisions at all (1:10).
study: Paul says humiliating those who have nothing is contempt for the Church. Who could feel out of place in my parish, and what might change that?
Jesus prays that we may be one “so that the world may believe”. What can I do this week to heal one division near me?

lead: Yesterday's plea for unity now takes shape in two pictures. Paul speaks of a body, Jesus of a vine. In each, the life comes from one source and passes through many parts. Neither picture allows anyone to say, “I do not belong”, or “I do not need the others”. Each teaches that Christ is manifested in the people who live from him.

r.h: One body with many members
set: Chapters 12–14 deal with spiritual gifts. Some Corinthians, it seems, prized speaking in tongues and looked down on those without striking gifts. Paul answers with a picture well known in the ancient world. The Roman historian Livy, for one, tells how the body was used as an image of society, to persuade the lower classes to keep their place. Paul turns the image around: in the following verses the weaker members are given greater honour (12:22–24).
str: v. 12: the body is one and has many members.
v. 13: the reason: one Spirit, one baptism.
vv. 14–16: the foot and the ear: no one may opt out.
vv. 17–18: if all were an eye: God arranged the members.
kw: For Paul more than an image of co-operation. In v. 12 he says, “so it is with Christ”, when we expect “with the Church”. The community is Christ's body.
The verb is in the past: a thing already done to us by God, in one Spirit. Unity is received before it is achieved.
An image of water given. The Spirit is the water of the new life.
vv: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.
Paul says “one” and “many” twice, in both directions. Unity does not erase difference, and difference does not break unity.
If the foot would say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
The foot's complaint is a sad one: it envies. Some who are told they have no gift believe it. Paul's answer is simple: you belong because of what God did, not because of how you compare.
But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.
God placed each member where it is. No one in the parish is an accident.
ch: The Catechism teaches that baptism makes us members of the Body of Christ (CCC 1267), and that “the body's unity does not do away with the diversity of its members” (CCC 791; see Lumen Gentium 7). St Augustine told the newly baptised at the Eucharist that they are themselves what they receive: you are the body of Christ, so be what you see (in substance).

r.h: The true vine
set: This speech belongs to Jesus' last discourse at the Supper. The vine was a known image of Israel in the Scriptures: God planted it and looked for fruit (Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21). The word “true” does not reject those texts. It says that God's care for his vine reaches its goal in Jesus, himself a son of Israel, and in those who live in him.
str: vv. 1–3: the vine, the grower and the pruning.
vv. 4–6: abide: the branch without the vine.
vv. 7–8: abiding, asking and bearing fruit.
vv. 9–10: abide in my love, by keeping my commandments.
kw: John's favourite word for discipleship, and it returns again and again here. It means staying, remaining at home with someone.
A play on words in the Greek: the grower “cleans” the branches (v. 2), and the disciples are already “clean” through the word (v. 3). Pruning is the work of his word.
vv: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.
Each “I am” in John tells who Jesus is for us. This one begins a family picture: the Father is at work among the branches.
Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
Good branches get cut. Not every hardship is punishment. A grower never prunes a branch he has given up on.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
Not “little” but “nothing”. And the promise comes first: much fruit.
As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
Now the image gives way to its meaning. The sap in this vine is the love of the Father and the Son.
ch: The Catechism lists the vine among the images of the Church (CCC 755), and it teaches that Jesus shares his own life with us: “Abide in me, and I in you” (CCC 787). It also says that the moral life grows from this union with him (CCC 2074). St Augustine stresses the word: the Lord does not say that without him you can do little, but nothing (in substance). The Eucharistic prayer in the Didache, an early Christian text, gives thanks over the cup for “the holy vine of David”.

qa: Does v. 6 mean God throws people away?

It is a warning, not a verdict on anyone. The branch that withers has cut itself off from the life on offer. The Church teaches that hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033). The reading's weight falls on the invitation, repeated again and again: abide.
study: Paul's foot says, “I do not belong”. Who do I know who feels that way, and how could I help that person find a place?
What has the Father pruned in my life, and what fruit came from it?

lead: Both readings are about those who have been far away being brought near. In Ephesians, Gentiles who were strangers to the promises are brought close by the blood of Christ, and a wall comes down. By the lake, the Risen Lord brings back a friend who had denied him, asking three times the only question that matters. Denha shows a God who does not stay on his side of the wall.

r.h: He is our peace
set: The letter's great theme is the unity of Jews and Gentiles in Christ. (On authorship: many scholars think that a close disciple wrote in Paul's name; others hold it is by Paul himself.) The writer addresses Gentile believers and asks them to remember how far off they once were: not to shame them, but so that they may be grateful. Israel is described here with honour: it has the covenants, the promise, hope and God.
str: vv. 11–12: remember what you were: far from the promises.
v. 13: but now, brought near.
vv. 14–16: Christ our peace: a wall down, one new humanity, reconciliation through the cross.
vv. 17–18: peace proclaimed; access to the Father.
v. 19: no longer strangers.
kw: Behind it is the Hebrew šālôm, wholeness. Here peace is a person: “he is our peace”.

Many scholars think the writer has in mind the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple which kept Gentiles from the inner courts, on pain of death. Josephus describes it and an inscription from it has been found. Others take the word as a picture of division in general.
The word for being admitted into the presence of a king. In one Spirit, both groups can come to the Father (v. 18).
vv: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
“But now” is the hinge. The words “far” and “near” come from Isaiah 57:19, which v. 17 echoes.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
The wall that falls is hostility. No people is being erased: Jews and Gentiles alike are reconciled in Christ.
He has abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances, that he might create in himself one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace,

This does not mean that God's moral law has ended (compare Matthew 5:17; Romans 7:12). It speaks of the Law as a barrier separating Jews from Gentiles. The Greek for “humanity” is anthrōpos: a new human being, Christ with us in him.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
Father, Son, Spirit: the whole Trinity in one short verse. Prayer itself is an act of peace.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes these verses in speaking of the Jewish people: by his cross Christ our Peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The same document says that the Church is nourished from the root of that good olive tree, and that the Jews remain dear to God. The Catechism teaches that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ, “our peace” (CCC 2305). So the Church may never treat any neighbour as beyond the wall.

r.h: Do you love me?
set: John 20 closes with what sounds like an ending (20:30–31). Many scholars therefore think chapter 21 was added soon after, by the evangelist or his circle. The scene is the Sea of Galilee after the Resurrection. The disciples have gone back to fishing, and Jesus has fed them breakfast on the shore, over a charcoal fire. Such a fire appears in only one other place in the New Testament: the fire where Peter stood warming himself when he denied the Lord (18:18).
str: v. 15: the first question and answer: “Feed my lambs.”
v. 16: the second: “Tend my sheep.”
v. 17: the third: Peter is hurt: “Feed my sheep.”
vv. 18–19: the prophecy of Peter's death and the call, “Follow me.”
kw: In vv. 15–16 Jesus asks with agapaō and Peter answers with phileō; at v. 17 Jesus uses Peter's word. Some Fathers and modern writers see a meaning here. Many modern scholars do not, as John often varies words without changing the sense. Either way, the threefold question remains the point.
Two verbs for the shepherd's work: giving food, and guiding and protecting. The flock stays “mine”, as Jesus says: Peter is given care of what belongs to Christ.
vv: Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?
He does not use the name Peter, “rock”, but his birth name. Peter once promised to lay down his life (13:37). Now he makes no boast and appeals only to what Jesus knows.
Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.

Peter's hurt is the beginning of healing. He no longer trusts his own record; he trusts the knowledge of the one he failed. (The POC has lambs and sheep in another order from the NRSV: the meaning is the same.)
But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.
Tertullian already reads this as Peter's crucifixion, which tradition places at Rome under Nero (in substance). The next verse says Peter's death will glorify God.
After this he said to him, “Follow me.”
The first call (Mark 1:17) is given again, after failure. There is no probation, only the same invitation.
ch: The Catechism sees in these words the pastoral office given to Peter, which is continued in his successors (CCC 553; 881); St Augustine says that the threefold confession answers the threefold denial, and that feeding the Lord's flock is the office of love (in substance). All authority in the Church is measured by this question. It is put to a man who has failed, and the office follows his answer of love.

qa: Do “agape” and “philia” mean a higher and lower love here?

That reading is well known and is often preached, and some Fathers noted the change. But many scholars doubt it, since John uses both verbs for the Father's love for the Son (3:35; 5:20) and for other loves too. It is safest to say the point lies in the three questions and in Peter's humility.
study: Whom do I treat as “far off”? What wall in my own heart does Christ want to break down?
Jesus does not ask Peter about his failure, only “do you love me?” How would I answer him today?

lead: Today's readings stand in a storm. A boat full of frightened disciples wakes a sleeping Lord: “do you not care?” Years later a letter bearing Peter's name replies: “he cares for you”, and it tells Christians under pressure to resist, steadfast in faith. The Church in India today honours St Devasahayam, a man of our own soil who lived those words to the end.

r.h: He cares for you
set: The letter is addressed to Christians scattered in Asia Minor (1:1), “exiles” who were suffering slander and hostility for their faith. It names Silvanus as its helper (5:12) and sends greetings from “Babylon”, a known code name for Rome (5:13). Some scholars think Peter wrote it through Silvanus; many think that a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, passing on his teaching. The Church receives it as God's word. The reading comes at the close, in advice to the community and its elders.
str: v. 5: humility toward one another.
vv. 6–7: under God's hand; cast your anxiety on him.
vv. 8–9: stay alert; resist the adversary, with believers throughout the world.
kw: A rare word from kombos, a knot: tie it on like a garment. Some see here the apron of a servant, and a memory of Jesus washing feet, though this cannot be proved.
The word Jesus uses when he tells us not to worry (Matthew 6:25–31 uses the related verb). The phrase in v. 7 echoes Psalm 55:22.
An opponent in a court of law. The devil is called the “accuser” in Revelation 12:10, and is real but not almighty: he can be resisted.
vv: for “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
The quotation is from the Greek of Proverbs 3:34, also quoted in James 4:6. Humility is the way grace enters.
Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you.
The verb is a strong one, used for throwing cloaks onto the colt (Luke 19:35). Anxiety is thrown, not kept. In the POC these words stand with v. 6.
Like a roaring lion your adversary the devil prowls around, looking for someone to devour.
An image with an edge in the Roman world, where Christians came to be thrown to beasts. The advice is alertness, not panic.
Resist him, steadfast in your faith, for you know that your brothers and sisters in all the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.
No one suffers for Christ alone. To know that is already a form of strength.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 7 when it speaks of God's providence: Christ invites us to filial trust in the Father, and St Peter repeats it (CCC 322). It teaches too that the devil's power is not infinite, and that he cannot prevent the building up of God's reign (CCC 395). Both are needed for a sane Christian life: trust without naivety, alertness without fear.

r.h: Even the wind and the sea obey him
set: Mark has spent the day with Jesus teaching parables from a boat (4:1). At evening they cross to the other side, the Gentile side of the lake (5:1). The Sea of Galilee is well known for sudden storms. For the Bible, however, the sea is more than weather. It stands for chaos, which only God can master (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:29). The story also recalls Jonah asleep in a ship during a storm (Jonah 1:4–6). Here it is the Lord himself who sleeps.
str: vv. 35–36: the crossing.
v. 37: the storm.
v. 38: Jesus is asleep, and the disciples' reproach.
v. 39: the rebuke and the calm.
vv. 40–41: two questions: his, and theirs.
kw: The same verb as when Jesus silences an unclean spirit (1:25). The storm is treated as an enemy.
Literally “be muzzled”. Mark also uses this verb at 1:25, so the same voice speaks to the demon and to the sea.
they were filled with great awe
Literally “they feared a great fear”, the phrase used of Jonah's sailors (Jonah 1:10, 16). They are less afraid of the storm now than of who is in the boat.
vv: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”
Only Mark mentions the cushion, and only Mark has this rude question. In the sleep of Jesus we see his true humanity, and in the question our own prayers.
He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
Note the contrast with “a great windstorm” (v. 37): the Greek also speaks here of a great calm. What God alone can do in the Psalms, Jesus does with a word.
He said to them, “Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?”
He calms the sea first and then speaks to them. The real storm is the fear inside.
Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
This is the question of Mark's Gospel, which the reader must answer. It is the question of Denha.
ch: Tertullian saw in this little boat a picture of the Church, tossed by the waves of the world while the Lord seems patiently to sleep, until the prayers of the saints rouse him (in substance). St Augustine told his people that when the storm rises in the heart, Christ is asleep there, because faith has gone to sleep: wake him, and all is quiet (in substance). The Church has never promised calm weather, but rather that he is in the boat.

qa: Why did Jesus sleep, if he knew the storm was coming?

Mark gives no reason. After a long day of teaching he may simply have been tired. It is a picture of real humanity and of complete trust in the Father. The Fathers saw both natures in this scene: as man he sleeps; as God he commands the sea.
rite: St Devasahayam was born Neelakanta Pillai and served as an official in the kingdom of Travancore. Baptised in 1745, he took the name Lazarus, Devasahayam in Tamil and Malayalam, “God is my help”. He treated all people as equals, refusing to treat anyone as untouchable. He was arrested, held in chains for nearly three years, and shot at Aralvaimozhy in 1752. Pope Francis canonised him on 15 May 2022, the first Indian layman to be canonised. His tomb is at Kottar. The Church honours his faith without any bitterness, and she prays today for those who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who have wronged them.
study: Peter says, “Cast all your anxiety on him.” What am I carrying this week that I need to throw onto the Lord?
St Devasahayam's faith changed how he treated people. What in my way of treating others does my baptism need to change?

lead: On the Fridays of Denha the Church remembers those who made Christ known, and today she remembers Peter and Paul. The four readings move from a closed door to an open Church. Elisha shuts the door and prays, and a dead child wakes. Peter puts everyone out, kneels, prays and says, “Tabitha, get up.” Paul counts what the Gospel has cost his body. At Caesarea Philippi Simon confesses who Jesus is and receives a new name and the keys. The calendar also joins John 21:15–19 to the Gospel, where the same Peter is asked three times about his love. The key words of the day are prayer, weakness and rock: the apostles' strength is never their own.

r.h: Elisha shuts the door and prays
set: Elisha worked in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC. The woman of Shunem, a village in the valley of Jezreel, had built him a small room on her roof, and he had promised her a son (4:8–17). Now the boy has died on her lap (4:20). She has laid him on the prophet's bed and ridden to Mount Carmel to find Elisha, refusing to leave him. Gehazi, the servant, has gone ahead and laid the prophet's staff on the child, with no result (4:31).
str: v. 32: Elisha finds the child dead on the bed.
v. 33: he closes the door and prays.
vv. 34–35: he lies on the child twice; the flesh grows warm, the child sneezes and opens his eyes.
vv. 36–37: the mother is called and receives her son.
kw: The story's turning point is this one verb. The staff has failed, and the prophet has no power of his own to use. Everything that follows comes after prayer.
The Hebrew keeps calling him the child, right up to the moment he is returned. He is not an example or a sign to the narrator. He is someone's little boy.
Seven is the Bible's number of fullness. The small, homely detail of the sneeze shows breath coming back, for breath is what God gave the first man (Genesis 2:7).
vv: So he went in and closed the door on the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.
Elijah did much the same for the widow's son at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:19–22). Jesus will one day tell his disciples to shut the door and pray (Matthew 6:6). The miracle takes place in hiddenness.
and while he lay bent over him, the flesh of the child became warm.
Mouth on mouth, eyes on eyes, hands on hands: the prophet gives his whole self to the child. The cure comes slowly and he does not stop at the first sign of it.
When she came to him, he said, “Take your son.”
Elijah, Elisha and Jesus all give a raised child back to the one who mourns (1 Kings 17:23; Luke 7:15). Nain, where Jesus raised the widow's son, lies close to Shunem on the same hill.
ch: Some early Christian writers saw in the prophet stretching himself over the small body a picture of the Son of God, who made himself small to give us life (in substance). The Catechism teaches that such raisings were real miracles and yet a return to ordinary earthly life, since those raised would die again; Christ's own Resurrection is of another order (CCC 646).

r.h: Tabitha, get up
set: After the conversion of Saul, Luke turns back to Peter, who is travelling among the believers on the coastal plain. At Lydda he has healed Aeneas (9:32–35). Joppa, the old port that is now Jaffa, lies a short journey away. These stories lead to the house of Simon the tanner (9:43) and on to Cornelius, the first Gentile household (Acts 10). The Church is about to grow beyond anything Peter had imagined.
str: vv. 36–37: Tabitha, her good works and her death.
vv. 38–39: Peter is called; the widows show him the clothes she made.
v. 40: he puts them out, kneels, prays and speaks.
vv. 41–42: she is restored to the community, and many believe.
kw: This feminine form of the word for disciple occurs only here in the New Testament. Luke gives Tabitha the title he gives to all who follow Jesus.
The Aramaic and the Greek names both mean gazelle. Luke gives both, the name used by Aramaic speakers and the name used by Greek speakers.
The word means mercy put into practice. The English word “alms” comes from it. Tabitha's charity has a very practical form: she sewed clothes for widows, who in that society had little protection.
vv: All the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
The best funeral sermon in the New Testament is preached without words, by women holding up what she had sewn. The early Church's care of widows is already seen in Acts 6:1.
Peter put all of them outside, and then he knelt down and prayed. He turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.”

Peter has seen this before. Jesus put the mourners out of the house of Jairus and said, Talitha cum (Mark 5:40–41). Peter copies the Master, with one difference: he kneels first, because the power is not his own.
This became known throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
They believed in the Lord, and not in Peter. The sign points away from the one who performs it.
ch: The Catechism lists clothing the naked among the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447), and Tabitha is one of its first saints in practice. Her story also shows how the apostles' ministry continues the ministry of Jesus: the same gesture, the same word, and the same Lord at work through them (CCC 1506).

r.h: The things that show my weakness
set: Paul is defending his work against rival preachers in Corinth, whom he calls with irony “super-apostles” (11:5). They seem to have boasted of their eloquence, their descent and their visions. Paul finds this foolish, and so he plays the fool on purpose: if there must be boasting, let him boast. This “fool's speech” runs from 11:1 to 12:13. He then turns the usual list of achievements upside down, for what he lists is what he has suffered.
str: vv. 21b–23a: his credentials: Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham, minister of Christ.
vv. 23b–27: his catalogue of labours and dangers.
vv. 28–29: the daily care for the churches.
vv. 30–31: the conclusion: he will boast of his weakness, and God knows that he does not lie.
kw: One of Paul's favourite words in this letter. A proper boast has its ground in the Lord (10:17). Here it has its ground in what looks like failure.
The same word Jesus uses for the worries that choke the word (Mark 4:19). In Paul it has been turned into love: the worry of a father for all his children.
It comes back again and again in these chapters, and it leads to the Lord's answer in 12:9: “my power is made perfect in weakness”.
vv: Five times I have received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one.

Deuteronomy 25:3 limits such a punishment to forty, and later Jewish law stopped at thirty-nine so as not to break the limit. Paul is writing as a Jew who still comes under the discipline of his own people, and he accuses no one here. He is listing his sufferings.
Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I received a stoning. Three times I was shipwrecked; for a night and a day I was adrift at sea;

Beating with rods was a Roman punishment (Acts 16:22–23); the stoning was at Lystra (Acts 14:19). The famous shipwreck of Acts 27 came later and is not among these three. Acts, then, tells only part of the story.
And, besides other things, I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches.
After the rods and the sea, this comes as the heaviest burden. Every pastor and every parent knows what he means.
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
ch: St John Chrysostom, who loved Paul deeply, wrote seven homilies in his praise. He marvels that one man in a mortal body could bear so much, with joy (in substance). St Clement of Rome, writing near the end of the first century, already holds up Peter and Paul together as examples of endurance, and speaks of Paul's chains and his stoning (1 Clement 5). The Catechism recalls the word Paul heard in his weakness, “My grace is sufficient for you” (CCC 1508).

r.h: You are Peter
set: Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, by a source of the Jordan, in Gentile territory. Herod's son Philip had rebuilt the town and named it in honour of the emperor. There was an old shrine to the god Pan there. In a place full of other claims to divinity, Jesus asks who he is. This is the turning point of Matthew's story, for straight after it he begins to speak of the Cross (16:21).
str: vv. 13–14: “Who do people say?” The answers are respectful and too small.
v. 15: “But who do you say?”
v. 16: Peter's confession.
v. 17: this was revealed by the Father.
vv. 18–19: the name, the Church, the keys.
kw: The Greek plays on the words. In Aramaic, which Jesus spoke, the name is Kepha (John 1:42), and many scholars think the same word stood in both places. “Rock” was not a common personal name at that time.
Among the Gospels only Matthew uses this word (here and in 18:17). In the Greek Old Testament it translates the assembly of God's people. “My” Church: Jesus gathers God's people around himself.
Isaiah 22:22 gives the image: Eliakim receives the key of the house of David, and what he opens no one shuts. The keys are the steward's authority in the king's house. The steward is not the king.
vv: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
Knowing what others say is not enough. The “you” is plural, and Peter answers for the group, but every believer has to give this answer in person.
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
This is a moment of Denha, the showing forth of the Lord. Faith is first of all a gift. Peter did not reason his way there; he received it.
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Hades is the place of the dead, and its “gates” are the power of death. The Church, built by Christ, will not be swallowed by death.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.
“Binding and loosing” was a way of speaking about forbidding and permitting, and also about excluding and restoring. In 18:18 the same power is given to the disciples together.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on the rock of the faith confessed by Peter, Christ built his Church (CCC 424), and that Peter's mission to keep this faith from failing and to strengthen his brothers rests on this promise (CCC 552–553). The office given to Peter is permanent and continues with the Pope, the head of the college of bishops (CCC 881–882; Lumen Gentium 22). St Leo the Great, preaching on the anniversary of his own election, says that Peter's firmness still lives on in the Church of Rome, and that the strength is Christ's (in substance).

qa: Is the rock Peter himself, or Peter's faith?

The Fathers say both, and St Augustine notes in his Retractations that either reading can be held. The Catechism keeps them together: the Church is built on the faith Peter confessed (CCC 424), and Christ made Simon himself the rock of his Church (CCC 881). The two do not compete, because Peter is rock only as the one who confesses Christ.
Did Tabitha and the Shunammite's son live for ever?
No. They returned to ordinary life and died later. Such signs announce the Resurrection of Christ, but his is different: he does not return to this life, he passes beyond death (CCC 646).
Why does Paul boast at all, after saying that boasting is foolish?
He is using the rivals' own method to show that it is empty. His list of glories is a list of beatings. The irony teaches that an apostle is measured by love and the Cross, and not by success.
rite: In the East Syriac year, the Fridays of Denha keep the memory of those who made the Lord known, and this second Friday belongs to Peter and Paul. As Thomas Christians we honour the Apostle who brought the faith to our land, and in today's Gospel we honour the rock on whom the whole Church stands. The Syro-Malabar Church lives its own East Syriac heritage in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. At the Holy Qurbana today we may pray for the Holy Father and for our Major Archbishop and bishops, that they may be like Peter in confession and like Paul in love for all the churches.
study: “But who do you say that I am?” How would I answer in my own words, without using a catechism's words?
Tabitha's witness was clothing she made for widows. What in my life would people hold up to show the love of Christ?
Paul says he is under daily pressure for all the churches. Whose cares do I carry in prayer each day?
Elisha and Peter both pray before they act. How often do I pray first when someone comes to me with a need?

lead: Both readings are about a word that does something. Paul traces the chain by which faith reaches a person: someone is sent, someone proclaims, someone hears, someone believes and calls on the Lord. In Capernaum people hear that word for the first time from the mouth of Jesus, and even an unclean spirit has to obey it. In this season of Denha, the Lord is shown forth by what he says.

r.h: Faith comes from what is heard
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long and painful reflection on his own people: how can the Gospel be for all, when many in Israel have not received it? He wrote about their “zeal for God” with love (10:1–2). This reading stands in the middle of that argument. It ends with questions that are carried on into chapter 11, where Paul insists that God has not rejected his people (11:1) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).
str: vv. 10–13: believing and confessing; no distinction; all who call will be saved.
vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent.
vv. 16–17: faith comes from hearing.
vv. 18–20: the word has gone out; Moses and Isaiah on those who were not seeking.
kw: To say the same thing, to declare openly. What the heart believes, the mouth says aloud: “Jesus is Lord” (10:9). Faith is more than private opinion.
The same Greek word means both the act of hearing and the message heard. Faith begins by receiving something from outside ourselves.
The work of a herald, who announces the words of another. The herald does not make up the message, and he has to be sent.
vv: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all and is generous to all who call on him.
Paul has used the same phrase about sin (3:22–23). The levelling is complete: all need mercy, and it is offered to all.
And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
He quotes Isaiah 52:7, the runner bringing news of God's victory to Jerusalem. Feet, usually dusty and overlooked, are here called beautiful because they have made the journey.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
This is the verse's plain teaching: faith has a history. Somebody told us. Each of us stands at the end of a long chain of people who were sent and who spoke.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to explain why the Church has an ordained ministry: no one can give himself the mandate to preach the Gospel, for he must be sent (CCC 875). It also teaches that the Church's mission flows from God's will that all be saved (CCC 851), and that God's covenant with the Jewish people has not been revoked (CCC 839).

r.h: A new teaching, with authority
set: This is the first public act of Jesus in Mark's Gospel, straight after the call of the four fishermen (1:16–20). Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee and became his home base (2:1). The synagogue was the place where the community met on the sabbath to hear the Law and the Prophets, and a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.
str: vv. 21–22: he teaches, and they are astounded.
vv. 23–24: the unclean spirit cries out.
vv. 25–26: the rebuke and the expulsion.
vv. 27–28: amazement, and the news spreads.
kw: The word means power that is rightly one's own. A scribe taught by handing on what the teachers before him had said, which was honest and valuable work. Jesus speaks in his own name.
The spirit knows what the crowd does not yet know. Peter uses the same title in John 6:69, but there as a confession of faith. Here it is a cry of fear (compare James 2:19).
Literally “be muzzled”, the word used for an ox in 1 Corinthians 9:9. Jesus does not accept testimony from this source.
vv: They were astounded at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Mark does not yet tell us what he taught. The first thing we learn about the word of Jesus is its effect.
and he cried out, “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.”
The “us” is telling. Evil recognizes what this Teacher's coming means. The first to name Jesus in public in this Gospel is his enemy.
But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!”
There is no ritual here and no long formula. Only a word. The man himself is not condemned; he is set loose.
He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.
The crowd joins teaching and exorcism: the word that instructs is the same word that releases people. The question “What is this?” will drive the rest of Mark's Gospel.
ch: The Catechism notes that the people were struck by Jesus teaching not as their scribes did (CCC 581), and that his expulsions of demons announce the coming of the Kingdom, the defeat of “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church continues this work, in the name of Jesus and by his authority, in the prayers of baptism (CCC 1673).

qa: Does “not as the scribes” mean that Jesus looked down on the teachers of Israel?

No. Mark is contrasting two ways of teaching, not judging a whole class of people. Jesus praises a scribe in Mark 12:34 and Matthew speaks of scribes trained for the Kingdom (13:52). The difference lies in who is speaking: the one whose own word has authority.
study: Who first told me about Christ? Have I ever thanked God for that person, or thanked that person?
Paul asks how anyone can hear without someone to proclaim. Is there someone who will hear about Christ only if they hear it from me?

lead: This Sunday asks who carries whom. In the desert Moses cries that the people are too heavy for him, and God shares his spirit with seventy elders. In Isaiah the gods of Babylon are loaded onto tired animals, while the Lord says to his people: “I have made, and I will bear.” Hebrews points to the rest God still holds open “today”. And in the Gospel John sees the Lamb of God, who takes away the weight no one else could lift. The key words are burden, rest and Lamb. Tomorrow the Three Days' Fast begins, and these readings tell us in whose strength we keep it.

r.h: Moses and the burden of the people
set: Israel has left Sinai and is in the wilderness. The people are weeping for the food of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic (11:4–6). God has been angry, and now Moses reaches breaking point. This is one of the rawest prayers in the Bible. God answers it in two ways: there will be help for Moses, and there will be meat for the people, in such quantity that it becomes a judgment (11:31–34).
str: vv. 11–15: Moses' complaint: why me? Am I their mother? Where shall I find meat? Kill me if this goes on.
vv. 16–17: God's answer to Moses: seventy elders will share the spirit and the burden.
vv. 18–20: God's answer to the people: meat for a month, until it disgusts them.
kw: From the verb “to lift, to carry”. It frames this passage (vv. 11 and 17). The word for what Moses cannot bear returns in the promise that others will bear it with him.

One who cares for a small child. Moses uses the language of conception, birth and nursing (v. 12): these are God's people, and God should be the parent. It is a bold prayer, and God does not rebuke it.
The spirit that rests on Moses is not reduced when it is shared. It is God's, not Moses' own, and God gives it as he wills.
vv: I am not able to carry all this people alone, for they are too heavy for me.
Scripture preserves this sentence for every parent, priest and carer who has felt it. The honest confession that one cannot go on is already a prayer.
If this is the way you are going to treat me, put me to death at once
Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (Jonah 4:3) will pray much the same. God does not take any of them at their word. He treats such a prayer as a cry of pain.
and I will take some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people along with you so that you will not bear it all by yourself.
God's answer does not remove the people. It spreads the load. Leadership among God's people is shared from the beginning, and it rests on the Spirit and not on ability alone.
because you have rejected the Lord who is among you
The fault named here is not hunger. It is the forgetting that the Lord is in their midst.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church's liturgy sees in the institution of the seventy elders, together with the priesthood of Aaron and the service of the Levites, a prefiguring of the ordained ministry of the New Covenant (CCC 1541). Jesus too sends out seventy, or seventy-two, as Luke's manuscripts differ (Luke 10:1). The Church also learns from Moses that intercession can be honest before God (CCC 2574–2577).

r.h: I will carry and will save
set: These chapters speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon, in the years when Cyrus of Persia was rising (he is named in 45:1) and before Babylon fell in 539 BC. Bel, a title of Marduk, was the chief god of Babylon, and Nebo (Nabu) was his son. At the New Year feast their statues were carried in great processions, and the names of kings such as Nebuchadnezzar contain the name of Nebo. For a defeated people the sight must have been overwhelming.
str: 45:18–19: the Creator made the earth to be lived in, and has spoken openly.
45:20–21: an appeal to the survivors of the nations; idols cannot save.
45:22–25: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!”
46:1–2: Bel and Nebo collapse on the backs of tired animals.
46:3–4: the Lord has carried Israel from the womb and will carry them into old age.
kw: The word used in Genesis 1:2 for the formless earth. God did not create the world to be a chaos (45:18). Exiles who felt that everything had fallen apart are told what the world is for.
a righteous God and a Savior
Monotheism here is not a cold claim about numbers. “There is no other” means that there is no other who saves. Môšîa‘ comes from the same root as the name of Jesus.
Both verbs appear in 46:4. The same root that names the idols as “things you carry” in 46:1 describes God carrying his people in 46:3–4. The chapter is built on this contrast.
vv: he did not create it a chaos, he formed it to be inhabited!
Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.
Astonishing words to be spoken to a captive people. The God of the exiles offers salvation to the whole world, including their captors.
To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.
Paul applies these words to Jesus in Philippians 2:10–11, and also in Romans 14:11. What the Lord says of himself here, the Church says of Christ.
Bel bows down, Nebo stoops, their idols are on beasts and cattle; these things you carry are loaded as burdens on weary animals.
This is a prophet's picture, not a record of events: Cyrus in fact honoured Marduk when he took Babylon. The point is what idols are: they have to be carried, and they cannot carry anyone.
even to your old age I am he, even when you turn gray I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.
In Hebrew the “I” is repeated emphatically. It is a promise for the end of life as much as for its beginning, and God speaks here like a mother with a child (compare 49:15).
ch: The Catechism quotes Isaiah 45:22–24 as a witness to Israel's faith in the one God, and notes how Paul's hymn in Philippians applies the words to Jesus (CCC 201). It also teaches that God's tenderness can be expressed in the image of motherhood, as well as fatherhood (CCC 239).

r.h: A sabbath rest still remains
set: Hebrews is a sermon to tired Christians, probably of Jewish background, whose author is not named. In 3:7–11 the preacher has quoted Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”, with its warning about the desert generation who did not enter the land. He now asks what God's “rest” really is. His method is to bring together Psalm 95:11 and Genesis 2:2.
str: vv. 1–2: the promise is still open; hearing without faith did not help them.
vv. 3–5: God's rest began at creation, and the psalm still speaks of it.
vv. 6–7: so God sets another day: “today”.
vv. 8–10: Joshua did not give the final rest; a sabbath rest remains.
kw: The word Psalm 95 uses in its Greek form. In the desert it meant the land; in Hebrews it means sharing God's own rest.
In the New Testament the word occurs only in 4:9. It suggests a keeping of the sabbath, a celebration, and not only a stopping of work.
The preacher's key word. David said “today” long after Joshua, and so the promise did not end with the entry into the land. Every “today” in which the word is heard is the same open door.
vv: For indeed the good news came to us just as to them; but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ here. One group speaks of people not united with those who listened (followed by the NRSV), another of a message not united with faith in the hearers. The Malayalam POC gives the plain sense: they did not believe. Either way, the word needs faith to do its work.
And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.
Genesis 2:2. God's rest is not tiredness but the completion and joy of his work, and this is what he wants to share.
For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not speak later about another day.
In Greek, Joshua's name is Iēsous, the same as Jesus. The preacher's first hearers would have caught this: the first Joshua led into the land, and the second leads into God's rest.
So then, a sabbath rest still remains for the people of God;
ch: The Catechism names “entering into God's rest” (Hebrews 4:7–11) among the Scripture's images of the blessed life (CCC 1720). It teaches that Christ's Sunday fulfils the spiritual truth of the sabbath and announces our eternal rest (CCC 2175). St Augustine begins his Confessions by telling God that our heart is restless until it rests in him, and he closes the City of God with the same vision of the eternal sabbath (in substance).

r.h: Here is the Lamb of God
set: John's Gospel does not narrate the baptism of Jesus directly. It gives us the witness of the Baptist, who says what he saw. The passage belongs to the opening week of the Gospel, marked by “the next day” (1:29, 35, 43). John has already told the priests and Levites that he is not the Messiah (1:19–27). Now the Baptist points away from himself to the one coming toward him, and that one is the centre of Denha.
str: v. 29: “Here is the Lamb of God.”
vv. 30–31: the one who ranks ahead of him, and why John baptized.
vv. 32–33: the sign: the Spirit descending and remaining.
v. 34: John's testimony.
kw: The title gathers several strands: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the lamb God provides (Genesis 22:8), and the Servant led like a lamb (Isaiah 53:7). Later this Gospel places the death of Jesus on the day of Preparation for the Passover (John 19:14) and applies to him the rule for the Passover lamb (19:36).
The Greek verb means both to lift up and to carry away. Both meanings fit: he takes the weight upon himself and removes it. “Sin” is singular: the whole power of sin in the world.
A favourite word of John. The Spirit does not merely touch Jesus; the Spirit stays. Later the disciples ask him where he stays (1:38), and he invites them to remain in him (15:4).
vv: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and declared, “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!
Moses could not carry the people. The Lamb carries what no one could: not only the people's complaints, but the sin of the whole world.
I myself did not know him; but I came baptizing with water for this reason, that he might be revealed to Israel.
The purpose of John's whole ministry is Denha: that he might be revealed. The prophet says twice that he did not know him, and that knowledge came as a gift.
I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.
The dove may recall the Spirit over the waters of creation (Genesis 1:2), or Noah's dove after the flood. John does not explain it.
And I myself have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God.

A note on the text. Most manuscripts read “the Son of God”, which the NRSV and the POC follow. Some ancient witnesses read “God's chosen one”. Both titles fit what the Father says at the baptism in the other Gospels.
ch: The Catechism says that John's title reveals that Jesus is at once the Suffering Servant who silently allows himself to be led to the slaughter and the Paschal Lamb, the symbol of Israel's redemption (CCC 608), and that the baptism of Jesus is the beginning of his mission as God's suffering Servant (CCC 536). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this verse, says that one Lamb died for all, in order to gain the whole flock for God the Father (in substance).

qa: Is it wrong to complain to God as Moses does?

No. The Psalms and the prophets are full of such prayers, and God answers Moses with help and without a rebuke. What the people did is different: they complained against God with their backs to him, while Moses complains to God with his face toward him (compare CCC 2574–2577).
Did the Jews lose God's rest, according to Hebrews?

No. The warning is about one generation in the desert, and it is addressed to the Christian hearers: “let us take care” (4:1). The preacher sees the same danger in the Church. The Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God has never revoked (CCC 121, 839).
If Jesus takes away the sin of the world, why is there still sin?

The Lamb's sacrifice is complete, and its power reaches every sinner. But it does not force anyone. We receive it through faith, baptism and repentance, and the struggle goes on in us until the end (CCC 1426, 1264). This is why we fast and confess.
rite: Tomorrow the Three Days' Fast begins, kept in the East Syriac tradition from the sixth century, when a plague in Persia ended after the people fasted and prayed. In Kerala Moonnu Nombu is especially loved at Kuravilangad, with its ship procession recalling Jonah's voyage. On this Sunday of Denha, the Holy Qurbana sets the fast in the right light. We do not fast in order to carry ourselves by our own strength. We fast to hand our burden to the Lamb, who carries it. Priests and catechists may remind families to keep the fast in a form suited to children and the elderly, following their own diocese's guidance. The Church Unity Octave also begins tomorrow.
study: Moses says, “I am not able to carry all this people alone.” Who in my life is carrying too much, and how could I share the load?
What am I carrying around that cannot carry me? What are my “Bel and Nebo”?
Isaiah 46:4 promises God's care to those who are growing old. How does this change the way I see old age, my own or others'?
What do I want to hand over to the Lamb of God during these three days of fasting?

lead: Today the Three Days' Fast begins, and the first voice we hear is a people crying to God from the ruins: “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down”. Habakkuk answers with trust when everything has failed: “yet I will rejoice in the Lord”. The First Letter to Timothy turns the fast outward, into prayer for everyone, because God “desires everyone to be saved”. Then Jesus tells us the condition of all mercy: a forgiven servant must forgive. So the fast's first lesson is this: we ask for mercy, we pray for all, and we let go of what others owe us.

r.h: O that you would tear open the heavens
set: Isaiah 63:7–64:12 is a long prayer of lament. Many scholars place these last chapters of Isaiah (56–66) after the return from exile, when Jerusalem was still poor and the Temple lay in ruins or had only just begun to rise; the verses after our reading speak of the “holy and beautiful house” burned by fire (64:11). In the Hebrew Bible the numbering differs by one verse, for 64:1 here is 63:19 there.
str: vv. 1–3: the cry: come down as at Sinai.
vv. 4–5a: no other God acts for those who wait for him.
vv. 5b–7: confession: we have sinned, we fade like a leaf.
vv. 8–9: “Yet, O Lord, you are our Father”: the appeal to the potter.
kw: A violent verb, used for tearing clothes in grief. Mark's Gospel uses a similarly strong Greek word when the heavens are torn apart at the baptism of Jesus (Mark 1:10). For the Church in Denha, that is the answer to this prayer.
This name for God is rare in the Old Testament, and it comes more than once in this prayer (63:16; 64:8). When the people have nothing else left to plead, they plead the relationship.
One who shapes clay with his hands, as God shapes the man in Genesis 2:7. The clay cannot save itself, but it does belong to the potter's hand.
vv: O that you would tear open the heavens and come down, so that the mountains would quake at your presence
The people recall Sinai and beg for it to happen again. This is the longing of the fast: not for a change in our circumstances first, but for God's own coming.
But you were angry, and we sinned; because you hid yourself we transgressed.
The Hebrew of this verse is notoriously difficult, and translations differ: the POC reads differently here. The prayer struggles honestly with how God's silence and our sin are bound up together.
We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.
Yet, O Lord, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.
“Yet” is the hinge of the whole prayer. Nothing has changed in the facts. What has changed is whom the people are looking at.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Israel called God “Father” as Creator of the world and as the one who made the covenant with his people (CCC 238). True conversion begins as a turning of the heart, and it is God who gives us the strength to begin anew (CCC 1431–1432). St Paul takes up the language of v. 4 when he speaks of what “no eye has seen” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

r.h: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord
set: Habakkuk is usually dated in the late seventh century BC, when Babylon was rising. In chapter 1 he argues with God about injustice, and in 2:4 he receives the great word, “the righteous live by their faith”. Chapter 3 is a psalm, with its own title and musical notes (3:1, 19). It pictures God coming as a warrior to save his people, as at the Exodus.
str: vv. 13–15: God comes to save: his enemies are crushed and the sea is trampled.
v. 16: the prophet trembles and waits quietly.
vv. 17–19a: his song of trust when nothing is left.
kw: “Your anointed” in v. 13 stands alongside “your people”. It probably means the king, or the people as a whole. The Church hears in the word the promise that is fulfilled in Christ.
It occurs in vv. 13 and 18, and it is related to the name of Jesus. The God of the battles is “the God of my salvation” for one person in the end.
“God, the Lord, is my strength.” The Hebrew word also means might or army. The prophet has no army and no harvest. God himself is his force.
vv: Though the fig tree does not blossom, and no fruit is on the vines; though the produce of the olive fails, and the fields yield no food; though the flock is cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
Every source of food in an ancient farm is named, and every one has failed. This is what it would be like when a plague or an invasion leaves nothing.
yet I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in the God of my salvation.
Joy here is not a feeling caused by events. It is a decision about God. Mary's song in Luke 1:47 has a similar ring.
God, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the feet of a deer, and makes me tread upon the heights.
The image also appears in Psalm 18:33. The man who was trembling (3:16) is now walking on the heights, though nothing around him has changed.
ch: St Augustine, in the City of God (18.32), reads this song as a prophecy of Christ (in substance). The Catechism says that hope keeps us from discouragement and sustains us in times of abandonment (CCC 1818), and that it gives joy even under trial (CCC 1820).

r.h: Prayers for everyone
set: The letter gives instructions for Church life. Its tradition names Paul as author; many scholars today think that it comes from a disciple writing in his name, while others keep to Pauline authorship. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case. Christians were a small minority under pagan rulers, and the “kings” they are told to pray for could also be those who persecuted them.
str: vv. 1–2: pray for everyone, including rulers.
vv. 3–4: God wants all to be saved.
vv. 5–6: one God, one mediator, a ransom for all.
v. 7: Paul's mission to the Gentiles.
kw: Four words for prayer, gathered together. The list covers need, worship, pleading for others and gratitude, and gives us the shape of the Church's common prayer.
One who stands between two parties to reconcile them. Christ can do this because he is God and “himself human”.
The price of setting captives at liberty. The word occurs only here in the New Testament, and it recalls Mark 10:45.
vv: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for everyone,
“For everyone” is repeated in this passage: for everyone, everyone saved, a ransom for all. No one is outside the Church's prayer.
who desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
This is one of the clearest verses about God's will for humanity. The fast of the Ninevites, a people outside Israel, shows the same will.
For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human,
The word “human” is emphasized. He mediates from our side of the gap, as one of us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the “one mediator” (CCC 618), that the Church's mission comes from God's will that all be saved (CCC 851), and that Christian intercession has no boundaries, and reaches even those who do us harm (CCC 2635–2636). The Second Vatican Council explains that Mary's and the saints' prayer does not take away from Christ's one mediation: it depends on it and shows its power (Lumen Gentium 60).

r.h: Forgive from your heart
set: Matthew 18 is the discourse on life in the Church. Peter has just asked how many times he must forgive: as many as seven times? Jesus answers, “seventy-seven times” (18:21–22). He then tells this parable, found only in Matthew, so that Peter may understand why.
str: vv. 23–27: the first account: an impossible debt is cancelled.
vv. 28–30: the second account: a small debt is not.
vv. 31–34: the king hears and judges.
v. 35: the lesson.
kw: A talent was worth about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was a day's wage. The sum is meant to be absurd: ten thousand was the largest number in Greek counting, and the talent the largest unit of money. No servant could ever pay it.

Literally moved in the bowels, the seat of compassion. The same verb is used of Jesus himself (Matthew 9:36; 14:14). The king gives far more than the slave asked for: he asked for time, and he receives release.
The parable's final words. Forgiveness is not a formula or a pretence that nothing has happened.
vv: And out of pity for him, the lord of that slave released him and forgave him the debt.
But that same slave, as he went out, came upon one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii;

A hundred denarii is about three months' wages, a real debt and not a small matter for a poor man. Compared with the first, it is almost nothing. His words are the same words he used before the king (vv. 26 and 29), and that is the point.
Should you not have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?
Here is the whole parable in one question. The “as” is the same as in the Lord's Prayer: “as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).
So my heavenly Father will also do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother or sister from your heart.
This is a parable's strong warning, and not a description of God's temperament. It says that a heart closed to a brother is closed to the mercy it needs.
ch: The Catechism says that this parable crowns the Lord's teaching on the communion of the Church, and that it is “in the depths of the heart” that everything is bound and loosed (CCC 2843). It adds that it is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offence, but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion (CCC 2843). God's mercy cannot reach a heart that has hardened itself against others (CCC 2840).

qa: Why do we fast on these three days?

The Three Days' Fast is the Church's way of doing what the people of Nineveh did: all together, in sackcloth of the heart, turning from evil and asking for mercy. In the East Syriac tradition it comes from a plague in Persia in the sixth century that ended after the people fasted and prayed. It is a preparation for the Great Fast and a share in the Church's penance (CCC 1438).
If only Christ is mediator, why do we ask the saints to pray for us?

Because the one mediation of Christ does not shut out our sharing in it. Asking a saint to pray is like asking a friend, as Paul asks the churches to pray for him (Romans 15:30). All intercession flows from Christ and leads back to him (Lumen Gentium 60, 62; CCC 970).
Must I forgive someone who keeps hurting me, and stay in harm's way?

Forgiving does not mean approving what was done, nor does it remove the need for justice or for protection. A person may and sometimes must leave danger, and still pray for the one who did the harm. Forgiveness is a work of grace that often takes time. A good priest or counsellor can help.
rite: Moonnu Nombu, the Rogation of the Ninevites, is one of the most treasured fasts of the Thomas Christians. Our churches fill for it, and Kuravilangad draws great crowds of pilgrims. Keep it as the Church asks and according to your own diocese's norms, and let it go together with prayer and works of mercy. Today is also the first day of the Church Unity Octave.
