The word about prayer “for everyone” applies very directly: we pray for our Christian brothers and sisters of other Churches, for the leaders of nations, and for those who suffer in many lands and for those who have wronged them.
study: Isaiah's people pray “Yet, O Lord, you are our Father” in the middle of ruins. Where do I need to say that “yet” today?
List the things in my life that have failed, in the manner of Habakkuk 3:17. Can I pray verse 18 after them?
Who is the person I find it hardest to include in “everyone”? Can I pray for them by name in this fast?
Is there a “hundred denarii” that I am still demanding from someone? What would it mean to release it?

lead: On the second day of the fast the readings look honestly at sin and at the way back. Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah, where they fast, say “We have sinned”, and find that a man's prayer stands between them and their fear. Isaiah says why God has seemed deaf: the fault is not in his ear, but in the barriers we have built. Paul then tells us what penance is for: to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, and to be made new from within. Jesus ends the day with two men in the Temple, and only the one who has nothing to offer goes home justified.

r.h: Return to the Lord with all your heart
set: The ark of the covenant has been captured by the Philistines and returned, and it has stayed for some twenty years at Kiriath-jearim while “all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord” (7:2). Samuel is the last of the judges and a prophet. He has been praying since he was a boy. Mizpah, in the hill country of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, was a place where Israel assembled.
str: vv. 3–4: Samuel's call: put away the foreign gods; Israel obeys.
vv. 5–6: the gathering at Mizpah: water poured out, fasting, confession.
vv. 7–8: the Philistines come, and the people beg Samuel to pray.
v. 9: the sacrifice and the cry; the Lord answers.
kw: The great word for repentance in the Old Testament. It is not firstly a feeling but a change of direction: “If you are returning… put away”.
Canaanite goddesses of fertility and war. People kept them alongside the Lord “just in case”. Samuel asks for an undivided heart: “serve him only”.
Here fasting goes with confession and prayer. It is the body's share in saying “We have sinned”.
vv: Direct your heart to the Lord, and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.
The order matters. The people want rescue, and Samuel speaks first of the heart.
So they gathered at Mizpah, and drew water and poured it out before the Lord. They fasted that day, and said, “We have sinned against the Lord.”

This rite with water is not found elsewhere in the Old Testament, and its exact meaning is not certain. It may express grief, or a heart poured out (compare Lamentations 2:19). The confession is plain: one sentence, with no excuses.
The people of Israel said to Samuel, “Do not cease to cry out to the Lord our God for us, and pray that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”
Repentance has not removed the danger; it has come at the very moment they turn back. Now they know where to look.
So Samuel took a sucking lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord; Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord answered him.
The lamb and the intercessor belong together. The Christian reader remembers Sunday's Gospel: the Lamb of God is also the one who intercedes for us (Hebrews 7:25).
ch: The Catechism describes how Samuel learned to pray from his mother Hannah and from Eli, and how he later came to know the cost of intercession: “far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you” (CCC 2578, quoting 1 Samuel 12:23). It teaches that interior conversion is expressed in visible signs, such as fasting and prayer (CCC 1430, 1434).

r.h: Barriers between you and your God
set: Many scholars place these chapters after the return from exile. The people have come home, but the great promises seem not to have come true. Fasting has not brought an answer (58:3). The prophet replies that God's arm is not the problem. After this indictment, the chapter moves on to a confession in the people's own voice (59:9–15) and the promise that a Redeemer will come to Zion (59:20).
str: vv. 1–2: God can save and can hear; sin has built the barrier.
vv. 3–4: hands, lips and courts: sin in daily life.
vv. 5–6: two pictures: adders' eggs and spider's webs.
vv. 7–8: the way of peace they do not know.
kw: From the verb bādal, to divide, used in Genesis 1 when God separates light from darkness. Sin does what creation did, but in reverse: it separates us from our God.
More than absence of war: wholeness, all things as they should be. The passage ends on this word, for sin is the road on which peace cannot be found.
What is right, and especially what is right in a court. The prophet's complaint against sin is very practical: lies, false cases, the innocent ruined.
vv: See, the Lord’s hand is not too short to save, nor his ear too dull to hear.
This answers the question that prayer so often raises: why is nothing happening? The fault is not on God's side.
Rather, your iniquities have been barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear.
The prophet is speaking to his own community, and so the words are for us: he is not pointing at outsiders. God has not walked away. The barrier is ours, and it can come down.
They hatch adders’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web;
Evil plans are compared to eggs that bring forth death and to webs that cannot be worn. All that busy work of sin makes nothing that can clothe anyone (59:6).
The way of peace they do not know, and there is no justice in their paths.
St Paul quotes vv. 7–8 in Romans 3:15–17, as part of his description of a humanity that needs grace, Jew and Gentile alike.
ch: The Catechism teaches that sin is before all else an offence against God and a rupture of communion with him, and that it damages communion with the Church (CCC 1440). The sacrament of Reconciliation is where the barrier comes down: “Be reconciled to God” (CCC 1442). Paul's use of this passage leads straight to the good news that we are justified by grace (Romans 3:24).

r.h: A living sacrifice
set: After eleven chapters on what God has done, Paul turns to how we are to live. “Therefore” in v. 1 holds the letter together: Christian conduct is an answer to the mercies of God already received. Chapters 12–15 are the moral part of the letter. The Roman community, with Jewish and Gentile members, had to learn to live as one body.
str: vv. 1–2: the offering of the body and the renewal of the mind.
v. 3: sober judgment about oneself.
vv. 4–5: one body, many members.
vv. 6–8: gifts that differ.
kw: Latreia is the word for liturgical service in the Temple. Logikos can mean spiritual or reasonable: worship that fits beings who think and love. Paul takes the language of the altar and applies it to the whole of life.

The same verb is used of the Transfiguration of Jesus (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2) and of Christians being changed into his image (2 Corinthians 3:18). It is in the passive voice and the present tense: let it keep being done to you.
From charis, grace. A gift is not a personal achievement. The list here runs from prophecy to acts of mercy, and it places them all on the same footing.
vv: I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.

The animals in the Temple died when they were offered. This sacrifice stays alive and goes on offering itself every day. The body, not only the soul, belongs in worship, and this is what our fasting says.
Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds, so that you may discern what is the will of God
There is a pressure from outside and a change from inside. The result is discernment: knowing what God wants, in a concrete situation.
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.
The last phrase goes further than saying that we all belong to Christ. We belong to each other.
the giver, in generosity; the leader, in diligence; the compassionate, in cheerfulness.
Mercy given with a long face is not quite mercy. This last word fits the fast well, for it is to be done without gloom (Matthew 6:16).
ch: The Catechism says that the moral life is spiritual worship, citing this verse (CCC 2031), and that by prayer we can discern what is the will of God (CCC 2826). The gifts of the Spirit are for building up the Church (CCC 799–801). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, asks how the body can be a sacrifice, and answers: let the eye look on nothing evil and it is a sacrifice; let the tongue speak nothing shameful and it is an offering; let the hand do no wrong and it is a whole burnt offering (in substance; Homily 20 on Romans).

r.h: Two men went up to the temple
set: Luke tells us the purpose before the story: it is for those “who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt”. This is a warning for anyone, the Christian reader first of all. The Pharisees were respected laymen, devoted to living the Law in daily life, and the first hearers would have expected this man to be the model of prayer. Tax collectors worked for the occupying power and were commonly despised as dishonest.
str: vv. 9–10: introduction: who is addressed and who the two men are.
vv. 11–12: the Pharisee's prayer.
v. 13: the tax collector's prayer.
v. 14: the verdict and the rule.
kw: The verb is related to the words used for atonement and the mercy seat (Hebrews 2:17; 9:5). It is more than “be nice to me”: it means be reconciled to me, take away my sin.
Declared and made right with God. This is a word we know from Paul, and Luke gives it here in the mouth of Jesus. The man did nothing except ask.
Literally “the rest”: the Pharisee sets himself apart from the rest of humanity. His words “like other people” show the real fault. His deeds are good. His way of seeing others is the problem.
vv: The Pharisee, standing by himself, was praying thus, ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people: thieves, rogues, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.

Standing to pray was usual. He does thank God, as good prayer should, but he is not asking for anything. “I” is the subject of nearly every sentence. He sees no need of mercy, and so he asks for none.
I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of all my income.

The Law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement. He does far more than is asked, and these things are good. In a week of fasting, we should notice this: it is possible to fast and yet to go home unchanged.
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even look up to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
No list, no comparison, and no promises. The Greek has “the sinner”, as if he were the only one. He stays far off, and yet he is the one who gets close.
I tell you, this man went down to his home justified rather than the other; for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but all who humble themselves will be exalted.
ch: The Catechism teaches that this parable concerns the humility of the praying heart, and that the Church continues to make the tax collector's prayer her own: “Kyrie eleison!” (CCC 2613; compare 2559). This prayer is at the root of the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern Churches (CCC 2667). The Catechism also reminds us that many Pharisees were close to Jesus and that some of them warned him of danger (CCC 575). St Augustine, preaching on this text, says that the Pharisee came to the doctor and showed only his healthy limbs, while the tax collector showed his wounds (in substance).

qa: Does the parable mean that fasting and tithing are worthless?
No. Jesus himself expects his disciples to fast and to give (Matthew 6:3, 16). The Pharisee's fault is not his fasting but his contempt. The fast has value when it makes us humble and merciful.
Is this parable an attack on the Jewish people or on Judaism?

No. Both men are Jews, praying in the Temple, and the Temple is the place where God's mercy is sought and given. Pharisees are not a symbol of a bad religion. The warning is meant for the Church's own members (CCC 575, 597).
What does “a living sacrifice” mean for ordinary people?
The farmer's work, the mother's sleepless night, the patient's pain and the honesty of a clerk can all be offered. At the Holy Qurbana these are joined to the one sacrifice of Christ (CCC 901, 1368).
rite: On this middle day of Moonnu Nombu, the tax collector's prayer fits the Church's mood well. Our Qurbana is full of the cry for mercy. If you can, make a good confession during these days. Let the fast of the body be matched by what Paul asks: a mind being renewed, a place taken in the body of Christ, and gifts used with cheerfulness. It is good to remember in prayer those who cannot fast because of sickness, and to help those for whom hunger is not a choice.
study: What “foreign gods” am I keeping alongside the Lord “just in case”? What would Samuel ask me to put away?
When my prayer seems unanswered, do I ask only what is wrong with God's hearing, or do I also ask about the barriers on my side?
Which part of my daily bodily life could I consciously offer as a “living sacrifice” today?
When I compare myself with others, do I come out better? What would it be like to pray without any comparison?

lead: On the last day of the fast we read the story that gave it its name. Joel calls the whole people, from the old to the infants at the breast, to the altar. Jonah walks into Nineveh with a short warning, and a great pagan city believes God. Paul uses the image of the potter to say that everything depends on God's mercy, which gathers people “not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles”. And Jesus warns that the best of fasts can end as a performance. The key words are together, who knows? and in secret. Today we also remember St Sebastian.

r.h: Sanctify a fast
set: We do not know Joel's exact date; many place him after the exile. The book opens with a terrible plague of locusts that has stripped the land (1:4), and it sees in it a warning of the Day of the Lord. In 2:12–14 God himself calls: “return to me with all your heart”. Our reading follows at once, and it is the practical order of service for a national day of penance.
str: vv. 15–16: the summons: the trumpet, the fast, the assembly; no one is exempt.
v. 17: the priests' prayer between vestibule and altar.
v. 18: the turning point: the Lord has pity.
v. 19: his answer: grain, wine and oil.
kw: The verb means to set apart for God. A fast is not merely a diet: it is a holy time, like a feast, called by the priests in the Lord's name.
To have pity, to look on with mercy. The priests offer no argument from the people's merit. Their argument is God's own name: “Where is their God?”
God's jealousy in Scripture is his passionate love for what is his own. The same word for God's anger against idols here turns into love for his land.
vv: gather the children, even infants at the breast. Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her canopy.

Even those excused from every other duty are called: a newly married couple (compare Deuteronomy 24:5) and babies who cannot understand. Sin and repentance concern a whole community, and this is why Moonnu Nombu brings whole families to church.
Between the vestibule and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep.
This was the place in the Temple court where the priests stood. The ministers of the altar begin the people's tears. A clergy that does not weep cannot lead a fast.
Then the Lord became jealous for his land, and had pity on his people.

The book turns on this verse. All the verbs of command have come before it, and now God acts. From here until the end, the book is a promise, which includes the pouring out of the Spirit (2:28–29; Acts 2:17).
ch: The Catechism cites Joel 2:12–13 when it teaches that the call of the prophets and of Jesus aims first at the conversion of the heart, and not first at outward works such as sackcloth and ashes (CCC 1430). Interior penance is expressed above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434), and the Church has her own seasons of penance, “intense moments of the Church's penitential practice” (CCC 1438).

r.h: The fasting of Nineveh
set: The Book of Jonah stands among the prophets, but it is a story about a prophet, not a collection of oracles. Many Catholic scholars read it as an inspired teaching story, while others read it more as history; its message stands either way, and Jesus himself uses it as a sign (Matthew 12:39–41; Luke 11:29–32). Nineveh was a capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC. To send a prophet there was to send him to the most feared enemy of his own people. Jonah has fled and has been thrown back on the shore. Now the word comes “a second time”.
str: vv. 1–4: the second call and Jonah's very short sermon.
v. 5: the people believe and fast.
vv. 6–9: the king and his decree.
v. 10: God sees, and relents.
kw: The verb used of Abraham in Genesis 15:6. Pagans in the great city do what Israel's prophet had refused to do. They “believed God”, and the story has barely begun.
The king's words in v. 9, and the same words appear in Joel 2:14. Repentance does not hold God to a contract. It trusts him without demanding.
A human way of speaking about God. He does not change in himself; the warning was given so that it might not have to be carried out. The threat was a mercy.
vv: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying,
Jonah's sin did not cancel his call. The God who gives Nineveh a second chance has already given Jonah one.
Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!

In Hebrew the sermon is five words. It does not even mention God or repentance. The verb can also mean “turned over”, as Sodom was overthrown (Genesis 19:25), and Nineveh is indeed turned around, by conversion. A note on the text. The Greek Septuagint here reads “three days”, whereas the Hebrew, followed by the NRSV and the POC, reads “forty”.
And the people of Nineveh believed God; they proclaimed a fast, and everyone, great and small, put on sackcloth.
It begins with the people, and only afterwards does the news reach the king (v. 6). The conversion rises from below.
When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

The ruler of the most powerful city gets down in the dirt, in contrast with Jonah, who has just fled. Even animals are made to fast in v. 7, which is both comic and serious, for the whole of creation shares in sin's consequences.
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God changed his mind about the calamity that he had said he would bring upon them; and he did not do it.
God does not see their sackcloth first. He sees that they have turned from their evil ways. So the decree in v. 8 mentions the violence in their hands. This is the true fast.
ch: Jesus says that “the people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment” (Matthew 12:41), and the Catechism notes that he spoke of the sign of Jonah when he pointed to his Resurrection (CCC 994). In the Syriac tradition the story of Nineveh has long been preached at this fast, and there are long metrical homilies on the repentance of Nineveh attributed to Mar Aprem.

r.h: Objects of mercy, from every people
set: Paul is in the middle of his reflection on Israel (Romans 9–11). If God chooses, why does he still find fault? This reading is his reply, and it is one of the hardest passages in his letters. It should be read through to the end of chapter 11, where he closes with mercy for all (11:32). The image of the potter is an old one: Isaiah 29:16; 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1–6; Wisdom 15:7.
str: vv. 19–21: the objection and the potter's answer.
vv. 22–23: God's patience with “objects of wrath” and his mercy toward “objects of mercy”.
v. 24: those objects of mercy are from Jews and Gentiles.
vv. 25–29: the proof from Hosea and Isaiah.
kw: The image says that the creature has no right to call the Creator to account. In Jeremiah 18 the potter reshapes a spoiled pot, and the people there are told they may repent.

The same word that is used for jars in a house (2 Timothy 2:20). Paul uses it to speak of those who receive wrath and those who receive mercy. In v. 22 he does not say that God prepared the first for destruction, while in v. 23 he does say that God prepared the second for glory.
A small part that stands for the whole, like the survivors in Isaiah. In chapter 11 Paul says that the remnant is a sign of hope for all Israel (11:1–5, 26).
vv: But who indeed are you, a human being, to argue with God?
Paul does not forbid honest prayer, which Scripture is full of. He rejects a claim to judge God from the outside.
What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience the objects of wrath that are made for destruction;

Notice “with much patience”. This is the patience shown to Nineveh. Paul asks a question, and he does not lay down a doctrine that God has created some people for hell. The Church teaches that “God predestines no one to go to hell” (CCC 1037).
including us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
Here is the point of the whole passage. God's mercy is wider than anyone had thought. The people of Nineveh were an early sign of it.
Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved.’
Hosea (2:23) spoke these words about Israel itself, restored after unfaithfulness. Paul now applies them to the Gentiles as well: the same mercy for all.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God predestines no one to go to hell, and that this comes only by a wilful turning away from God (CCC 1037). God's eternal plan includes each person's own response to his grace (CCC 600). The Church's relationship with the Jewish people is unique, for to them belong the covenants, and the gifts of God are irrevocable (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: Your Father who sees in secret
set: The Sermon on the Mount has just taught a righteousness deeper than the outward rule (Matthew 5). Chapter 6 now takes the three great works of Jewish piety, almsgiving, prayer and fasting, and gives each the same pattern: do not do it to be seen; the Father sees in secret. Our reading is the first of the three. Jesus takes for granted that his disciples will do these things: he says “whenever you give alms”, not “if”.
str: v. 1: the general warning.
v. 2: what not to do.
vv. 3–4: what to do, and the promise.
kw: Literally “righteousness”: right conduct before God. It is the same word as in 5:6 and 5:20. Jesus does not abolish the practice. He changes the audience.
Originally a stage actor, wearing a mask. Jesus is warning his own disciples about the temptation to perform, and he is not describing a whole people or all of their worship.
A commercial word found on receipts: “paid in full”. Applause is a real reward, but nothing further is owing.
vv: Beware of practicing your piety before others in order to be seen by them; for then you have no reward from your Father in heaven.
This does not contradict “let your light shine” (5:16). There the purpose is that others may give glory to the Father; here the purpose is one's own glory. The question is who is meant to be seen.
So whenever you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by others.
We have no evidence of actual trumpets being blown: this is a vivid picture, of the kind Jesus loves. Today the trumpet may be a plaque, a list of donors, or a post on a phone.
But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
Taken literally this is impossible, and that is the point. Forget it yourself too.
so that your alms may be done in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
Some later manuscripts add “openly”, a word not in the best witnesses. The secret is not empty, for someone is looking. The whole of Christian hiddenness lives on this: the Father sees.
ch: The Catechism says that the New Law practises the acts of religion, namely almsgiving, prayer and fasting, directing them to the “Father who sees in secret” (CCC 1969), and that interior penance can be expressed in fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). St Peter Chrysologus preaches that prayer, fasting and mercy are three things that are one, and that they give life to each other: fasting is the soul of prayer, and mercy is the lifeblood of fasting (in substance; Sermon 43).

qa: Did Nineveh's repentance last?

Nineveh later fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC (see the Book of Nahum). The Book of Jonah does not deny this. Its point is that God wants the repentance of every people, and that he hears it at once. Each generation must turn for itself.
Does Romans 9 mean that God creates some people to be damned?

No. The Church teaches that God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037), and that he “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4). Paul's question is about God's freedom to show mercy to the Gentiles and to Israel. It ends in the words “that he may be merciful to all” (Romans 11:32).
Should I never let anyone know what I give?

Sometimes a good deed will be seen, and even should be, as with the Church's public works of charity. The question is whose glory I am seeking. Where possible, keep your own giving private, and let the giving be for the sake of the poor and the Father.
rite: Moonnu Nombu ends today, and tomorrow we give thanks. Like Nineveh, the Church has fasted as one people. The calendar notes that the Third Qudasha is used today, and it gives other readings for St Sebastian. Sebastian is remembered by tradition as a Roman soldier who strengthened Christians in prison and gave his life for Christ. He is greatly loved in Kerala, and his name is carried by many of our people, some of our bishops among them. Let this fast end with mercy done in secret and with faith confessed without fear, and let us pray for all who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who wronged them.
study: Joel calls even infants and newly married couples to the fast. How do we make the Church's fasts something that our whole family shares, in ways fit for each person?
Jonah's sermon had five words in Hebrew. What short word from God has been waiting for a response from me?
“Who knows?” said the king of Nineveh. How do I pray when I have no guarantee of the result?
Is there something good I do that I secretly want others to notice? What would it mean to do it for the Father alone?

lead: The fast is over, and the day after it is a day of thanksgiving. The readings tell us what God was doing during the fast. Ezekiel gives us God's oath: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked”. Micah sings of a God who throws our sins into the sea. The elder writes to Gaius of his joy that his children walk in the truth. And Jesus tells of the shepherd and the woman who search until they find, and of the joy in heaven when a sinner turns. The word for today is joy, and first of all the joy of God.

r.h: Why will you die, O house of Israel?
set: Ezekiel is a priest among the exiles in Babylon, in the sixth century BC. Chapter 33 stands at the turning point of the book: he has been appointed a watchman (33:1–9), and very soon the news will come that Jerusalem has fallen (33:21). The people have stopped making excuses and have fallen into the opposite danger, which is despair: “how then can we live?” The same teaching appears at more length in chapter 18.
str: v. 10: the people's despair.
v. 11: God's oath and his plea.
vv. 12–13: the righteous who sin cannot trust in their past.
vv. 14–16: the wicked who turn shall live, and their sins will not be remembered.
kw: The strongest oath in the Bible. God has nothing greater to swear by than his own life, and he uses it to swear that he does not want the sinner to die.
The repeated word is a plea. A judge does not plead with the guilty, but this God does.
Something taken as security for a loan, such as a poor man's cloak (Exodus 22:26). Conversion here is highly practical: give it back.
vv: Our transgressions and our sins weigh upon us, and we waste away because of them; how then can we live?
This is true guilt, and it could lead either to God or to despair. Judas and Peter both knew this weight. The difference lies in what one does next.

As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from their ways and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways; for why will you die, O house of Israel?
This is one of the great verses on God's heart in the whole Old Testament. See also 18:23, 32. It is echoed in 2 Peter 3:9.
None of the sins that they have committed shall be remembered against them; they have done what is lawful and right, they shall surely live.
God's memory of sin ends with conversion. Yet the same passage warns that past goodness is not a bank account (33:13). What matters is the direction of one's life today.
ch: St Clement of Rome, near the end of the first century, already quotes this teaching to urge repentance on the Church of Corinth (1 Clement 8, in substance). The Catechism teaches that conversion is a turning of the whole life to God, and that it is God who gives the heart strength to begin anew (CCC 1431–1432). Giving back what has been taken is also a matter of justice: restitution is part of repentance (CCC 2412).

r.h: Who is a God like you?
set: Micah preached in Judah in the eighth century BC, defending the poor. The book's closing verses (7:8–20) read like a liturgy, and many scholars think that they were shaped in the time after the exile. Lady Zion speaks in the first person, in darkness but with hope. The final hymn is a song to God's mercy, and in Jewish custom these verses are read at the Tashlikh rite at the new year, when people go to flowing water and symbolically cast off their sins.
str: vv. 8–9: Zion's confession of trust: “when I fall, I shall rise”.
v. 18: “Who is a God like you?”
v. 19: he will tread down our iniquities and cast our sins into the sea.
v. 20: the oath to Abraham and Jacob.
kw: who is a God like you?
A play on the prophet's own name: Mîkāyâ means “Who is like the Lord?” The book closes by repeating its author's name as a question of praise.
God's covenant love, which holds firm when we do not. It occurs in v. 18 and again in v. 20. “He delights in showing clemency”: mercy is what he enjoys.
Often paired with ḥesed, as in Exodus 34:6. In v. 20 the two words round off the book, both resting on what God promised long ago.
vv: Do not rejoice over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be a light to me.
A verse for the morning after any failure. Falling is not the last event. The Christian also hears here the light that the season of Denha proclaims.
I must bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he takes my side and executes judgment for me.
She accepts what she has done, without self-pity. The judge she has sinned against will turn out to be her advocate.
He will again have compassion upon us; he will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea.

After three days with Jonah, this comes as a fine picture. The sea that was once Jonah's punishment and the Egyptians' end becomes the place where sins are lost, as Pharaoh's army was (Exodus 15:4–5).
ch: The Catechism says that God keeps steadfast love for thousands, and that in spite of human unfaithfulness he reveals himself as rich in mercy (CCC 211). The forgiveness of sins that the prophets long for comes in Christ, who gave his Church the power to forgive (CCC 976, 981).

r.h: Walking in the truth
set: This is the shortest book of the Bible in Greek, a real private letter of the kind found in the ancient world. The writer calls himself “the elder”. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, while many scholars see a leader of the Johannine communities. Travelling preachers needed hospitality from local Christians, and some leaders were refusing it (Diotrephes in v. 9). Gaius has welcomed them. This is one of very few glimpses of how the first mission actually paid its way.
str: vv. 1–2: greeting and prayer for his health.
vv. 3–4: joy at Gaius's faithfulness.
vv. 5–6a: his welcome of strangers.
vv. 6b–8: send them on, and so become co-workers with the truth.
kw: The word occurs in each of the first four verses except v. 2, and again in v. 8. Truth in John is not only something one thinks: one walks in it, loves in it and works with it.
A technical word in the early Church for equipping travellers with food and money for the next stage of the journey (compare Romans 15:24; Titus 3:13).
Those who stayed home become partners in the mission. Those who feed the preacher share in his preaching.
vv: Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, just as it is well with your soul.
An ordinary greeting from a letter of the time, turned into a prayer. It shows care for the whole person. It is not a promise of wealth.
I have no greater joy than this, to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
Every parent and every priest can pray this verse. Here is the joy that the day's other readings speak of, but now in a human heart.
for they began their journey for the sake of Christ, accepting no support from non-believers.
Literally “for the sake of the Name”. They would not take money from pagans, so that the Gospel would not look like a religious trade. Therefore someone had to help them.
Therefore we ought to support such people, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.
ch: The Catechism teaches that all members of the Church share in the apostolate, each in his or her own way (CCC 863). The Didache, an early Christian writing, gives rules for welcoming travelling teachers, which show how important this was (Didache 11–13). The whole Church's support of mission work continues this today.

r.h: Rejoice with me
set: Luke 15 is the heart of Luke's Gospel: three parables of the lost, of which the third is the Prodigal Son. The occasion is given in vv. 1–2. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near, and the Pharisees and scribes object that Jesus eats with them. In that culture, sharing a table meant accepting someone. Jesus' answer is addressed to good people, and it is an invitation: come in to the feast.
str: vv. 1–3: the complaint and the occasion.
vv. 4–7: the lost sheep.
vv. 8–10: the lost coin.
kw: The same kind of word that the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel in the desert (Exodus 16:2). It is a warning for anyone who thinks that the Father's house is theirs alone.
The word occurs in each story. What is lost still belongs to the owner. This is why he goes after it.
It runs through the chapter. The stories are less about the sheep and more about the one who finds it. Luke 15 reveals what makes God happy.
vv: This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.
It was meant as an accusation, and it has become one of the best descriptions of Jesus. It is also a description of the Holy Qurbana.
Which one of you, having a hundred sheep and losing one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it?
“Until he finds it”. The search has no time limit. Honest shepherds might well answer “not me”, and this is why the parable is so surprising.
When he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders and rejoices.
There is no word of blame. The shepherd carries the sheep himself. This is the same picture as Sunday's first readings: God carries his people.
Or what woman having ten silver coins, if she loses one of them, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?
Jesus pairs a man's work with a woman's, and God is pictured in both. A drachma was about a day's wage: for a poor house, this is real money.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
At the end of a fast, this is the verse to remember. The joy is first in heaven.
ch: The Catechism points to these parables as the revelation of God's mercy to sinners (CCC 1846; compare 1439), and it recalls that Jesus scandalized the Pharisees by eating with tax collectors and sinners (CCC 588; compare 1443). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, says that the shepherd laid the sheep on his shoulders because in taking our human nature Christ bore our sins (in substance; Homily 34 on the Gospels).

qa: If God does not want the death of the sinner, why is there a hell?

Because God does not force love. The Church teaches that hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from God, and that God predestines no one to it (CCC 1033, 1037). This is why he pleads so hard: “why will you die?”
Were the ninety-nine in the parable truly in no need of repentance?

This is gentle irony. All of us need repentance (Luke 13:3). Jesus is inviting those who think they do not need it to come and share the joy. Many Pharisees were close to Jesus, and the door is held open for them, as it is for us (CCC 575).
Should every Christian support missionaries?

Yes, each in the way open to them: with prayer, offerings and hospitality. The Church teaches that the whole Church is missionary (CCC 849–856). In many of our parishes, Mission Sunday and support of mission dioceses continue what Gaius did.
rite: In the East Syriac tradition, the Thursday after the Three Days' Fast is a day of thanksgiving for the mercy received, and the calendar calls it so. The readings are the right ones for it: we have asked for mercy, and now we hear how much God desired to give it. At today's Holy Qurbana, give thanks not only for what we received in the fast, but for God's own joy. Keep something of the fast's fruit: one forgiveness offered, one sin confessed, one work of mercy continued, and let them be the first steps toward the Great Fast.
study: Do I know people who have given up, saying, “How then can we live?” How could I bring them Ezekiel 33:11?
Micah says God “delights in showing clemency”. Do I believe that God enjoys forgiving me? How would it change my confession if I did?
Who are the “Gaius” in my life, who quietly welcome and support the Church's mission? How can I become a co-worker with the truth?
What did this fast bring me that I want to keep? Whom should I now go out and search for?

lead: On this Friday of Denha the Church remembers Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, and the four readings show what their work is about: God making himself known. On Carmel, Elijah prays that a wavering people may know who God is, and fire answers. In Acts the same God works through the apostles among the sick of Jerusalem. Paul tells the Corinthians what it costs to carry this message, and calls himself their father through the gospel. In Matthew, Jesus names the Twelve and sends them out with empty hands. The Evangelists did in writing what the Twelve did by voice. The key words are know, sent and without payment.

r.h: The fire that answers
set: The scene belongs to the ninth century BC, in the northern kingdom of Israel. King Ahab and Queen Jezebel have promoted the worship of Baal (16:31–33), who was honoured as the god of storm and rain. So the drought announced by Elijah (17:1) challenges Baal on his own ground. On Mount Carmel Elijah puts the question plainly: “How long will you go limping with two different opinions?” (18:21). The prophets of Baal have cried out all day, and “there was no voice, no answer, and no response” (18:29). Now it is Elijah’s turn.
str: vv. 30–32: Elijah repairs the broken altar with twelve stones.
vv. 33–35: wood, the bull, and water poured three times until the trench is full.
vv. 36–37: a short prayer at the hour of the offering.
v. 38: the fire falls.
v. 39: the people fall on their faces and confess.
¶ The reading stops before v. 40, the killing of the prophets of Baal. That verse belongs to the violence of that age and is no pattern for Christians.
kw: The name means “my God is the Lord”. The whole story is the prophet’s name turned into an event, and the people’s final cry almost repeats it.
The regular offering of the afternoon (18:29, 36). Elijah acts at the hour of Israel’s own worship, as if to bring a straying people back into its proper rhythm.
The confession of v. 39. The words answer the question of v. 21: if the Lord is God, follow him. The people who “did not answer him a word” at the start now find their voice.
vv: First he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been thrown down;

Before he asks for anything he repairs. The twelve stones (v. 31) are striking, because the kingdom had long been divided and Elijah is standing in the north. He builds for the whole family of Jacob, the Israel that God intends.
Answer me, O Lord, answer me, so that this people may know that you, O Lord, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.

After a whole day of shouting by others, this prayer is brief. Elijah does not ask to be proved right. He asks that the people may know God, and he sees that even their turning back is God’s own work.
Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and even licked up the water that was in the trench.
The water poured in a time of drought made any trick impossible. Everything on the altar is taken, even the stones and the water.
The Lord indeed is God; the Lord indeed is God.
ch: The Catechism counts this among the great prayers of the Old Testament, and it notes that the Eastern liturgies repeat Elijah’s plea, “Answer me”, in the Eucharistic epiclesis (CCC 2583). The Letter of James holds him up as “a human being like us” whose prayer was heard (James 5:17). Sirach calls him “a prophet like fire” (Sirach 48:1). Mar Ephrem loved this language: fire and Spirit are in the womb of Mary, in the Jordan, in our baptism, and in the bread and the cup (Hymns on Faith 10, in substance). That is why this reading suits Denha.

r.h: Signs through the hands of the apostles
set: This is the third of Luke’s short summaries of life in the first community (compare 2:42–47 and 4:32–35). The apostles have already been warned by the authorities (4:18), and the grave story of Ananias and Sapphira has just been told (5:1–11), which helps to explain why “none of the rest dared to join them” (v. 13). The believers meet in Solomon’s Portico, a colonnade on the east side of the Temple court (see 3:11; John 10:23). They are still Jews praying in their own Temple.
str: v. 12: signs through the apostles, and the community together in the Portico.
vv. 13–14: outsiders keep their distance, the people respect them, and believers are added.
v. 15: the sick are laid in the streets for Peter’s shadow.
v. 16: crowds come from the towns around Jerusalem, and all are cured.
kw: The words Peter used of Jesus himself at Pentecost (2:22). What the apostles do continues what the Lord did. A sign is a deed that points beyond itself.
The form suggests that God is the one who adds. Growth in Acts is his gift, not the result of good planning alone.
The verb used for Peter’s shadow in v. 15. It is also the word for the power of the Most High overshadowing Mary (Luke 1:35) and for the cloud at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:34).
vv: Now many signs and wonders were done among the people through the apostles.
The Greek says literally “through the hands of the apostles”, as the Malayalam POC keeps it. The hands are theirs; the power is not.
in order that Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he came by.

Luke does not teach that shadows have power. He reports the faith of simple people, as with the fringe of Jesus’ cloak (Mark 6:56) and later with Paul’s handkerchiefs (Acts 19:12). God is pleased to work through created things and through people, and the sacraments rest on the same truth.
A great number of people would also gather from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all cured.
ch: The Church continues this ministry to the sick. The Catechism teaches that the Lord sends his disciples to heal in his name (CCC 1506–1507), and it also says honestly that even the most intense prayers do not obtain the healing of every illness (CCC 1508). St Luke, whom tradition honours today, wrote this book as the second part of his work (Acts 1:1), so that the story of Jesus should not end with the Gospel but go on in the Church.

r.h: A father through the gospel
set: Paul wrote to Corinth from Ephesus in the mid-50s. The community he founded is split into parties around favourite teachers (1:12; 3:4), and some members think they have already arrived: “Already you have become rich!” (4:8). His answer is sharply ironic. If they are kings, what does that make the apostles?
str: v. 9: the apostles as the last act in a public show.
v. 10: three contrasts: fools and wise, weak and strong, disrepute and honour.
vv. 11–13: the actual life of an apostle, and its answers: bless, endure, speak kindly.
vv. 14–16: the tone changes: not shame, but a father’s warning.
kw: The word for a theatre or what is shown in one. Paul pictures the condemned brought on last in the arena, with the world and the angels as the audience.
Words for what is scraped off and thrown away. No stronger words could be found, and Paul uses them of himself.
The household slave who took a child to school and watched his conduct. Such a person can correct a child, but he is not its father.
A strong verb. For Paul, proclaiming the gospel gives life, and he uses the same language of those he brings to faith (Philemon 10).
vv: We are fools for the sake of Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
This is irony, not self-pity. The Corinthians measure success as the city does. Paul has already said that the message of the cross looks like foolishness (1:18).
When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;
This is the Sermon on the Mount lived in a working life. Paul adds that he grows “weary from the work of our own hands”, a thing educated Greeks tended to look down on.
For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
“In Christ Jesus” and “through the gospel” are the limits of this fatherhood. He does not take God’s place. The life passes through him from Christ.
I appeal to you, then, be imitators of me.
He later adds the condition that explains it: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1).
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this verse when it asks priests to care, as fathers in Christ, for those they have begotten spiritually through baptism and teaching (Lumen Gentium 28). On this day the passage can be applied to the Evangelists too. They too are fathers in faith, and those who first carried their books often paid the price Paul describes.

r.h: He called them by name and sent them
set: This is the beginning of the second of the five great discourses in Matthew (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25). Just before it Jesus sees the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” and tells his disciples to pray for labourers (9:36–38). Now those who were told to pray become the answer to their own prayer.
str: v. 1: authority given to the Twelve.
vv. 2–4: the names.
vv. 5–6: where to go: first the lost sheep of Israel.
vv. 7–8: what to do: proclaim and heal, without payment.
vv. 9–10: what not to take.
vv. 11–15: how to enter a house, and how to leave one.
kw: From a verb meaning to send. Matthew uses this noun only here (10:2). A person sent with authority acts in the name of the one who sends him.
“You received without payment; give without payment.” The whole mission rests on this word. The gospel is a gift, and it cannot become a trade.
The very words of John and of Jesus himself (3:2; 4:17). The apostles add nothing to the message; they carry it further.
vv: These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, also known as Peter,

Twelve recalls the twelve tribes: Jesus is gathering the whole of Israel (19:28). Only here in the lists is Matthew called “the tax collector” (10:3; compare Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15). The Gospel that bears his name does not hide where he came from. Thomas stands beside him. The lists differ a little: Luke has Judas son of James where Matthew has Thaddaeus, and some manuscripts of Matthew read Lebbaeus.
Go nowhere among the Gentiles, and enter no town of the Samaritans,

This is the order of God’s plan: Israel first (compare Romans 1:16). The same Gospel ends with “make disciples of all nations” (28:19). Between those two commands the Gentile centurion and the Canaanite woman have already appeared (8:5–13; 15:21–28).
You received without payment; give without payment.
Take no gold, or silver, or copper in your belts,

The lack of baggage is itself a message: God provides, and the messenger depends on those who receive him. Mark allows a staff and sandals (Mark 6:8–9), so the point is the attitude, not an exact rule of equipment. The early Church manual called the Didache warns that a travelling apostle who asks for money is a false prophet (Didache 11, in substance).
ch: The Catechism sees in the Twelve, representing the tribes of Israel, the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765), and it says that the whole Church is apostolic because she is sent into the world (CCC 863). On the Evangelists, the Second Vatican Council teaches that what the apostles preached at Christ’s command, they and apostolic men handed on in writing under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (Dei Verbum 18). The Catechism calls the Gospels the heart of all the Scriptures (CCC 125) and gives them unique honour in the Church’s worship (CCC 127). St Irenaeus compared the four Gospels with the four winds and the four corners of the earth, so that the one Gospel reaches everywhere (Against Heresies 3.11, in substance).

qa: Did the four men named really write the Gospels?

The Church teaches firmly that the four Gospels are of apostolic origin (Dei Verbum 18). Ancient tradition names Matthew and John from the Twelve, and Mark and Luke from the circle of Peter and Paul. Many scholars today think that disciples and communities also had a hand in the final form of some of these books. The Church’s concern is that they faithfully hand on what Jesus did and taught, under the Spirit’s inspiration (Dei Verbum 11, 19).
Jesus says, “call no one your father” (Matthew 23:9). So why do we call priests “father”?

Jesus is warning against claiming the honour that belongs to God alone. The same New Testament has Paul writing “I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). A spiritual father is a channel of what comes from the Father, never his rival.
Did Peter’s shadow really heal people?

Luke reports what the people hoped and that the sick were cured. He does not say the shadow had power of its own. The healer is the risen Lord, who works through his apostles and meets people in their simple faith.
rite: The Fridays of Denha keep a line of witnesses: in this year’s calendar, St John the Baptist, Sts Peter and Paul, the Evangelists, and St Stephen. We who received the faith through the tradition of Mar Thoma hear him named today among the Twelve, and we hear the four Gospels read at every Holy Qurbana. When the Gospel is read and we stand, we are standing before the words that these men handed down at great cost.
study: Elijah repairs the altar before he asks for fire. What in my family’s prayer needs repairing first?
Paul says that he blesses when reviled. Whom would I find hardest to bless this week?
“You received without payment.” What have I received in the Church that I can give without counting the cost?
Which of the four Gospels do I know least? How could I begin to read it this year?

lead: Both readings are about standing firm when it costs something. Paul asks the Philippians to hold together under pressure and calls their suffering a gift. In the district of Tyre and Sidon a Gentile mother will not go away, even when she meets silence and a hard saying. Faith here is not a feeling but a refusal to let go.

r.h: Citizens worthy of the gospel
set: Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), and its people were proud of their Roman citizenship. Paul founded the Church there and was flogged and jailed in that city (Acts 16:19–24). He now writes from prison again (1:13); whether in Rome or elsewhere, scholars still discuss. He has just said that he hopes to return. Whatever happens to him, he says, one thing matters for them.
str: v. 27: live as worthy citizens, and stand together.
v. 28: do not be frightened by opponents.
vv. 29–30: suffering is a grace, and they share Paul’s own struggle.
kw: From polis, a city. Literally “live as citizens”. In a colony proud of Rome, Paul speaks of another citizenship: “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20).
An athlete’s word. The opponents are outside; the team must not be fighting within. Paul is thinking of unity as much as of courage (see 4:2).
From charis, grace. Paul uses the language of gift for suffering, which is the last thing we would expect.
vv: standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel,
Soldiers and athletes stand this way. A Church that quarrels within cannot withstand pressure from without.
he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well
Paul does not call suffering good in itself. To suffer for Christ is to share his life, and so even this can be received as a gift.
ch: The Second Vatican Council calls martyrdom an exceptional gift and the supreme test of love, and it says that all must be prepared to confess Christ before others even along the way of the cross (Lumen Gentium 42). In the second century St Polycarp wrote his own letter to this same Church and remembered Paul’s teaching among them. We pray today for those who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who wrong them.

r.h: Even the dogs eat the crumbs
set: Jesus has just argued about clean and unclean with Pharisees and scribes (15:1–20). Now he goes to the district of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile land on the Phoenician coast. Mark calls the woman a Syrophoenician (Mark 7:26). Matthew uses the old biblical word “Canaanite”, which recalls the people of the land from Israel’s earliest story.
str: vv. 21–22: the woman’s cry.
vv. 23–24: silence, the disciples’ impatience, and the limit of his mission.
vv. 25–26: she kneels; the hard saying.
v. 27: her reply.
v. 28: his praise, and the healing.
kw: The cry that the Church has kept in her liturgy in Greek, Kyrie eleison. A Gentile woman prays it here, and she also gives him the title “Son of David”.
A diminutive form, used of small dogs in a home, as her reply about the table suggests. Commentators warn that this softens the saying but does not remove its sting. “Dogs” was a known insult.
Only here and with the centurion (8:10), another Gentile, does Jesus praise faith in this way in Matthew. Just one chapter before, he said to Peter, “You of little faith” (14:31).
vv: But he did not answer her at all.
Prayer sometimes meets silence. She does not take silence for a final answer.
But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
The shortest prayer of the passage. The verb is the one used of the Magi, who also came from the Gentiles to worship him (2:11).
Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.
She does not dispute the order of God’s plan. She accepts it and finds room inside it. Her wit is the wit of faith: there is so much bread at this table that the crumbs are enough.
Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.
ch: The Catechism names the Canaanite woman among those whose prayer of faith Jesus heard (CCC 2616). The Church has seen in her a sign of what Denha proclaims: the salvation first offered to Israel reaches the nations (CCC 543). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, admired how the woman’s perseverance won what the disciples’ request could not (Homilies on Matthew 52, in substance).

qa: Was Jesus insulting the woman?

The words are hard, and it is better not to explain them away. Jesus is stating the order of his mission to Israel (15:24; compare 10:5–6). Many commentators think he draws out her faith, and the end of the story supports this: few in Matthew are praised as she is.
study: What do I do when God seems silent in response to my prayer?
Paul links courage with unity. Where is my parish or family weakened by a quarrel inside it?

lead: Denha celebrates the manifestation of the Lord, and today’s Gospel is the first sign at Cana, where he “revealed his glory”. The other readings prepare the way. In the wilderness God asks Moses, “Is the Lord’s power limited?” and shares his spirit far beyond what anyone expected, but his gift of quails is grabbed with craving. In Isaiah idols have to be carried on shoulders, while the true God speaks and acts. Hebrews shows who is at work: a priest who “continues forever” and “always lives” to intercede. At Cana a mother notices a need and tells the servants to obey, and water fills six stone jars and becomes wine. The line runs from craving to abundance, and its key words are spirit, glory and sign.

r.h: Is the Lord’s power limited?
set: Israel has left Sinai and is on the march. The people, tired of manna, crave the food of Egypt (11:4–6). Moses breaks down: “I am not able to carry all this people alone” (11:14). God answers with two promises: seventy elders will share his burden, and the people will have meat. Moses cannot see how (11:21–22). Today’s reading begins with God’s reply.
str: v. 23: God’s question.
vv. 24–25: the seventy at the tent receive a share of the spirit.
vv. 26–30: Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp; Joshua objects; Moses answers.
vv. 31–32: a wind brings the quails.
vv. 33–35: the plague, and the place named Kibroth-hattaavah.
kw: is the Lord’s hand too short?
The NRSV’s “Is the Lord’s power limited?” renders a vivid Hebrew picture, which the Malayalam POC keeps: “has my hand become short?” The same image returns in Isaiah 50:2 and 59:1.
The same Hebrew word stands in v. 25 (“spirit”) and v. 31 (“wind”). The breath that fills the elders is the breath that drives the quails. Both come from the Lord.
The word means strong desire, the same craving that began the chapter (11:4). The sin is not hunger. It is the greedy grabbing of a gift, as though God would not give enough.
vv: The Lord said to Moses, “Is the Lord’s power limited? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not.”
The whole of today’s Sunday is an answer to this question.
and when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied. But they did not do so again.

A note on the text. The Hebrew means that this happened once, a sign that the elders had been given authority. The Latin Vulgate understood it the other way, that they did not cease. The modern versions, with the NRSV and the POC, follow the first sense.
But Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit on them!”

Joshua is loyal, and his loyalty is too small. Moses wants nothing for himself. The spirit is not his property, and Eldad and Medad are in the list even though they stayed in the camp (v. 26). Jesus later answers John the same way: “Do not stop him” (Mark 9:39).
But while the meat was still between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the Lord was kindled against the people,
Psalm 78 sings of this story (78:26–31). Paul uses it as a warning for Christians that they should not crave what is evil (1 Corinthians 10:6).
ch: Moses’ wish is fulfilled at Pentecost, when Peter says that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh (Acts 2:17). The Church teaches that the whole People of God shares in Christ’s prophetic office (CCC 785; Lumen Gentium 12). An ancient ordination prayer for presbyters recalls these seventy elders (the Apostolic Tradition, in substance). So the passage guards two truths together: God gives authority to some, and the Spirit is not limited to them.

r.h: Gods who must be carried
set: This part of Isaiah speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon, before 539 BC. Great processions carried Babylon’s gods through the city. Just before our reading, the prophet pictures Bel and Nebo, the chief gods, loaded on tired animals as refugees (46:1–2), and then the Lord says to Israel, “even when you turn gray I will carry you” (46:4). The contrast is the heart of the chapter: Babylon carries its gods, and Israel’s God carries Israel.
str: v. 5: God’s question: to whom will you liken me?
vv. 6–7: the satire: gold, a goldsmith, shoulders, and silence.
vv. 8–11: remember: God alone declares what is to come, and he calls a “bird of prey”.
vv. 12–13: his salvation is near, even to the stubborn.
kw: Most commentators take this as Cyrus of Persia, already named in 44:28 and 45:1, who came from the east and took Babylon. God can use a foreign king who does not know him.
Literally “righteousness”. For this prophet, God’s righteousness is his faithful action to save. In v. 13 the NRSV rightly translates it “deliverance”.
In v. 13 God calls Israel his glory, his adornment. Israel does not glorify God by being impressive. God shows his glory by saving her.
vv: If one cries out to it, it does not answer or save anyone from trouble.
It stands where it is put. It is the exact opposite of the God who hears.
remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is no one like me,
Israel’s faith is built on memory. To remember what God has done is the best defence against worshipping what looks strong today.
I bring near my deliverance, it is not far off, and my salvation will not tarry; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory.
Simeon’s words about the child Jesus may echo this promise: “a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32). That is a verse for Denha.
ch: The Catechism teaches that idolatry is not only about false pagan worship. It remains a constant temptation to faith, whenever we honour and revere a creature in place of God, such as power, pleasure, race, ancestors, the state or money (CCC 2113). The test Isaiah gives still works: does the thing I rely on carry me, or do I have to carry it?

r.h: The priest who lives forever
set: Hebrews 7 has been reading Psalm 110:4 line by line: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek”. Melchizedek stands outside the line of Levi, and the promise comes with God’s oath (7:20–22). Now the author draws the conclusion: what kind of priest do we actually have? Its author is not named, and the Church received it among the letters linked with St Paul.
str: vv. 23–24: many priests because they die; one because he lives.
v. 25: so he can save for all time, and he intercedes.
v. 26: the fitting high priest.
v. 27: no daily offerings; he offered himself once.
v. 28: the law appoints weak men; the oath appoints a Son.
kw: It means both lasting and not able to be handed on. Aaron’s office passed from father to son at death. Christ’s has no successor, because he has not died out of it.
The phrase can mean both “for all time” (NRSV) and “completely” (POC: പൂർണമായി). Both are true of him.
To approach someone on behalf of another. The risen Lord is not idle in heaven. He pleads for us.
Sacrifice is finished, not because it is forgotten, but because it is complete.
vv: but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever.
Consequently he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
This may be the most comforting verse in the letter. At this moment someone is praying for me whom the Father cannot refuse.
this he did once for all when he offered himself.

Priest and victim are the same. No earlier priest could offer himself, and no later one needs to offer anything else. The argument speaks of “day after day” although the great atonement was yearly: the author is thinking of the whole system of offerings, and of the contrast with once.
but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
“Made perfect” does not mean he was once sinful. It is the language of being fitted for an office, here through obedience and suffering (compare 2:10; 5:8–9).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it speaks of Christ’s entry into heaven as our high priest (CCC 662), and of the intercession of Christ on which all Christian intercession depends (CCC 2634). Only Christ is the true priest, and the others are his ministers (CCC 1545, quoting St Thomas Aquinas). When the Church offers the Holy Qurbana, she does not add to the one sacrifice; it is made present (CCC 1366–1367).

r.h: The first of his signs
set: In the longer form the Gospel starts with Philip and Nathanael. Philip says, “Come and see”, and Jesus promises Nathanael, “You will see greater things than these” (1:46, 50). Cana is the first of those greater things. Cana was a village in Galilee, and Nathanael came from there (21:2). The “third day” (2:1) recalls for many commentators the day on which the Lord appeared in glory at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), and for every Christian reader the day of the Resurrection.
A village wedding could last several days, and for the wine to run out would have been a real shame for the family. The hosts’ honour was at stake.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: a wedding, his mother, the disciples.
vv. 3–5: the shortage, the exchange, and her word to the servants.
vv. 6–8: the jars filled and drawn.
vv. 9–10: the steward tastes and calls the bridegroom.
v. 11: John’s conclusion: sign, glory, faith.
kw: Not rude in Greek, but strange for a son to his mother. In John, Jesus addresses her in this way only here and at the Cross (19:26). At Cana and at Calvary she is more than a family member; she has a place in the work of the hour.
In John this means the hour of the Cross and glorification (12:23; 13:1; 17:1). At Cana it has not yet come, yet the sign points forward to it.
John’s word for what the others call mighty works. A sign shows who Jesus is. Cana is the “first” or “beginning” (archē) of signs, the word with which his Gospel opens (1:1).
In the Old Testament, the weight and shining presence of God. The Word “lived among us, and we have seen his glory” (1:14). Here it is seen first by a few, at a family celebration.
vv: When the wine gave out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”
She does not tell him what to do. She simply presents the need. This is the model of Christian intercession.
And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what concern is that to you and to me? My hour has not yet come.”

The phrase “what concern is that to you and to me?” is a Semitic idiom found also in Judges 11:12 and 1 Kings 17:18. It marks a distance and does not by itself mean refusal, since he acts a moment later. He is saying that his work follows his Father’s hour, not family need alone.
His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
Her last words in this Gospel. For many commentators they recall the words of Israel at Sinai, “Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do” (Exodus 19:8). Every Marian devotion ends here.
Now standing there were six stone water jars for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.

Stone did not contract ritual uncleanness in Jewish practice, and such jars have been found by archaeologists in the land. The total is between about 450 and 700 litres, a huge amount. The prophets foretold wine in plenty for the days of the Messiah (Amos 9:13; Isaiah 25:6). Jesus does not smash the jars. He fills them to the brim.
But you have kept the good wine until now.
The steward speaks more truly than he knows. God kept his best until now.
Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
This is the point of the entire story. There is no word of what the guests thought. The sign is complete when the disciples believe (compare 20:31).
ch: The Catechism draws three lessons from Cana. It is a confirmation of the goodness of marriage (CCC 1613). It is an announcement of the Eucharist: the new wine of the Kingdom, become the Blood of Christ (CCC 1335). And it shows Mary’s intercession, at a feast that is a sign of the wedding of the Lamb (CCC 2618). The Second Vatican Council says that she, moved with pity, brought about by her intercession the beginning of the signs (Lumen Gentium 58).

St Cyril of Jerusalem argued from this miracle to the Eucharist: if he once changed water into wine, why not believe that he changes wine into his Blood? (Mystagogical Catecheses 4, in substance.) St Augustine remarked that the Lord who did this once at Cana does the same every year in the vineyards, and that we have stopped wondering (Tractates on John 8, in substance).

qa: Was Jesus being disrespectful to his mother?

No. “Woman” was a respectful form of address, though unusual from a son, and he uses it again from the Cross, when he gives her to the beloved disciple (19:26). She takes no offence, and he does what she has asked.
Does the Gospel look down on Jewish rites of purification?

No. John notes the jars and their purpose with care. Jesus, his mother and his disciples are all Jews at a Jewish wedding. The sign says that what God promised to Israel is coming to fullness in a new and overflowing way. The Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God has never revoked (CCC 121, 839).
If Christ is the only high priest, what are our priests?

They share in his one priesthood as his ministers (CCC 1545). When a priest offers the Holy Qurbana, it is Christ who acts through him. Hebrews excludes any rival priesthood or any sacrifice added to his. It does not exclude ministers of his own.
rite: Denha means “dawning” or manifestation. In the Syro-Malabar season it is the shining of the Lord’s glory, first at the Jordan and now at Cana. At every Holy Qurbana a little water is mingled with the wine, and in the same Qurbana the Spirit is called down on the offerings. The people of Kerala know what a wedding means to a family, and how much a mother sees before anyone says a word. Today’s Gospel brings that ordinary knowledge to the altar.
study: God asks Moses, “Is the Lord’s power limited?” In what part of my life do I act as if it were?
Joshua wanted to stop those who were outside the group. Whose gifts in my parish do I find hard to welcome?
What do I rely on that I have to carry, rather than the God who carries me?
Mary said, “They have no wine.” What need in my family or village can I bring to Jesus in the same simple way this week?

lead: Today’s readings set two great calls side by side. A shepherd in the wilderness hears “Moses, Moses!” from a burning bush. A persecutor on the road hears “Saul, Saul!” from a light in the sky. The God who says “I am” to Moses says “I am Jesus” to Saul. Years later Paul looks back and says only: “by the grace of God I am what I am.” The parable of the labourers explains that grace: the wage is not earned by the hour, and the owner goes out even at the end of the day. The key words are called, grace and last.

r.h: The bush and the Name
set: Moses, raised in Pharaoh’s house, has killed an Egyptian and fled to Midian (2:11–22). He is now keeping someone else’s sheep. Meanwhile the Israelites groan under slavery, and God has heard (2:23–25). Horeb is another name for the mountain also called Sinai, where Moses will one day return with the whole people (3:12).
str: vv. 1–3: Moses comes to Horeb and sees the bush.
vv. 4–6: God calls him: holy ground, and the God of the fathers.
vv. 7–10: God has seen, heard, known, and come down, and so he sends Moses.
vv. 11–12: “Who am I?” “I will be with you.”
vv. 13–14: “What is his name?” The Name is given.
kw: A thorny desert plant, and the word sounds like Sinai. God does not appear first in a temple or a palace, but in a low and common shrub.
The answer of those who are ready to be sent, as with Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8). Ananias gives the same reply in today’s second reading.

The Hebrew can also mean “I will be who I will be”. The name given as YHWH comes from the same verb. Just before this God promises, “I will be with you” (3:12), with the same word ’ehyeh. His name is a promise of presence. The Greek Bible has “I am he who is”. Out of reverence Jewish tradition does not pronounce the Name, and says “Lord” instead (CCC 209).
vv: he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.
The fire does not need the bush for fuel, and God does not need the world to exist. Yet he comes into it without destroying it.
Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.
Nothing is holy about the land itself. It is holy because God is there. Holiness begins with distance and reverence, as the Catechism notes (CCC 208).
I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry
Four verbs in a row (vv. 7–8): seen, heard, known, come down. Having named himself the God of the fathers, this is what God says next about himself: he is not far from suffering.
But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?”
God does not answer the question. He does not say who Moses is. He says who will be with him.
I am who I am
ch: The Catechism gives a whole section to this passage (CCC 203–213). God reveals himself as the living God, who is also near and saves (CCC 205–207), and the Name reveals a mystery that goes beyond what we can name (CCC 206). St Gregory of Nyssa saw in the bush that burned and was not consumed a figure of the Virgin, who bore the divine light and was not harmed (Life of Moses 2, in substance). Jesus himself uses the passage to teach the resurrection (Mark 12:26). Today the Church hears it beside the road to Damascus.

r.h: Saul, Saul
set: Saul first appears at the stoning of Stephen (7:58; 8:1). Paul later describes himself as a Pharisee and a zealot for his ancestors’ traditions (Philippians 3:5–6; Galatians 1:13–14). Damascus, a city in Syria with a Jewish community, lay some 200 km from Jerusalem. The followers of Jesus there are called those of “the Way” (9:2). Acts tells this story three times (chapters 9, 22 and 26), a sign of how central it was to Luke. Paul’s own brief account is in Galatians 1:15–17. His name is not changed here: Acts goes on calling him Saul, and later says “Saul, also known as Paul” (13:9). Jews in the Roman world often had two names.
str: vv. 1–2: Saul’s plan.
vv. 3–9: the light and the voice, and three days of blindness and fasting.
vv. 10–16: the Lord and Ananias: a vision, an objection, a command.
vv. 17–19: hands laid on him, the scales, baptism, food.
vv. 20–22: he proclaims in the synagogues the one he came to oppose.
kw: “Why do you persecute me?” Saul thought he was attacking men and women. The voice says “me”. Christ is one with his Church.

An early name for the Christian movement (see 19:9, 23; 24:14). It is a life to be walked before it is a doctrine to be defended. The Malayalam POC renders it with a phrase meaning “the Christian way”.
Literally “a vessel of choice”; the NRSV has “an instrument whom I have chosen”, and the POC keeps “vessel”. A vessel does not fill itself. It carries what it is given.
vv: He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
God calls by name, twice, as with Abraham and Moses. There is no accusation of a crime and no sentence, only a question. The text mentions no horse; that comes from later Christian art.
He asked, “Who are you, Lord?” The reply came, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
The whole of Paul’s later teaching on the Body of Christ is already here.
“Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem;
Ananias has good reason to be afraid. He is one of the great minor figures of the Bible. He objects honestly, then goes.
So Ananias went and entered the house. He laid his hands on Saul and said, “Brother Saul,
“Brother”: the first word a Christian says to him. Paul was received into the Church through the hands and courage of a man we know nothing else about.
And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and his sight was restored. Then he got up and was baptized,
Sight and baptism come together, and the early Church called baptism “enlightenment” (CCC 1216).
and immediately he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”

The Catechism notes that this confession stands at the centre of the apostolic faith (CCC 442). In v. 22 Saul is a Jew arguing with fellow Jews in the synagogue; the phrase “the Jews who lived in Damascus” does not set Christians against a people. That division lay in the future.
ch: St Augustine often returned to the words “why do you persecute me?”, saying that the Head in heaven cries out on behalf of his members on earth (in substance); this is the teaching of the whole Christ (CCC 795). St John Chrysostom preached a series of homilies in praise of St Paul, and he never tired of the grace that turned such zeal to Christ. The Church does not celebrate today a change of character only, but the risen Lord who met him. Paul himself lists it among the appearances of the risen Christ, as the next reading shows.

r.h: Last of all, to me also
set: Some in Corinth were saying “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Before he answers them, Paul reminds them of what they already received. Writing in the mid-50s, he quotes a formula that he himself was given, and many scholars think it goes back to within a few years of the events. The Catechism points to this same text as very early witness (CCC 639).
str: vv. 1–2: the gospel they received and stand in.
vv. 3–5: the formula: died, buried, raised, appeared.
vv. 6–8: the list of witnesses, ending with Paul.
vv. 9–10: the least of the apostles, and God’s grace.
kw: Technical words for passing on a tradition faithfully. Paul has no private gospel. He stands in a line.
The word used four times here (vv. 5–8), and the same one the Greek Bible uses for God appearing to people. The risen Lord is the one who acts, and he lets himself be seen.
A very strong word: a birth before its time, a miscarriage. He may have been taking up an insult used about him. Someone not ready, brought to life by God’s power alone.
vv: For I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures,
and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures,

“Buried” underlines that he really died. “Raised” is a passive: the Father’s act. No single Old Testament verse is quoted; the whole of the Scriptures is seen as pointing to it (compare Isaiah 53; Hosea 6:2).
Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.
