Paul puts Damascus in the same list as Easter morning. It was not a private inner experience in his eyes but a meeting with the risen one.
For I am the least of the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
He never forgets it. Grace does not erase memory, but heals it. The Latin word paulus means “small”.
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain.
“Grace” occurs three times in this one verse. It answers “I am who I am” in the first reading. The Lord alone can say that sentence of himself; everyone else must say it Paul’s way.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage as a chief witness to the Resurrection, a real event known from those who met the Lord (CCC 639, 642). The Church’s faith rests on the apostles’ testimony, handed on. So every Creed we recite in the Holy Qurbana has this ancient formula within it. The grace Paul speaks of is that which comes first: it is God who begins, and merit is itself his gift (CCC 2007–2008).

r.h: Those who came last
set: The parable is found only in Matthew. Peter has just asked, “What then will we have?” (19:27), and Jesus has answered with a saying: “many who are first will be last, and the last will be first” (19:30). The parable then illustrates that saying, and it ends with the same words reversed. Day labourers were hired in the marketplace, and the Law required them to be paid the same day, before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14–15).
str: vv. 1–2: dawn: the agreement, the usual daily wage.
vv. 3–7: the owner goes out again and again, even at five o’clock.
vv. 8–10: evening: the payment, starting with the last.
vv. 11–12: the grumbling.
vv. 13–15: the owner’s reply.
v. 16: first and last.
kw: A Roman silver coin, the normal pay for a labourer’s day. It was roughly enough to keep a family for a day. Nobody is paid less than that.
A cool form of address, used as an address in Matthew only with people in the wrong: here, for the man without a wedding robe (22:12), and for Judas (26:50).
The owner’s question in v. 15 is literally “Is your eye evil because I am good?”. Envy looks at another’s blessing as if it were a loss.
vv: They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’
They were not lazy. They were unwanted. The owner’s going out so late has no business reason. It only makes sense if he is thinking about them.
Call the laborers and give them their pay, beginning with the last and then going to the first.
The order is the point of the story. If he had paid the first ones first, they would have gone home content and we would have no parable.
These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.
They have a real case, and every honest reader feels it. The word “equal” is the one they cannot bear.
Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or are you envious because I am generous?
He has done no wrong to anyone (v. 13). Justice is the floor of God’s dealing with us, not the ceiling.
So the last will be first, and the first will be last.

A note on the text. Many later manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate add “for many are called, but few are chosen”, which comes from 22:14. The oldest manuscripts do not have it here, and the NRSV and the POC omit it.
ch: The Fathers read the hours in more than one way. St Gregory the Great took them as the stages of a human life, so that no one should despair at any age (Homilies on the Gospels 19, in substance). The Easter sermon that bears the name of St John Chrysostom, still read in the Byzantine East, welcomes those who came at the eleventh hour (in substance). The Catechism teaches that we have no strict right to merit before God (CCC 2007), and it ends the section with St Thérèse, who wished to appear before God with empty hands (CCC 2011). Some older readings took the first-hired as Israel and the latecomers as the Gentiles, but the parable says that the owner keeps his agreement with the first, and the Church teaches that God’s covenant with Israel stands (CCC 839).

qa: Was Paul a Jew who left his faith?

Paul never stopped being a Jew. He calls himself “a member of the people of Israel” (Philippians 3:5) and insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). In Galatians he describes the event in the language of a prophet’s call (Galatians 1:15; compare Jeremiah 1:5). “Conversion” is the Church’s traditional word, and a true one, because he turned wholly to Christ; many scholars also stress that it was a call.
Did his companions hear the voice or not? Acts 9:7 and 22:9 seem to differ.

Acts 9:7 says they “heard the voice but saw no one”; 22:9 says they “saw the light but did not hear the voice”. A common explanation is that they heard a sound but did not understand the words, since the Greek verb can mean both. In either telling, the call is meant for Saul alone.
Is the owner unfair to the workers? Does this parable teach us how to pay wages?

No. It is about God’s generosity, not labour policy. Nobody gets less than was agreed. The Church teaches firmly that a just wage is a duty, and that to withhold it can be a grave injustice (CCC 2434).
rite: In our Holy Qurbana the Epistle is called the reading of the Apostle (Sliha), and many of these readings come from Paul. Today we meet the man behind the letters we hear Sunday after Sunday. Today also ends the Octave of Prayer for Christian Unity. Ananias’s first word to a man who had come to bind him was “Brother”. In Kerala, where the children of Mar Thoma are found in several Churches, this is a word to pray with and to practise.
study: Moses asks “Who am I?” and receives a promise instead of an answer. Where do I need that same promise now?
Ananias went although he was afraid. Who is the person God may be asking me to call “brother” or “sister”?
Paul never forgets what he did, and he never despairs about it. How do I hold my own past before God?
Do I secretly feel that I deserve more from God than others do? Which of the workers do I resemble?

lead: Both readings turn on the word “today”. Hebrews takes it from Psalm 95: the promise of God’s rest is still open, today, to those who listen. At Nazareth, Jesus has just said that “today” the Scripture is fulfilled, and his own townspeople cannot bear where this leads. One reading warns against a hard heart; the other shows us one.

r.h: The rest that is still open
set: Hebrews has just quoted Psalm 95 at length (3:7–11) and recalled the generation of the Exodus, who refused to enter the land at Kadesh after the report of the spies (Numbers 14; Hebrews 3:16–19). They heard God’s word and did not enter. The author now says to his tired Christian listeners: the promise did not end with them.
str: v. 1: the promise is still open, so let us take care.
v. 2: they heard good news as we do, and it did not profit them.
vv. 3–5: God’s rest goes back to the seventh day of creation (Genesis 2:2).
vv. 6–7: so God sets another day: “today”.
kw: In Psalm 95 and Numbers it means the land. Hebrews reads deeper and sees God’s own rest, the rest of the seventh day, which believers are invited to share. The land was only its sign.
The word Hebrews repeats from the psalm (3:7, 13, 15; 4:7). Every time the psalm is sung, that day is here.
vv: while the promise of entering his rest is still open, let us take care that none of you should seem to have failed to reach it.
but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ in this verse. The NRSV reads “not united by faith with those who listened”; others read that the word was not joined with faith in those who heard, which is close to the Malayalam POC, “they did not believe it”. In both readings hearing without faith does not help.
“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
The author says “through David”, because the Greek Bible heads the psalm with his name. His argument is simple: if God was still saying “today” long after Joshua, then the promise is still open now.
ch: The Catechism says that when the Church celebrates the mystery of Christ, one word marks her prayer: “Today!” (CCC 1165). The Fathers loved this rest. St Augustine begins his Confessions by telling God that our heart is restless until it rests in him (Confessions 1.1). Each Sunday’s Holy Qurbana is a foretaste of that rest.

r.h: He passed through the midst of them
set: The scene begins in the synagogue at Nazareth. Jesus has read from Isaiah 61, “to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor”, and has said, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:19, 21). Luke places this visit at the very start of the ministry, like a programme for everything that follows. The people of Nazareth have heard of what was done at Capernaum, though Luke has not yet narrated it (compare 4:31).
str: v. 22: amazement, and the question: “Is not this Joseph’s son?”
vv. 23–24: the proverb and the saying about the prophet.
vv. 25–27: Elijah and the widow; Elisha and Naaman.
vv. 28–29: rage, and the attempt to kill him.
v. 30: he goes on his way.
kw: A play on words that English loses. Jesus proclaims the “acceptable” year of the Lord (v. 19), and then says that no prophet is “accepted” in his hometown (v. 24). The same Greek word stands in both places.
Literally “the words of grace”. The grace is in what he says as well as in how he says it, and they cannot accept where it reaches.
vv: yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon.
See 1 Kings 17:8–16. The widow belonged to the very region of Baal’s worship, the Gentile coast.
and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.
See 2 Kings 5. Jesus says nothing against Israel here. He reminds his hearers from their own Scriptures that God’s mercy has never been limited by a border.
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.
Luke does not explain how. The hour of his death will come in Jerusalem (compare 9:51; 13:33), not on a hillside at the hands of neighbours. Nothing stops his road.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Kingdom, first announced to the children of Israel, is meant for people of all nations (CCC 543). Luke will show this at length in Acts. The people of Nazareth stand for no nation; their reaction is the human one, found in any town, when a familiar person speaks God’s word and the word reaches beyond us.

qa: Why did they become so angry so quickly?

The two examples Jesus gives are of outsiders favoured by God while Israel’s own in need waited. Those who felt they had the first claim on him heard that God’s mercy was going elsewhere. Familiarity had already prepared the ground: “Is not this Joseph’s son?” Any parish or family can do the same.
rite: Today India keeps Republic Day, recalling the Constitution that came into force on 26 January 1950. The Gospel offers a word for such a day: to love one’s own place is good, and to think that God’s mercy stops at its border is a mistake. We give thanks for our country, pray for those who govern it, and ask for hearts that do not harden. The calendar also recalls today Sts Timothy and Titus, Paul’s trusted fellow workers.
study: What word of God have I been putting off until tomorrow?
Is there anyone close to me whom I have stopped listening to because I know them too well?

lead: Both readings ask how a Christian tells the true voice from a false one. Paul is alarmed that the Galatians are turning to “a different gospel”, and he insists that there is only one. Jesus speaks of sheep who follow the shepherd because they know his voice, and run from a stranger. In the season of Denha, when Christ is shown to the world, the question is simple: whose voice do I know?

r.h: There is no other gospel
set: Paul had brought the Gospel to the Galatians, Gentile converts in the Roman region of Galatia in Asia Minor. After he left, other Christian teachers came and insisted that these converts must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses (5:2–3; 6:12–13). This was a dispute among believers in Christ, and Paul, himself a Jew (2:15), argues it from the Scriptures of Israel. His answer is that salvation comes through the grace of Christ, received in faith, and that nothing can be added to it as a condition.

In his other letters to churches, some word of thanks or blessing follows the greeting. Here there is none. After the greeting of vv. 1–5 he goes straight to the problem, and the first readers would have felt the omission.
str: vv. 6–7: Paul’s astonishment: they are deserting the one who called them.
vv. 8–9: a solemn curse, said twice, on anyone who changes the Gospel.
v. 10: Paul tests his own motives: God’s approval or people’s?
kw: A word used of someone changing sides or moving allegiance. The tense is present: they are in the middle of turning, and so can still be stopped. Paul says they are deserting not a teacher but “the one who called you”, that is, God.

Paul uses two words. They are turning to a “different” gospel (heteron), which is not “another” one (allo) at all, because there is no second Gospel to choose. What they are being offered only carries the name.

In the Greek Old Testament this word translates ḥērem, what is handed over to God for destruction. Paul is not yet using it as the later Church’s formal term of excommunication. He places the false preacher under God’s judgment, and he does not exempt himself.
vv: not that there is another gospel, but there are some who are confusing you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ.
For Paul “gospel” is not yet a book. It is the preached message of what God has done in Christ, the Crucified and Risen One. To change it is to change Christ.
But even if we or an angel from heaven should proclaim to you a gospel contrary to what we proclaimed to you, let that one be accursed!
Paul places even himself under the curse. The authority of the Gospel does not depend on the preacher, however great. The truth does not belong to the one who proclaims it.
If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ.
The word for servant is doulos, a slave. Perhaps someone had accused Paul of softening his message to win converts. His sharp words here are his reply. A servant has one master.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Magisterium “is not superior to the Word of God, but is its servant” (Dei Verbum 10; CCC 86). The Church guards the Gospel; she does not own it. St Vincent of Lérins, writing in the fifth century, dwells on this very verse in his Commonitorium: the faith handed down may be understood more deeply, but it may never be changed into something else (in substance). The Catechism gives the same reason for the Church’s care for doctrine: the faith is a gift received from the apostles and passed on (CCC 171).

r.h: He calls his own sheep by name
set: There is no break between chapter 9 and chapter 10. Jesus has just given sight to a man born blind, and the man has been driven out for confessing him (9:34). Jesus now speaks to those Pharisees who questioned the man (9:40). He has shown what a shepherd does, in contrast to those who cast out a sheep.

The background is the Old Testament image of God and Israel’s leaders as shepherds, above all Ezekiel 34, where God condemns shepherds who feed themselves and promises to shepherd his people himself. Psalm 23 stands behind it too. A village sheepfold was often a walled enclosure with one gate, where more than one flock could spend the night. In the morning each shepherd called, and his own flock came out to him.
str: vv. 1–3a: gate and wall: the thief climbs in, the shepherd enters by the gate.
vv. 3b–5: the voice: he calls, leads out and walks ahead; the sheep follow him and run from a stranger.
v. 6: they do not understand. Jesus will explain in the verses that follow (10:7–18).
kw: John’s word for this kind of teaching (see also 16:25, 29). It is a veiled saying, a picture whose meaning has to be opened. It is not the usual word for “parable” in the other Gospels.
The word recurs in vv. 3, 4 and 5. The sheep do not follow an argument or a uniform; they follow a voice they have heard many times. Knowing it takes long acquaintance.
God says to Israel, “I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1). At the tomb the Risen Lord will say one word, “Mary!”, and she will know him (20:16).
vv: The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
“Leads them out” recalls the leader Moses prayed for: one who “shall lead them out and bring them in”, so that the people “may not be like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17).
When he has brought out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice.

“Brought out” is the same Greek verb used when the blind man was driven out (9:34). The man who was thrown out by others has in truth been led out by the Shepherd. And this shepherd walks in front: he goes first into every danger, in the end into death itself (10:11).
They will not follow a stranger, but they will run from him because they do not know the voice of strangers.
The healed man has just done this: he would not be argued out of what he knew.
ch: The Second Vatican Council gathers this chapter into its teaching on the Church: she is “a sheepfold whose one and indispensable door is Christ” (Lumen Gentium 6; CCC 754). St Gregory the Great, preaching on the Good Shepherd, asks his hearers whether they truly know him, and says that he means knowing not by faith alone but by love (in substance). The voice of Christ is learned by long listening, in Scripture and in the Holy Qurbana.

qa: Paul sounds intolerant. Should Christians speak like this today?

Paul’s fierce words are aimed at those who were changing the message and harming new believers, not at people outside the Church or searching for God. The Letter to the Ephesians, from the same Pauline tradition, asks us to speak “the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). The Church holds both together: firmness about the Gospel, and respect and gentleness toward every person (CCC 2104–2106).
study: When have I been tempted to want a gentler Gospel, or to preach one, in order to please people?
How have I learned to recognise the Shepherd’s voice? What in my daily life helps me to hear it, and what drowns it out?

lead: Today’s readings show what moves a person toward Christ and then toward others. In the Gospel it begins with a word from John the Baptist, a question from Jesus and a long afternoon in his company; then Andrew cannot keep the news to himself. In the Epistle Paul names the force behind all of it: “the love of Christ urges us on”. The Church also remembers St Thomas Aquinas, whose great learning grew from the same seeking and staying.

r.h: The love of Christ urges us on
set: Paul is defending his ministry to a community that has been unsettled. Some of the Corinthians had been impressed by rival preachers, whom he later calls “super-apostles” (11:5), and his own weakness and sufferings counted against him. Just before this passage he has spoken of the judgment seat of Christ, before which all must appear (5:10). That is “the fear of the Lord” with which v. 11 opens.
str: v. 11: Paul works in the fear of the Lord, and God knows his heart.
vv. 12–13: he is not boasting, but giving them an answer to those who boast in appearances.
v. 14: the real motive: Christ’s love, and his death for all.
kw: The verb means to hold fast, press in on, control. Its sense is stronger than encouragement: Paul feels hemmed in by this love, with no way of acting except from it.

The Greek could mean our love for Christ or Christ’s love for us. The next words, about his death for all, point to the second as the main sense. What presses on Paul is the love Christ has shown him.

The same verb is used of Jesus when people said “He has gone out of his mind” (Mark 3:21). Perhaps Paul was mocked for his ecstasies and his intensity. He answers: if I seem mad, that is for God; if sensible, that is for you.
vv: so that you may be able to answer those who boast in outward appearance and not in the heart.
Literally, “in the face”. It is an old test of true and false religion: “the Lord looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all; therefore all have died.

Paul’s reason is a conviction about a fact. Christ’s death was “for all”, in their place and for their sake, and so all humanity is touched by it. The next verse adds what follows: those who live should live no longer for themselves. The Malayalam POC says this love ഉത്തേജനം നൽകുന്നു, “gives us energy”, a fair rendering of the same inner force.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it explains that Christ’s sacrifice has its value from his love “to the end” (CCC 616), and again when it speaks of the Church’s missionary drive: “the love of Christ urges us on” (CCC 851). That Christ died for all, without exception, is the Church’s constant teaching (CCC 605).

r.h: Come and see
set: John’s Gospel counts the first days of Jesus’ ministry carefully: “the next day” (1:29, 35, 43). John the Baptist has already pointed out Jesus and borne witness to him. Now the witness has its effect: his own disciples leave him for the one he points to. The Baptist does not hold them back.

Unlike the other Gospels, where Jesus calls the first disciples from their nets, John tells of a first meeting in the circle of the Baptist. The two accounts need not conflict. One of the two disciples is named Andrew; the other is unnamed, and an old tradition sees in him the beloved disciple behind this Gospel.
str: vv. 35–37: the Baptist points; two disciples follow.
vv. 38–39: the first words of Jesus in this Gospel; they stay with him.
vv. 40–42: Andrew finds Simon and brings him; Jesus gives him a new name.
kw: Jesus’ first words in John are a question, and it reaches every reader. At the end of the Gospel, in the garden, the Risen Lord asks Mary Magdalene nearly the same: “Whom are you looking for?” (20:15).

“Where are you staying?” “They remained with him.” A plain word that John fills with meaning: at the Last Supper Jesus will say, “Abide in me as I abide in you” (15:4). Discipleship begins with staying.
The look is given twice: the Baptist looks at Jesus (v. 36) and Jesus looks at Simon (v. 42). The verb suggests a close, attentive gaze. Jesus sees in Simon what he will become.
vv: and as he watched Jesus walk by, he exclaimed, “Look, here is the Lamb of God!”

The title gathers the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the Servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). John’s Gospel will set Jesus’ condemnation on the day of Preparation for the Passover, at about noon (19:14).
He said to them, “Come and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day. It was about four o’clock in the afternoon.
The Greek says “the tenth hour”, as the POC keeps it. An eyewitness remembers the hour he first met the Lord. Jesus gives an invitation rather than an explanation.
He brought Simon to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You are to be called Cephas” (which is translated Peter).
Cephas is Aramaic for “rock”, and Peter comes from the Greek for the same. In the Bible a new name means a new calling (Genesis 17:5; compare Matthew 16:18).
ch: The Catechism notes that John the Baptist, looking at Jesus, pointed him out as the Lamb of God (CCC 608). It teaches that the Lord made Simon first among the Twelve, the rock of his Church (CCC 552), and that the handing on of the faith means leading people to Christ (CCC 425). St John Chrysostom admires Andrew’s haste: he does not keep the treasure to himself, but runs to share it with his brother (in substance).

qa: Does the Fourth Gospel contradict the others about the call of the first disciples?

The Synoptic Gospels tell of a call by the Sea of Galilee (Mark 1:16–20). John tells of an earlier meeting near the Jordan. Many readers take these as two stages: first an encounter, later the decisive call to leave everything. Each Gospel also shapes its account for its own teaching.
rite: St Thomas Aquinas (died 1274), a Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church, lectured on both St John’s Gospel and the letters of St Paul. The early accounts of his life say that he heard the Lord ask what reward he wanted, and that he replied: nothing but you, Lord. A great scholar and the two fishermen of the Gospel asked one question and found one answer. The Latin calendar keeps his memorial today, and our own Eastern tradition, which loves its great teachers, can honour him gratefully.
study: If Jesus turned to me today and asked, “What are you looking for?”, what would I honestly say?
Who brought me to Jesus, as Andrew brought Simon? To whom might I say “Come and see”?

lead: On this Friday of Denha the Church keeps the memory of St Stephen, the first martyr, and the four readings follow a single thread: the blood of the innocent and what God does with it. Naboth is stoned on false evidence so that a king can have a vineyard, and God sends Elijah to name the crime. Stephen is stoned after a hearing with false witnesses, but he sees the heavens opened and dies forgiving. Paul, who once stood by at that stoning, describes from the inside what it is to carry the death of Jesus so that his life may be seen. And Jesus, in Matthew, grieves over the long line of the murdered and longs to gather his people under his wings. The key words are witness, blood and glory. Denha means the dawning, the rising of Christ’s light, and today that light shines in a dying man’s face.

r.h: Naboth’s vineyard
set: Ahab ruled the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, from his capital at Samaria, with a second palace at Jezreel in the fertile valley. His wife Jezebel was the daughter of the king of the Sidonians (16:31), and she brought with her the worship of Baal. The chapters around this one are the great contest between that court and the prophet Elijah (1 Kings 17–19).

The story turns on two ideas of land. For Israel the land belongs to God: “the land is mine; with me you are but aliens and tenants” (Leviticus 25:23). Each family holds its portion as a trust from him, to pass on. The king therefore has no right to it. Jezebel’s question, “Do you now govern Israel?”, comes from another idea of kingship altogether, in which a king’s desire is law.
str: vv. 1–4: Ahab’s offer, which is fair by its own lights, and Naboth’s refusal.
vv. 5–10: Jezebel’s plan, in letters under the royal seal.
vv. 11–14: the city’s elders carry it out, and Naboth is stoned.
vv. 15–16: Ahab goes down to take possession.
vv. 17–21: the word of the Lord comes to Elijah, who meets Ahab in the vineyard.
¶ The reading stops at the sentence of judgment. The story goes on: Ahab humbles himself and God delays the punishment (21:27–29), and the sentence falls in time (22:38; 2 Kings 9:26).
kw: Naḥălâ is the family’s share in the land God gave. For Naboth it is not property to be priced. His refusal is an act of faith, which is why he swears by the Lord.
Literally “sons of worthlessness”. The Law demands at least two witnesses for a death sentence (Deuteronomy 17:6), so Jezebel supplies two. She keeps the form of the Law in order to break it.
have you killed, and also taken possession?

Two verbs, and each is heavy. Rāṣaḥ is the verb of the commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Yāraš is the word for Israel’s taking possession of the land as God’s gift. Elijah’s question sets the gift and the crime side by side.
vv: “The Lord forbid that I should give you my ancestral inheritance.”
Naboth’s whole speech in the story is this one sentence. He is a small man with one sentence, and it costs him his life.
She wrote in the letters, “Proclaim a fast, and seat Naboth at the head of the assembly;
This is the cruelty of the plan: a religious fast, a seat of honour, the name of God. A fast suggested that some grave sin had to be put right. Religion itself is made the instrument of the crime.
So they took him outside the city, and stoned him to death.

The elders know the Law: a blasphemer is stoned outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). So Stephen will be dragged out of the city and stoned (Acts 7:58), and Jesus will suffer “outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
Have you killed, and also taken possession?

The letters were written by Jezebel and carried out by others, and Ahab’s hands look clean. God addresses him all the same. A person is answerable for what he profits from and does not stop. The question echoes the first one God asked about a murder: “What have you done?” (Genesis 4:10).
Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, O my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you. Because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the Lord,
Ahab offered to buy a vineyard, and in the end the one who has been sold is himself.
ch: St Ambrose wrote a whole treatise on this chapter, On Naboth, and says that the story is old in time but happens every day (in substance). St Paul VI quotes that treatise in Populorum Progressio 23: what you give the poor is not from what is yours, you are returning what is theirs. The Catechism teaches that the right to private property does not cancel the original gift of the earth to all humanity (CCC 2403), condemns the unjust taking of what belongs to others (CCC 2409), and names false witness as a grave offence against justice (CCC 2476). The blood of the innocent is among the sins that cry out to heaven (CCC 1867). Many Christian readers have also seen in Naboth a figure of the Innocent One, put to death on false testimony.

r.h: The first martyr
set: Stephen was one of the seven chosen to serve the tables of the Greek-speaking widows in Jerusalem, “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (6:5). The Church remembers them as the first deacons, though Acts does not yet use that title. His preaching brought him before the council, with false witnesses saying that he spoke against the Temple and the Law (6:11–14), and he answered with the long speech of chapter 7, retelling Israel’s story.

Acts tells us that the speech ended with a hard reproach (7:51–53), in the voice of the prophets. Stephen speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews. The men who killed him were a particular crowd in a particular hour, and Luke’s account has an uncertain legal shape: it reads more like an eruption of fury than a formal sentence.
str: v. 54: the fury of those who hear.
vv. 55–56: the vision: the glory of God, and Jesus standing.
vv. 57–58: they cover their ears, drive him out and stone him; a young man named Saul holds the coats.
vv. 59–60: two prayers, and his death.
¶ Luke has shaped the scene on the death of Jesus in his own Gospel: both are falsely accused (Luke 23:2; Acts 6:13), both commit their spirit, and both pray for those who kill them (Luke 23:34, 46).
kw: A long, fixed look. His accusers see only him; he looks beyond them. Luke uses the same word earlier when the council looks at Stephen and sees his face “like the face of an angel” (6:15).

Jesus had said that the Son of Man would be “seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke 22:69). Here he stands. Some see a host rising to welcome; others see a witness rising to speak for one who is on trial.
Outside the Gospels this full title occurs only here. Jesus used it of himself before his judges; now the man on trial for his name sees it fulfilled (Daniel 7:13).

The “witnesses” who lay their coats down are called martyres. Later Paul will call Stephen “your witness” (Acts 22:20), using the same word. In this story we can almost see the word beginning to mean what “martyr” means now: one who bears witness with his life.
vv: But filled with the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Stephen has just told how the God of glory appeared to Abraham (7:2) and how God does not live in houses made by hands (7:48). Now he sees that glory himself, with no temple around him, out in the open under a shower of stones.
But they covered their ears, and with a loud shout all rushed together against him.
Some will not hear, as Stephen has said (7:51). It is a warning for every believer, since any of us may be tempted to cover our ears to an uncomfortable truth.
and the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Deuteronomy 17:7 makes the witnesses throw the first stones, and they lay aside their coats for the work. Here is the first mention of the man who will be the Apostle Paul. He will later be stoned himself (2 Corinthians 11:25).
While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Jesus prayed this prayer to the Father (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays it to Jesus. This early Christian is calling on Jesus as Lord, as one prays to God.
Then he knelt down and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he died.
Greek: “he fell asleep” (ekoimēthē), the Christian word for the death of the faithful. The POC keeps it (മരണനിദ്ര, the sleep of death). After such a death, the word is a word of peace.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473), and teaches that the forgiveness of enemies is where Christian prayer reaches its height (CCC 2844). St Fulgentius of Ruspe, in a sermon on St Stephen, says that love was his weapon and that by his love he won Saul, his persecutor, to be his companion in heaven (in substance). A saying handed down under St Augustine’s name makes the same point: had Stephen not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul. St Gregory the Great explains the standing Christ: to sit belongs to a judge, to stand to one who fights or helps (in substance).

r.h: Carrying the death of Jesus
set: Paul has just said, “we have this treasure in clay jars, so that it may be made clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God” (4:7). Today’s reading unpacks that sentence. He has known real danger; earlier in the letter he speaks of an affliction in Asia so heavy that he despaired of life (1:8), and later he lists beatings, shipwreck and a stoning (11:23–27).

He is answering those who thought a true apostle should look impressive. His argument is the opposite: the weakness of the messenger is where the power of God can be seen, because the pattern of the Apostle’s life is the pattern of Jesus’ death and resurrection.
str: vv. 8–9: four contrasts: afflicted but not crushed, and so on.
vv. 10–12: the principle: death at work in us, life for you.
vv. 13–15: faith that speaks, resting on the hope of resurrection.
vv. 16–18: therefore we do not lose heart: what is passing and what is eternal.
kw: A play on words in Greek: “at a loss, but not utterly at a loss”. Paul allows himself to be perplexed. Faith is not always having an answer.
Not the usual word for death: it suggests the process of dying, a wasting away. Paul’s daily exhaustion for the Gospel is itself a sharing in Christ’s dying.

Literally “the outer man” and “the inner man”, as the POC has it. Paul does not despise the body, for he expects its resurrection (v. 14). He means the visible life that wears out and the life in Christ that grows.

In Hebrew, “glory” (kābôd) comes from a root meaning heavy. Paul, thinking as a Jew in Greek, sets a light and brief trouble against a heavy and eternal glory. The POC speaks more simply of അനുപമമായ മഹത്വം, glory beyond compare.
vv: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair;
These words could be said of Stephen. They are not a boast, for the power is God’s.
always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our bodies.

“Made visible” is a word for Denha. The Risen Jesus is shown to the world in the bodies of those who suffer for him. Paul says simply “Jesus” again and again in these verses, the human name of the one who really died.
So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.
This verse speaks to the sick and the old as much as to apostles.
For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,
Paul, who has listed his sufferings, calls them “slight”. He can do so only by placing them on the scale beside what is to come.
because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen; for what can be seen is temporary, but what cannot be seen is eternal.
This is exactly what Stephen did (Acts 7:55).
ch: The Catechism applies the image of the clay jars to the whole Christian life: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (CCC 1420). Because Christ has in some way united himself with every person, all are offered a share in the paschal mystery, and he calls his disciples to take up their cross (CCC 618). The sick, too, are united to his Passion by the grace of the Anointing (CCC 1521). The Church does not call suffering good in itself. She teaches that, joined to Christ, it can bear fruit.

r.h: As a hen gathers her brood
set: These are the last words of Jesus’ public teaching in Matthew, spoken in the Temple before he leaves it (24:1). The chapter is a series of woes addressed to “scribes and Pharisees”. Its language is the hard language of the prophets, who rebuked their own people out of love. It is also a family dispute. Jesus himself was a Jew, and he agreed with the Pharisees on many things (see 23:2–3; CCC 575–576). Many scholars think that Matthew’s sharpness also reflects the painful tension of his own day, when Christian Jews and synagogue leaders were separating.

Israel’s own Scriptures confess the rejection and killing of prophets (Nehemiah 9:26; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Jesus does not stand outside this history as an accuser. He places himself within it, as the last of the rejected messengers, and he weeps for the city.
str: v. 34: “I send you prophets, sages, and scribes”: messengers and their fate.
vv. 35–36: from Abel to Zechariah: the whole history of innocent blood.
v. 37: the lament over Jerusalem.
vv. 38–39: the empty house, and the promise of a greeting to come.
kw: Abel’s blood “is crying out to me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Hebrews says that the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): Abel’s cries for justice, and Jesus’ for mercy.
I desired / you were not willing
The same verb on both sides. It is one of the most moving lines in the Gospels, and it shows a God who desires, and who allows himself to be refused. God does not force love.

The word means a bird, here a mother hen. Scripture speaks of refuge under God’s wings (Ruth 2:12; Deuteronomy 32:11). Jesus uses the image for himself, and it is a very humble one: not an eagle, but a farmyard bird.
vv: Therefore I send you prophets, sages, and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town,
“I send”: Jesus speaks with the authority of God. Matthew’s readers would have recognised their own missionaries here (compare 10:17, 23), and Christians have long heard Stephen in this verse.
from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

Abel is the first murder in the Bible. The Zechariah killed in the Temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22) is probably meant as the last, because in its usual order the Hebrew Bible closes with Chronicles. There he is the son of Jehoiada; Zechariah son of Berechiah is the name of the prophet (Zechariah 1:1), and Matthew’s wording may join the two. The “you” is the language of prophetic accusation, addressed to that generation’s leaders. It is not a charge against the Jewish people as a whole.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
The doubled name is the sound of grief (compare “O my son Absalom”, 2 Samuel 18:33). “Stones those who are sent”: in Acts the next in line is Stephen.
See, your house is left to you, desolate.

“Your house” is the Temple, and it may also mean the city and its people. The language echoes Jeremiah 22:5. The Temple was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70. Jesus speaks as one in sorrow, not with satisfaction.
For I tell you, you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’
The last word is not doom. The verse quotes Psalm 118:26, the greeting of pilgrims, and it looks forward to a day of welcome.
ch: The Catechism counts the blood of Abel among the sins that cry out to heaven (CCC 1867). It teaches firmly that the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living, nor against Jews today (CCC 597; Nostra Aetate 4), and that “the glorious Messiah’s coming is suspended at every moment of history” until he is recognised by all Israel (CCC 674, citing this verse with Romans 11). St Paul says that God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). St Augustine loved the image of the hen: no other bird is so plainly weakened by caring for her chicks, and so she pictures the Wisdom of God made weak for our sake (in substance).

qa: If God sees everything, why did he let Naboth and Stephen die?

Scripture does not explain this in a sentence. It does show that God is not silent: he sends Elijah to the vineyard, and he opens the heavens for Stephen. The innocent are not forgotten, and their blood has a voice before him. The full answer the Christian has is the Cross and Resurrection, where God himself enters the suffering of the innocent. The Catechism says that faith gives no quick answer to evil, and that the whole of the Christian message is the response (CCC 309).
Does Matthew 23 or the death of Stephen mean that the Jewish people are to blame?

No. Jesus, Stephen, Paul and the first believers were Jews, and those who killed Stephen were one angry crowd in one place. The Church teaches that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed, and that the guilt of those events cannot be laid on all Jews of that time, or on Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). These passages call every believer to examine himself: where have I covered my ears?
Why is Stephen remembered in Denha, if the Latin calendar keeps him on 26 December?

The East Syriac tradition gives the Fridays of this season to those through whom Christ was made known. A martyr is a witness, and so he belongs to a season about the showing of Christ. The two calendars honour the same saint from different angles: the Latin one places the first martyr beside the Child born for us, and ours places him among the witnesses who made the Lord known.
rite: In our tradition a martyr is a sahada, from the Syriac word for a witness, just as the Greek martys in Stephen’s story means a witness. To Syro-Malabar ears “Sahada” is an old and loved title. The Holy Qurbana stands where Stephen stood: he saw the heavens opened and Jesus at the right hand of God, and we pray before that same Lord. Those who suffer for Christ in many lands today are his brothers and sisters. We pray for them, and with Stephen we pray for those who wrong them. A family with a quarrel over land or an old wrong will find today’s readings close to home: Naboth’s story warns us about greed, and Stephen’s prayer shows the way out of revenge.
study: Naboth said one sentence and held to it. What is there in my life that I would refuse to sell at any price?
Ahab’s hands looked clean. Are there wrongs that I benefit from without having done them myself?
“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Whom do I find it hardest to pray this for?
Paul says the life of Jesus is made visible in our bodies. Whose patient suffering has shown me Christ?

lead: Both readings are about belonging to God and how it shows. John assures believers that they have eternal life, and draws the conclusion: they pray with confidence, intercede for a brother or sister who sins, and keep away from idols. In the Gospel Jesus tells people who claim descent from Abraham that true kinship with God is seen in hearing his word and in doing what Abraham did. On the eve of the Lord’s Day we ask whose family we resemble.

r.h: That you may know that you have eternal life
set: This is the close of the First Letter of John, written probably toward the end of the first century. The Church’s tradition links it with St John the Apostle; many scholars think of a writer from the circle formed by his teaching. A painful split lies behind it: some had left the community (2:19), and those who remained were shaken and needed assurance.

The letter has already said both that “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1:8) and that “those who have been born of God do not sin” (3:9). Today’s ending holds the same tension. A believer may fall, but sin is no longer his home, and the community prays him back to life.
str: v. 13: why John has written: so that you may know.
vv. 14–15: confidence in prayer.
vv. 16–17: prayer for a brother or sister who sins.
vv. 18–20: three times “we know”.
v. 21: the last line: keep yourselves from idols.
kw: Originally the citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly. Here it is the believer’s open, unafraid way of speaking to God as a child to a father.

Literally “sin toward death”. John does not define it. In the setting of this letter many scholars think of a deliberate rejection of Christ and of the community, like that of those who left. It is not the same as the fully developed teaching on sin, though the Church finds the root of that teaching here.

A surprising last word, since the letter has not spoken of idols before. It can refer to pagan images, which were everywhere in the cities of that time, and also to any false god or false picture of God, set against “the true God” of the previous verse.
vv: If you see your brother or sister committing what is not a mortal sin, you will ask, and God will give life to such a one
The first response to a brother’s sin is prayer, before criticism. God gives life through the prayer of the community. John does not forbid prayer for the other case; he only declines to command it.
We know that those who are born of God do not sin, but the one who was born of God protects them, and the evil one does not touch them.

A textual note: the manuscripts differ here. Some say that the one born of God “protects him”, the reading the NRSV takes as Christ protecting the believer, and the POC makes this plain (ദൈവപുത്രൻ അവനെ സംരക്ഷിക്കുന്നു). Others say that the believer “keeps himself”. The point stands in both: the safety of the believer is not his own achievement.
He is the true God and eternal life.

The Greek could point back to the Father or to “his Son Jesus Christ”, the nearest name. Many Christian readers from early times have read it of Christ, and it is one of the few places in the New Testament that may call him God outright.
ch: The Catechism cites this passage for the distinction between mortal and venial sin, “already evident in Scripture” (CCC 1854; see 1857–1861). It presents intercession as a sharing in the prayer of Jesus (CCC 2634–2635), and it teaches that idolatry reaches far beyond pagan worship: a person commits idolatry whenever he honours and reveres a creature in place of God, whether power, pleasure, money or anything else (CCC 2113).

r.h: Whoever is from God hears the words of God
set: The scene is the Temple in Jerusalem around the feast of Tents (chapters 7–8). The hardest debate in this Gospel is under way. It began with “the Jews who had believed in him” (8:31), and it grows steadily more tense, until they take up stones (8:59). All the speakers are Jews, Jesus included. The Vatican’s 1974 Guidelines on Nostra Aetate note that “the Jews” in John sometimes means, according to the context, the leaders or the adversaries of Jesus. Many scholars think that this Gospel’s language also carries the hurt of a later separation between John’s community and the synagogue.
str: vv. 39–41a: “Abraham is our father”: children act like their father.
vv. 41b–43: “one father, God himself”: then you would love the one he sent.
vv. 44–47: two families, truth and the lie; the test is hearing.
kw: Literally “the works of Abraham”. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6) and welcomed those God sent to him (Genesis 18). The argument is that kinship shows in conduct, the point John the Baptist makes in Matthew 3:9.

Literally “man-killer”. It looks back to Genesis: the serpent’s lie that led to death, and Cain, whose killing of his brother 1 John 3:12 ascribes to “the evil one”. Wisdom 2:24 says that “through the devil’s envy death entered the world”.
In John’s language, as in the Hebrew šāma‘, to hear includes to accept and obey. The same theme as the sheep and the voice in chapter 10.
vv: They answered him, “Abraham is our father.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing what Abraham did,
Jesus does not deny their descent. In v. 37 he says, “I know that you are descendants of Abraham.” He speaks of living up to it.
You are from your father the devil, and you choose to do your father’s desires.

This is the hardest verse, and it has been cruelly misused in history. Jesus is speaking to people in that hour who are planning to kill him (v. 40), and his charge concerns that plan and the lie behind it. He is not describing a people. The Church utterly rejects any such use of it (Nostra Aetate 4).
Whoever is from God hears the words of God.
This is the positive rule, and it is addressed to every reader, today’s Christians first.
ch: The Catechism uses this verse in its teaching on truthfulness: the Lord denounces lying as the work of the devil (CCC 2482). St Augustine, preaching on this chapter, explains that these hearers were Abraham’s children by birth but not by imitation, and likewise that no one is a child of the devil by nature. God is the creator of all, and one becomes the devil’s child only by imitating him (in substance). The Church teaches that Jesus’ conflict with some authorities of his time cannot be turned into a charge against the Jewish people (CCC 597–598).

qa: Did Jesus call the Jewish people children of the devil?

No. Jesus was addressing particular opponents who were seeking his death, in a debate among Jews, and he says the same sort of thing to Peter when Peter resists the Cross: “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:23). The Church rejects any teaching that the Jews are accursed (Nostra Aetate 4), and she honours them as the people to whom God first spoke, whose calling he has not revoked (CCC 839). The verse searches every believer: whenever I live by a lie, whose child am I acting like?
study: John’s first response to a brother’s sin is prayer. For whom do I need to pray instead of criticising?
What half-truth have I grown used to living by? What would it mean for me to hear the words of God about it today?

lead: In Denha the Church asks how God makes himself known, and the four readings give an answer that moves from a voice to a lifted-up Son. Deuteronomy forbids seeking the future through diviners and promises instead a prophet like Moses, with God’s words in his mouth. In Isaiah the God of the exile says, “I am the Lord your God, who teaches you”, and sighs over a people who did not listen. Hebrews tells tired believers to imitate Abraham, who trusted God’s sworn promise and waited. In John the prophet like Moses speaks to Nicodemus by night: as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son must be lifted up, because God so loved the world. The Genesis story of Abraham’s only son lies behind Hebrews and, for many readers, behind John as well. The key words are hear, wait, lifted up and light.

r.h: A prophet like Moses
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses’ last words on the plains of Moab, with Israel about to enter the land. Chapters 16–18 describe the offices that will guide the people: judges, the king, priests and prophets. Just before our reading (18:9–12), Moses lists the practices of the surrounding nations: divination, soothsaying, sorcery, consulting the dead.

The point is that Israel does not need to pry into the future or force the hand of the unseen. God himself will speak. The people had asked for this at Horeb, when they were terrified by the fire and the voice (5:23–27; Exodus 20:19). God’s reply is one of the tenderest moments in the book: “They are right in what they have said.”
str: v. 13: the principle: be wholly the Lord’s.
v. 14: not the way of the nations.
v. 15: the promise: a prophet like Moses, and the command to heed him.
vv. 16–18: its origin at Horeb, in the people’s fear and God’s answer.
¶ The passage goes on to ask how a true prophet can be told from a false one (18:19–22).
kw: It means whole, without blemish; the same word describes a sacrificial animal, and Noah (Genesis 6:9). God says to Abraham, “walk before me, and be blameless” (Genesis 17:1). The POC keeps this sense (കുറ്റമറ്റവൻ). Undivided trust is what is asked.

At first this may well have meant the line of prophets God would send, one after another. But Deuteronomy ends by saying, “Never since has there arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses” (34:10). The promise stayed open, and in Jesus’ time people were waiting for “the prophet” (John 1:21; 6:14).
you shall heed such a prophet
Literally “to him you shall listen”. On the mountain of the Transfiguration, with Moses present, the voice from the cloud will say of Jesus, “listen to him!” (Matthew 17:5).
vv: Although these nations that you are about to dispossess do give heed to soothsayers and diviners, as for you, the Lord your God does not permit you to do so.
This is a word against fear as much as against superstition. Divination tries to control what only God holds. Those who know the Father do not need to.
The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people; you shall heed such a prophet.
“From among your own people”: the Word comes in a human voice, from a brother. St Peter and St Stephen both apply this verse to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37).
I will put my words in the mouth of the prophet, who shall speak to them everything that I command.

See Jeremiah 1:9. Jesus says of himself, “the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak” (John 12:49). In Jesus the Word does not merely enter a mouth: the Word has become flesh.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that Christ, the Word made flesh, completes and perfects revelation (Dei Verbum 4). He is anointed prophet as well as priest and king (CCC 436). The Catechism also repeats Deuteronomy’s warning: God can reveal the future to his prophets, but all forms of divination are to be rejected, including horoscopes, astrology and palm reading, because they conceal a desire for power over time and history (CCC 2115–2116). The sound attitude is to put oneself confidently into the hands of Providence (CCC 2115).

r.h: I am the Lord your God, who teaches you
set: Isaiah 40–55 speaks to the exiles in Babylon in the years before the Persian king Cyrus took the city (539 BC) and allowed them to return. Chapter 48 closes the first part of this section, and it is a sharp one: God reminds a stubborn people that he has told them everything in advance. The great deliverance is about to happen. The one “the Lord loves”, who will act against Babylon (v. 14), is understood to be Cyrus, named earlier (44:28; 45:1).

The exiles saw the gods of Babylon carried in great processions, and they might well have thought that Babylon’s gods had won. Isaiah’s answer is that only the Lord made the heavens and the earth, only he has told the future, and only he can redeem.
str: vv. 12–13: “I am He”: the Creator summons his people.
vv. 14–16: God has called the one who will overthrow Babylon; a new voice speaks in v. 16b.
vv. 17–19: the Teacher’s sorrow: “O that you had paid attention”.
v. 20: the command to leave Babylon, and to shout the news to the ends of the earth.
kw: A solemn self-naming of God that recurs in these chapters (41:4; 43:10). Together with “I am the first, and I am the last” it lies behind the words of the Risen Christ in Revelation (Revelation 1:17).

In Israel’s law the gō’ēl is the near relative who steps in to buy back a kinsman’s land or liberty (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49). To call God gō’ēl says that he treats his people as his own family, and pays what is owed. The verb returns in v. 20.

The NRSV has “prosperity” and “success” in v. 18; the Hebrew words are šālôm (wholeness, peace) and ṣədāqâ (righteousness, right relation), which the POC renders സമാധാനം and നീതി. Together they mean life as God meant it to be.
vv: Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last.
The people’s first duty is the same as in Deuteronomy: listen.
And now the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.

A sudden new speaker. The text does not say who he is; many scholars think of the prophet himself, or of the Servant of the following chapter (49:1). Some early Christian writers, Origen among them, heard here the Son, sent by the Father with the Spirit (in substance).
Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.
God describes himself as a teacher and a guide. What he commands is for our good, not for his. Diviners promise to tell what will happen; God shows the road.
O that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your prosperity would have been like a river, and your success like the waves of the sea;

This is not anger but longing. Psalm 81:13 sighs in the same way: “O that my people would listen to me”. Compare Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem. The images of river and waves are precious in a dry land: a life that keeps flowing.
Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy,
A new Exodus. The news of it is for “the end of the earth”: the reach of God’s saving act is already wider than Israel.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God is Truth and his teaching is trustworthy, because his words are true and his law is truth (CCC 215). It also says that he is the first and the last (CCC 198), the beginning and the end of everything, in words taken from these chapters of Isaiah. The Letter to the Hebrews calls Christ the one who is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), and the Book of Revelation gives him this very title of God: the first and the last. On a Sunday of Denha the reading tells us that the One who showed himself in Christ is the Teacher who has been patiently leading his people all along.

r.h: Through faith and patience
set: Hebrews is a sermon (13:22) written to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were growing tired. Its author is not named, and the Church received it among the letters linked with St Paul. The verses just before today’s reading are among the sternest in the New Testament: those who fall away after being enlightened cannot be restored, and land that bears only thorns is close to being cursed (6:4–8). This is a warning and not a limit on God’s mercy: the Church teaches that there is no offence, however serious, that she cannot forgive (CCC 982).

Now the preacher changes his tone. He has spoken severely so as to wake them, but he is confident of better things. The ground of hope that he gives them is not their strength. It is God’s oath to Abraham, which he goes on to expound (6:16–20).
str: vv. 9–10: reassurance: “God is not unjust”, and he remembers their love.
vv. 11–12: the appeal: keep going to the end, imitate those who inherit.
vv. 13–15: Abraham: God swore by himself, and Abraham waited.
kw: The word has already appeared at 5:11, where the NRSV translates it “dull”. These are the only two uses in the New Testament. The danger is not persecution here but slowly losing interest.
A full, settled certainty. Hebrews uses it again at 10:22 for the assurance of faith as we draw near to God. Hope has its own kind of confidence.
Literally “long-spiritedness”, the opposite of a short temper. It is not passive. It is the staying power of those who keep believing when nothing seems to be happening.

An oath calls on someone greater to guarantee it. God has no one greater, and so he swears by himself (Genesis 22:16). Hebrews brings out the wonder of this: God himself stoops to reassure a doubting people.
vv: For God is not unjust; he will not overlook your work and the love that you showed for his sake in serving the saints, as you still do.
“The saints” here means fellow Christians, probably the poor or imprisoned among them (10:32–34). Their love is what the preacher sees and praises first. Service of others is itself service of God.
so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
This looks ahead to the great roll of witnesses in Hebrews 11. Christian life is learned by imitation.
When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself,
The oath of Genesis 22:16–17 comes after Abraham was willing to offer Isaac, “your only son”. So Hebrews and today’s Gospel stand on the same mountain.
And thus Abraham, having patiently endured, obtained the promise.
Abraham was seventy-five when the promise came (Genesis 12:4) and a hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 21:5). Even then he saw only the beginning of what was promised (Hebrews 11:13).
ch: The Catechism presents hope as “the sure and steadfast anchor of the soul” (CCC 1820, quoting Hebrews 6:19) and names Abraham as the one who hoped against hope (CCC 1819). It presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146). The Council of Trent cited Hebrews 6:10 in its teaching on merit (Decree on Justification, chapter 16). The Catechism explains that merit before God rests wholly on his grace and on his choice to associate us with his work (CCC 2006–2011). St Augustine says that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts (in substance).

r.h: So must the Son of Man be lifted up
set: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader, comes to Jesus “by night” (3:1–2). Jesus speaks to him of being born from above, “of water and Spirit” (3:5). Then Nicodemus fades from view, and the talk opens out into one of the most famous passages of the Bible. He does not vanish from the Gospel: he defends Jesus before the council (7:50–51) and comes to his burial with myrrh and aloes (19:39). The man who came in the dark ends in the light.

The background is Numbers 21:4–9. When the people in the desert were bitten by serpents, God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and those who looked at it lived. The Book of Wisdom had already explained this carefully: “the one who turned toward it was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all” (Wisdom 16:7).
str: vv. 14–15: the serpent and the Son of Man.
v. 16: the heart of the matter: God’s love and God’s gift.
vv. 17–18: sent to save, not to condemn.
vv. 19–21: light and darkness: judgment as what people do with the light.

¶ Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, so it is not clear where Jesus’ words end and the evangelist’s reflection begins. The NRSV marks a new speech at v. 16 and continues to v. 21; many commentators think that from v. 16 the evangelist himself is speaking. The teaching has the same authority either way.
kw: John uses this verb for the Cross (8:28; 12:32–33), and it also means to be exalted. In this Gospel the two are one movement: the Cross is already the throne.
In v. 16, “so” does not only mean “so much”. It also means “in this way”: this is how God loved, by giving. The way of giving tells us the measure.

“One of a kind”, the only child. The Latin tradition read “only-begotten”, as the POC’s ഏകജാതൻ also suggests. Hebrews 11:17 uses the same word of Isaac, and the words “your son, your only son” (Genesis 22:2) stand behind this verse for many readers.
Both a sentence and a separating. In John the light itself divides: God does not come to condemn, yet people’s response to the light shows what they are.
vv: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,

“Must” (dei) is the Gospel’s word for God’s plan. The serpent was the very image of what was killing them. So Christ takes on what kills us: God “made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
“For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.
In John, “the world” is often the place that resists God. This makes the verse more astonishing: God loved a world that did not love him. The word is “gave”, and it includes the giving on the Cross.
“Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
Compare 12:47. The Son’s purpose is salvation. This is what the season of Denha shows the world.
And this is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.
Judgment is not the arbitrary act of an angry God. The light comes, and we are shown to ourselves. Nicodemus came by night.
But those who do what is true come to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that their deeds have been done in God.
To “do what is true” is a Semitic phrase: truth is something done. The last words give all the credit to God.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it says that the Word became flesh so that we might know God’s love (CCC 458). Christ did not come to condemn; whoever rejects the grace offered judges himself, and “receives according to his works” (CCC 679). God predestines no one to go to hell (CCC 1037), and Christ died for all without exception (CCC 605). St Augustine draws out the comparison with the serpent: those bitten in the desert looked and lived, and so those wounded by sin look in faith on the death of Christ and are healed (in substance). St John Chrysostom notes that God gave not a servant or an angel but his only Son, and that the greatness of the gift shows the greatness of the love (in substance). The Catechism also names the bronze serpent as an image God himself permitted, which pointed to salvation through the incarnate Word (CCC 2130).

qa: Wasn’t the bronze serpent an idol? Why would God command such an image?

The serpent was not worshipped in Numbers, and God saved through it, as Wisdom 16:7 explains. When people later burned offerings to it, King Hezekiah rightly broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). The difference is what the Catechism teaches: an image pointing beyond itself to God’s saving work differs from an idol taking God’s place (CCC 2129–2132).
If “whoever believes” has eternal life, what of those who have never heard of Christ?

John 3 speaks to those to whom the light has come and who refuse it. The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, may attain eternal salvation, always through the grace of Christ (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). This is no reason to be careless about mission: God wants all to know the truth (CCC 851).
Is it wrong for Christians to check a horoscope or an auspicious time?

The Church says plainly that consulting horoscopes, astrology and omens contradicts the honour and loving trust we owe to God alone (CCC 2116). This is a word to believers about their own trust in God. A Christian can plan wisely and consult experts, while placing the future in the hands of the Father who teaches and leads him.
rite: Denha, “the dawning”, celebrates the Lord’s baptism and his showing to the world, and today’s Gospel, spoken to a man who came in the dark, is a Denha Gospel: “the light has come”. Its talk of being born “of water and Spirit” (3:5) belongs to the same mystery, for baptism was anciently called enlightenment (CCC 1216). The St Thomas Cross, so dear to our Church, shows the Cross as the sign of life and glory, its ends blossoming. It is a fitting picture of John’s “lifted up”, in which death and exaltation are one. At the Holy Qurbana we look with faith on the One lifted up, as the bitten Israelites looked, and we are healed. Today the Church also remembers St John Bosco, who with patience and joy brought the poor boys of Turin to the light of Christ.
study: When I am afraid about the future, where do I turn? How does Deuteronomy 18 speak to that?
“O that you had paid attention!” Where do I hear God’s sorrow, and not his anger, in my own failure to listen?
Abraham waited about twenty-five years for Isaac. What am I still waiting for from God, and what does waiting ask of me?
Is there a deed in my life that I would rather keep from the light? What would it take to bring it there, perhaps in the sacrament of Reconciliation?
